Sova Rani Guha alias Sova Rani Gupta ------ Appellant 
vs
Abdul Awal Mia and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment: MH Rahman J: This appeal by special leave, at the instance of defendant No. 6, is directed against the judgment and decree of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 327 of 1980 decreeing the respondent-plaintiffs' suit in part. 2. Respondent Nos. 1-3 filed the suit, Title Suit No. 11 of 1972 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali, for partition claiming 0.3077 acres in the suit property and for a declaration that the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 145 of 1954 of the First Court of Munsif, Patuakhali was fraudulent and collusive and not binding on them. Their case, in brief, is that the Suit lands, recorded in CS Khatian No. 406 of mouza Patuakhali, subsequently in SA Khatian Nos. 729 and 1721, were auction purchased by Aswini Kumar Dhar, Indra Bala Dhar and Jogesh Chandra Dey in equal shares. On 14 November 1969 Manzur Murshed, the predecessor of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the 1/3rd share of Indra Bala Dhar. On 25 February 1970 the same parties purchased the shares of the successor-in-interest of Aswini Kumar Dhar. 3. Defendant No. 5, Golap Mani, contested the suit asserting, inter alia that the plaintiffs obtained their documents from fictitious persons; that she was one of the auction-purchasers; that the compromise decree was legal and valid; that her share of eight annas was subsequently recorded on 27 May 1954 in a mutation case and that she had already filed Title Suit No. 298 of 1979 in the First Court of Munsif, Patuakhali for permanent injunction and got an interim order. Defendant No. 7 supported her claim. 4. Defendant No. 6, Sova Rani Guha is the present appellant. Her case is that the plaintiffs' documents are collusive and fraudulent; that defendant No. 5 had no right or title in the suit land and that her father-in-law Monoranjan Guha took settlement of the suit land from Umesh Chandra Dey, his three brothers and Sister Tanu Bala Dey. In the certificate case Umesh Chandra Dey, Dinesh Chandra Dey, Gouranga Chandra Dey, Tanu Bala Day, Indra Bala Dhar and her husband Aswini Kumar Dhar were the auction purchasers. This defendant purchased the 8 annas share of Dinesh Chandra Dey by a registered Kabala dated 1 January 1970. She is living in a dwelling house on the suit land since the settlement. Under section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and section 4 of the Partition Act 1893 the plaintiffs being stranger purchasers are not entitled to get any possession. She paid rent to the Government and tax to the municipality but the dakhilas and tax-receipts were looted during disturbance. 5. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that it was barred by res judicata and not maintainable in the absence of any prayer for setting aside the compromise decree. On appeal the appellate Court decreed the suit and held that the plaintiffs were entitled to a two-third share in the partible property. It was further held the compromise decree was obtained by fraud; and that defendant No. 6 could not formally prove her sale deed. 6. Against the appellate Court's judgment three separate revisional applications were filed by defendant No. 5, defendant No. 6 and the heirs of defendant No. 7. The High Court Division modified the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. The compromise decree was found to be valid. The plaintiffs were declared to be entitled to get 0.0675 acres as their share by partitioning the suit property. 7. The appellant contends that the High Court Division did not consider her Civil Revision No. 327 of 1980 and failed either to affirm or reverse the finding of the appellate Court as regards her claim in the suit land. It is submitted that the compromise decree having been signed by one Kanai Lal Dhar, having no authority to sign on behalf of the other defendants, and that the predecessor-in-interest of defendant No. 6, not being a party to the compromise, there was no basis for holding that the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 145 of 1954 was valid and legal. It is urged that as the certified copy of Kabala, Ext. A II, was exhibited without any objection, and that an explanation was given for non-production of the original Kabala, the High Court Division ought to have reversed the finding of the Appellate Court that the Ext. A II was not admissible in evidence. The appellant further submits that the appellate Court and the High Court Division did not consider her possession in the suit land and her right to buy off the plaintiffs' share, if found entitled to, under section 4 of the Partition Act. 8. The appellate Court disbelieved the compromise decree mainly on the ground that fraud was apparent on the face of the record because the defendants appeared and filed the compromise petition before the summons was issued and served, and that Kanailal Dhar was not authorized to act on behalf of all the defendants. The High Court, Division after giving good reasons, upheld the compromise decree. It was held that under sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure the defendants could appear at the presentation of the plaint and admit the plaintiffs' claim and there was no necessity for issuing any summons upon the defendants. It was further found that Kanailal Dhar acted on behalf of all the defendants and that defendant No. 5 after obtaining the compromise decree filed a mutation case under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and got her name recorded. 9. The appellant's papers concerning the pattan and the original kabala were not before the court. The appellant was not examined and there was no explanation as to why she could not be examined. Her husband DW 3 Satya Ranjan Guha said in cross examination that the attesting witnesses of the pattan migrated to India and none of them was available. Papers of Umesh were also missing. As the pattani papers were looted away the pattani land was kabala purchased by his wife. The kabala i.e. Ext A II was executed and registered at Dhaka and the appellant's husband acted as the identifier. Umesh, a police constable posted at Manikganj, could have been examined for proving the execution of the kabala, but he was not examined. The deed-writer and the attesting witnesses were also not examined. The plaintiffs suggested that the kabala was executed by false personification and it was a fake and collusive document for which no consideration was paid. 10. A registered sale deed is the primary evidence of the interest sold. Under section 74 (2) of the Evidence Act, 1882 public record of a private document like a sale-deed when kept in the office of the Sub-Registrar to which the public generally have access falls within the category of public document and a certified copy of such a document can be adduced as a secondary evidence, though the reception of such evidence will be of a weak character in place of the registered document evidencing the sale. 11. Where a case for the reception of secondary evidence is made out under the provisions of section 65, a certified copy of a registered document becomes admissible in proof of the existence, condition and contents of the original document under the provision of section 57(5) of the Registration Act, but the contents of the documents may not be conclusive evidence. 12. The production of a certified copy of a sale-deed does not, however, warrant the presumption of due execution of the original document. A party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even in a case where a document is exhibited without objection the Court is to be satisfied as to the execution of the document. 13. The appellant's husband who claimed to have identified the executant, Umesh, is the only witness testifying as to the sale deed. There is no explanation why the executant of the sale-deed and the scribe and the attesting witnesses could not be examined to prove the transaction. The appellant's evidence as to her title and possession and her entitlement under section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 was not at all satisfactory. The appeal is dismissed. No costs. End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 281 of 1991.
lawyer:
ABM Khairul Haque with Mrs. Snigdha Haque, Advocates ----- For the Appellant.
Nurul Islam Chowdhury with Md. Omar Farook, Advocates -----For the Respondent No.4.
parties:
Sonali Bank ----- Appellant
Vs
Hare Krishna Das & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: This appeal is at the instance of the plaintiff from the decree dated 30-9-1984 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional First Court, Chittagong, in Money Suit No. 11 of 1984.

2. The Sonali Bank, KC Dey Road Branch, Chittagong as plaintiff filed the aforesaid Money Suit against the defendants for realisation of Taka 1,52,650.46 being the principal amount of loan including interest as on 31-8-1982 with a further prayer of pendente lite interest @ 20% per annum from the date of filing of the suit till recovery of the decretal dues with cost.

3. The case of the plaintiff is that the defendant No. 1 took a loan of Taka 1,00,000.00 on 24-10-1979 from the plaintiff for his fishing business against the guarantee of the defendant Nos.2-4. The loan was repayable within 31-3-1980 by fortnightly instalments from the sale proceeds of raw/dry fish. The defendant No. 1 availed the said loan on 24-10-1979 and the defendants executed and delivered the following sets of documents to the plaintiff namely, the DP note for Taka 1,00,000.00 dated 24-10-79, DP note delivery letter for Taka 1,00,000.00 dated 24-10-79, memorandum of deposit of title deeds and a tripartite agreement dated 24-10-79. The defendants also executed balance confirmation slips. The loan was given to defendant No.1 under a scheme slip. The loan was given to defendant No. 1 under a scheme of the Government namely, "Shamudrik Matsha Ahrahan Rin Prakalpa", Anorganisation named and styled "Dubla Fishermen's Group" was formed which was run by the defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 4. The defendant No.1 utilised the said loan but did not make payment and or square up the loan together with interest within the stipulated period leaving the outstanding amount at Taka 1,52,650.46 as on 31-8-80. The further case of the plaintiff is that on the basis of promissory note, the agreement of guarantee and the said tripartite agreement, the defendants are jointly and severally liable to square up the outstanding amount and the plaintiff is legally entitled to realise the said amount from the defendants. The defendants did not payoff the loan despite repeated demands and notices. Hence the suit.

The defendant Nos. 1-3 did not contest the suit. The defendant No. 4 filed written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable and there is no cause of action for the suit. The suit is false and fabricated. That the suit is bad for non-joinder of parties.That this defendant is not a necessary party. Since this defendant is admittedly a guarantor he has no liability to pay the debt of the borrower. The plaintiff Bank must realise the entire amount of loan with interest from the borrower by attaching the personal properties of the borrower and after doing all these if there remains any amount to be paid to the Bank then and then only the guarantor will be followed up to pay the said unrecovered amount. This defendant did not sign any balance confirmation certificate nor did he create any equitable mortgage in favour of the plaintiff Bank. The defendant No. 1 in collusion with the plaintiff obtained some signatures of the defendant on some blank papers. This defendant is not aware of any tripartite agreement which might have been created with those signed blank papers. The further case of this defendant is that he did neither create any promissory note nor he has signed any other documents as alleged by the plaintiff. He did not take the loan and, as such, he is not liable to pay the claimed amount. The plaintiff cannot get any relief in the suit and there cannot be any direction upon this defendant to pay the decretal amount unless the decretal amount, if any, is first of all recovered from the other defendants who were allowed to take the loan. There cannot be any personal decree against this defendant, so the suit must fail.

4. In the light of the aforesaid pleadings the trial Court framed four issues. At the trial the plaintiff examined one witness and exhibited certain documents in support of their case. The defendant No. 4 examined himself as DW 1 in support of his case but did not exhibit any document.

5. The trial Court after considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant No.4 and ex parte against others without cost holding that the plaint is not a plaint in terms of Order 7 rule 1 of CPC and that the very plaint on the pleadings of the plaintiff were prepared completely contrary to the documents of the plaintiff. The trial Court also found that the plaintiff is not entitled to get any relief in the suit on the basis of mere admission of the defendant No. 4 that he was the guarantor of the loan.

6. Mr. Khairul Haque, the learned Advocate who appeared for the appellant Bank, submitted that the learned court below erred in .law in holding that the DP note dated 24th September, 1979, Ext. 1 executed by the defendant No. 1 and endorsed by the remaining defendants on its reverse is meaningless paper. He further submitted that the trial Court erred in law in holding that the defendants are not responsible for the dues of the plaintiff in spite of admitted endorsement on the Demand Promissory Note by the defendants No. 2-4 making themselves jointly and severally liable as sureties/guarantors for payment of the plaintiffs dues under the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The learned lawyer of the appellant Bank also submitted that the learned court below should have decreed the suit on the basis of the admitted exhibits on record which proved the case of the plaintiff beyound and shadow of doubt. His further submission was that since the defendant Nos. 1-3 did not contest the suit the trial Court seriously erred in law in not decreeing the suit against them at least. The learned Advocate of the appellant with much emphasis submitted that the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaint is not a plaint as per provision of Order 7 rule 1 of Civil Procedure Code is misconceived. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that the irregularities in the Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deed, Ext. 4, cannot cause any impediment in the instant case in granting decree for recovery of outstanding dues on the basis of primary securities since it is not a mortgage suit. Mr. Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate, who appeared for the respondent No. 4, submitted that the onus is on the plaintiff to prove his case and in the instant case the plaintiff has not been able to prove their case. He further submitted that there is nothing on record to show the liability of defendant No. 4 as there is no evidence to show that defendant No. 4 was a guarantor. The final submission of the learned Advocate of the respondent is that the admission of defendant No. 4 that he is a guarantor is not enough to bind him in view of section 31 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate further tried to submit that the admission of his client is no admission in the eye of law and the Ext. 1 is not a Demand Promissory Note as per provision of Negotiable Instruments Act and, as such, the trial Court did not commit any illegality or irregularity in dismissing the suit

7. Now let us consider the respective submissions of the learned lawyers on the basis of the pleadings of the parties, evidence and materials on record. In this case it is admitted that the plaintiff granted a loan of Taka 1,00,000.00 to the defendant No. 1 on 24-10-79 and he also availed of the same. It is also admitted that defendant No. 4 is a guarantor of the loan. It is the case of the plaintiff that to secure the loan the defendants executed and delivered the following documents in favour of the plaintiff:

1. DP note for Taka 1,00,000.00 dated 24-10-79.

2. DP Note delivery letter for Taka 1,00,000.00, dated 24-10-79

3.	Memorandum of deposit of title deeds and

4.	Tripartite agreement between the borrower, defendant No. 4 and the plaintiff.

8. The said documents were also proved by the plaintiff at the trial but the trial Court took exception to the fact that in the memorandum of deposit of title deed Ext. 4 it is mentioned that certain title deeds are deposited by the defendant No. 1 but the schedule of Ext. 4 is left blank. So, no equitable mortgage was created and the plaintiff unnecessarily incorporated the same document in the plaint and also brought it in evidence before the court. The trial Court, therefore, found that the plaint is not a plaint as per provision of Order 7 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is true that a plaintiff must give such particulars as will enable the defendant and the court to ascertain whether in fact or in law the cause of action did arise as alleged or not. It is also equally true that the pleadings should not be construed too narrowly and every variance between pleading and proof is not fatal. In construing the plaint the court must have regard to all the relevant allegations in it and must look to the substance of the matter and not its form.

<u>9. The purpose of pleadings is to pinpoint the matters of controversy between the parties and to enable the contesting parties to meet their respective cases. If at the trial a plaintiff fails to prove some of his allegations that does not necessarily mean that the suit shall fail. The fate of the suit depends on the overall evidence and materials on record. We fail to understand why the learned Court below took exception with regard to the irregularities in the memorandum of deposit of title deed Ext. 4. Ext. 4 allegedly created an equitable mortgage in favour of the plaintiff to secure the interest of the plaintiff. Even if the creation of the equitable mortgage is found to be defective or if there is no equitable mortgage then also the plaintiff is entitled to succeed in the suit if they can successfully prove their other material allegations i.e. taking of loan by the defendant No. 1 and his failure to repay the same. We have perused the plaint and we find that all the requirements of Order 7 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure have been fulfilled by the plaintiff and by no stretch of imagination it can be said that the plaint in the instant case is not a plaint as per Order 7 rule 1 because of the embodiment of the statement regarding memorandum of deposit of title deeds. It appears to us that the learned Subordinate Judge absolutely misconceived and misconstrued the provision of Order 7 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>10. Ext. 1 is the Demand Promissory Note. The learned lawyer of the respondent No. 4 submitted that it is not a Demand Promissory Note as per law. The Demand Promissory Note has been defined in section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, to be a promissory note, the document in question-</u>

<u>(a) must be an instrument in writing (b) must not be a bank-note or a currency note (c) must be signed by the maker; and (d) must contain an unconditional undertaking to pay a certain sum of money.</u>

<u>(i) Only to a certain person, (ii) to the order of certain person; or (iii) to the bearer of the instrument: or (iv) only to, or to the order of, certain person: or (v) only to a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument.</u>

<u>The question, whether a particular document is a promissory note or not, has to be decided with reference to-</u>

<u>(1) the description of the instrument, (2) the language of the instrument taken as a whole, (3) the circumstances under which the document came to be executed; (4) the intention of the parties manifest on the face of the document and (5) the surrounding circumstances.</u>

<u>So, where the instrument clearly indicates the promissor and the promisee and contains a definite promise to pay, it is a promissory note. We have carefully scrutinised Ext. 1 and we find that all the requirements of law to make it a promissory note are found to be present in it and, as such, we have no hesitation to arrive at a decision that it is a Demand Promissory Note as contemplated in the Negotiable Instruments Act.</u>

11.Now let us see if the defendant No.4 can be treated as a guarantor of the loan in question. Ext.l is the Demand Promissory Note drawn by the defendant No.1 in favour of Mr. Korban Ali (the defendant No. 4) and Dubla Fishermen's Group or order. On the reverse of the said Demand Promissory Note it was endorsed the Sonali Bank or order by said M/S. Korban Ali (defendant No. 4) and two other persons on behalf of Dubla Fishermen's Group.It. thus.appears that the demand promissory note was duly endorsed by the defendant No. 4 along with two others in favour of the plaintiff Bank. Ext. 2 is the demand promissory note delivery letter dated 24-10-1979 whereby the said demand promissory note was handed over to the plaintiff with the waiver of the dishonor notice. The maker of the promissory note is the principal debtor or the party primarily liable on the instrument. The endorser of a demand promissory note engages that on due presentment it will be paid according to its tenor, and that, if it is dishonored, he will compensate the holder or any subsequent endorser. Section 38 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, provides that, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the maker of a promissory note is bound to pay the amount thereof to the holder on demand and in default of such payment, such maker or accept or is bound to compensate the holder of the note for any loss or damage sustained by him or caused by such default. Section 37 of the Act states that as between the maker and endorser, the endorser is liable as a surety, the maker being liable as principal debtor. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Act namely, sections 4, 14, 15, 32 48 and 50 it appears to us that the defendant No. 4 in the instant case is a surety guarantor of the principal debtor, the defendant No. 1. The submission of the learned Advocate of the respondent No. 4 that there is no evidence to show that the defendant No. 4 is a guarantor appears to us to be of no substance.

12. The defendant No. 4 in his written statement took up the plea that the plaintiff cannot pursue the guarantor without first realising the amount from the borrower i.e. the principal debtor. But, however, he has given a go-by to this at the trial and candidly admitted in his examination- in-chief that he is the guarantor of the loan of Taka 1,00,000.00 of the defendant No. 1 along with defendant Nos. 2 and 3. In cross examination he has reiterated that he is the guarantor of the loan of defendant No.1 and also admitted the endorsement on the demand promissor note. He also admitted his signature on Ext. 2 Demand Promissory Note delivery letter. These are the admitted pieces of evidences which show that the defendant No. 4 is one of the guarantors of the loan and, as such, he must bear the responsibility of the guarantor under the law.

13. As to the liability to repay the outstanding amount of the loan the responsibility of the principal debtor is co-extensive with the guarantor. The priority of the choices to seek repayment from either the principal debtor or the guarantor rests with the creditor. The liability of the guarantor is in no way dependent upon the principal debtor. Without even seeing the principal debtor for the repayment of the loan the creditor may choose to proceed against the guarantor. The guarantor is liable to pay even where the creditor omits to sue the principal debtor. The guarantor's liability is not deferred until the creditor exhausts his remedies against the principal debtor. His liability is immediate. We have already found that the defendant No. 4 is a guarantor of the loan. He also candidly admitted the same position in his evidence but the trial Court refused to decree the suit on his admission on the ground that "the exhibited documents and plaintiff cannot expect any relief on the basis of the confused evidence."The said finding of the trial Court is erroneous and without any basis at all.

<u>14. The learned Advocate of the respondent submitted that the admission of his client is not sufficient to bind him in view of section 31 of the Evidence Act. This section deals with the effect of admissions with regard to their conclusiveness. It means that admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted and the party is at liberty to prove that these were made under mistake of law or fact, or were untrue or were made under threat, inducement or fraud. In the instant case the defendant No. 4 in his written statement clearly admitted that he is the guarantor of the loan. In his examination-in-chief he stated that he is the guarantor and so also in his cross examination. There is nothing on record to show that he made the admission on mistake of law or fact or for some other reasons. He made it clear in his cross examination that he knows the responsibility of the guarantor. We therefore, find this submission devoid of any substance.</u>

<u>15. It is true that the onus is on the petitioner to prove his case and in the instant case on perusal of evidence and materials on record we find that the plaintiff have been able to prove their case against the defendants. Besides, there is another aspect of the case which has been lost sight of by the learned Subordinate Judge that is, that the liability of the principal debtor is co-extensive with the guarantor. A creditor can pursue either the principal debtor or the guarantor according to his sweet will to realise his dues or can proceed against both simultaneously. In the instant case the defendant No. 1 is the principal debtor and defendant Nos.2-4 are guarantors. The defendant Nos. 1-3 did not contest the suit The case of the plaintiff with regard to defendant Nos. 1-3 remains uncontested. Moreover, the plaintiffs,have proved their case against them by cogent evidence. In view of that matter we do not find any reason why the learned Subordinate Judge did not decree the suit at least against defendant Nos. 1-3 and the judgment is not sustainable on that count also.</u>

<u>We have perused the materials and evidence on record and we have already found that the plaintiff have been able to prove their case against all the defendants who are jointly and severally liable to repay the loan. It appears to us that the learned court below failed to appreciate the true import and tenor of the relevant provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and the learned Subordinate Judge is absolutely ignorant about the relevant provisions of the said Act. The learned Subordinate Judge on a total misconception of law and facts misconstrued and misinterpreted the evidence and materials on record and most illegally dismissed the suit although the plaintiffs have successfully proved their case. In the result the appeal is allowed without cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 30-9-84 passed in Money Suit No. 11 of 1984 of the 1st Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, are set aside. The suit is decreed with cost.</u>

End.

case_source:
(From the judgment and order dated 9.2.1989 passed by the
High Court Division, Barisal Bench, Barisal in Civil Revision Case Nos. 103 and 104 of 1982).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman J: These two appeals, Civil Appeal No. 19 of 1990 and Civil Appeal No. 20 of 1990, are disposed of by this judgment. Appellant filed two suits, Title Suit Nos. 52 and 53 of 1971, in First Court of Munsif, Pirojpur for a declaration that he purchased the respective suit lands from proforma defendant Nos. 2 and 3 (Respondent Nos. 3 and 4-6) for valuable consideration by three registered Kabalas in the name of defendant No. 1 Sarbeswar Ghose. The latter's heirs are respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The suits were compromised between the plaintiff appellant and defendant No. 1 by a solenama dated 22.9.1971. Both the suits were decreed on compromise against deceased defendant No. 1 and ex parte against proforma-defendant Nos. 2 and 3, against whom the appellant did not pray for any relief.

2. On 6th April, 1982 defendant Nos. 2 and 3 filed two applications for setting aside the ex parte decrees under Article 3 of the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1972 (PO No. 12 of 1972). By separate orders Dated 30th April, 1982 those applications were allowed, the decrees were set aside and the suits were restored to their files and numbers for re-hearing. The appellant moved unsuccessfully two revisional applications before the District Judge and thereafter before the High Court Division.

3. Leave was granted to consider whether the compromise decrees were outside the mischief of PO No. 12 of 1972, particularly when as alleged by the appellant, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 having sold out their interest in the suit lands had no longer any subsisting interest to contest the suits. PO No. 12 of 1972 was promulgated on 6th February, 1972 to provide for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings and for the nullification of all judgments, decrees and orders passed ex parte or in default of compliance with certain directions in certain legal proceedings. Article 3 of the PO No. 12 reads as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, all judgments, decrees or orders passed ex parte by any Court or Tribunal or orders disposing of matters due to default in compliance with any direction of any Court or Tribunal in any legal proceedings at any time after the 1st day of March, 1971, and before the commencement of this Order are hereby declared null and void and the proceedings shall, on the commencement of this Order, continue in accordance with the Law."

<u>4. The appellant's contention is that the compromise decrees were not ex parte decrees as defendant No. 1 was very much a party to the same. It is further contended that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 did not deny that they sold the suit lands to defendant No. 1 and hence they had no subsisting interest in the proceedings to file the applications for restoration of the suits. In support of his first contention the learned counsel for the appellant relied on Mokbul Ahmed and others Vs. Ali Ekabbar and others 35 DLR 86. In that case plaintiff filed a title suit for declaration of title in the suit land against principal defendants Nos. 1-9 and proforma defendant Nos. 10-17. Defendant Nos. 1 to 9 entered appearance, but later on compromised the suit with the plaintiff. The ex parte decree passed in that suit was subsequently set aside and the suit was restored to its file and number.</u>

<u>5. In setting aside the Order of restoration the learned Single Judge observed:</u>

<u>"It is patent that only ex parte judgments, decrees or orders passed during the period mentioned in article 3, of PO 12 of 1972 came under the mischief of the section. Compromise decrees did not come within the mischief of the section. There is no doubt that the decrees against defendants 10-17 came under the mischief of article 3 of PO 12 of 1972 but this by itself could not justify the setting aside of the decree as a whole and restoration of the suit without a finding that if ex parte decree against defendants 10-17 was null and void, the compromise decree against defendants 1-9 could not be maintained."</u>

<u>6. In that decision the compromise decree was upheld and it was ordered that the ex parte decree against defendants 10-17 be set aside and their names be struck off the decree. In that case no one appeared for the proforma-defendants and it was not agitated how in view of the clear language of Art. 3 of PO No. 12 of 1972 a part of the decree namely, the compromise decree in favour of defendants 1-9 could be severed and saved from the decree that was passed ex-parte against the other defendants. The law in the case reported in 35 DLR 86 has not been correctly decided. In the instant case in refusing to interfere with the restoration of the two suits under Art. 3 of PO No. 12 of 1972, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has correctly laid down the law. We approve the following observation made by the learned Judge:</u>

<u>"The expression "proforma defendant" does not appear in any provision of the Code of Civil Procedure; the term indicates that for the sake of form the so-called proforma defendant was made a party in the suit. In the instant case although no relief has been claimed against defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the claim of the plaintiff is based on the averment that he purchased the suit lands from defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and as such the plaintiff made them parties to the suit. The decrees passed on 22.9.1971 show that the suit was decreed ex parte against defendant Nos. 2 and 3. As such defendant Nos. 2 and 3 has locus standi to invoke the provisions of Art. 3 of PO No. 12 of 1972. Even if they did not file any application the decree became null and void by operation of law inasmuch as the provision of Art. 3 of PO No. 12 of 1972 provided that such decree passed within the time mentioned therein were declared null and void by that provision of law."</u>

<u>We do not find any substance in the appellant's second contention. In their applications under Article 3 of PO 12 of 1972 defendant Nos. 2 and 3 did not deny the sale but they asserted that they had their ancestral homestead in the suit lands and they were co-sharers of the holding and the suits were decreed on compromise in their absence. The case made out by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was good enough for the restoration of the suits under Art. 3 of PO No. 12 of 1972. The defendants-respondents were not required to disclose what stand or plea of defence they would take in their written statements which could only be filed after the restoration of the suits. Accordingly, we uphold the decision of the High Court Division and dismiss the two appeals. As no one appears for the respondents there will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Revision Case No. 5381 of 1991 (Dhaka) No. 265 of 1986 (Ctg.)
lawyer:
Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate with Mostafa Niaz Muhammad, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Khademul Islam Chowdhury, with Md. Omar Farook, Advocates ------ For the Opposite Party No.1

Abdus Sattar ------ Petitioner

Abdul Karim  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule is against the judgment and decree dated 7-7-86 passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Patiya in Other Appeal No. 50 of 1967 reversing the Judgment and decree dated 5-1-67 passed by the 2nd Court of Munsif, Patiya, Chittagong in Title Suit No. 60 of 1965 (wrongly typed in the certified copy as TS No. 60 of 1956.

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are, that the petitioner herein as plaintiff No. 2 along with his father Jeabat Ali, since deceased, as plaintiff No.1, instituted a Title Suit No. 60 of 1965 on 27-11-65 for declaration of their riyati interest and for confirmation of possession from beyond the statutory period of limitation with regard to the suit pond and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the suit pond and from giving any fencing and/or any obstruction and also from cutting any trees and enjoying any fruits and from catching any fish from the suit pond. The suit land described in the schedule as RS Plot No. 1362 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 333 having an area of 1 Kani 2 gandas and the nature of the suit land is pond and its bank.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that, the pond originally belonged to one Girish Chandra Mohajan who died leaving 4 sons namely, Nishi Chandra, Ram Chandra, Mahendra Lal and Manindra Lal and also a grandson namely, Profullah Kumar, son of Jogesh Chandra who predeceased Girish Chandra Mohajan. The heirs of Girish Chandra Mohajan settled the pond with the plaintiffs namely, Jeabat Ali and Ayub Ali at a rental of Taka 8.00 about 25 years back and since then the plaintiffs have been possessing the said pond and its bank. Defendant No. 38, Profullah Kumar gave out that he got the suit pond in his share by amicable settlement amongst the co-sharers. The defendant No. 37, Manindra Lal Mohajan who acted as Karjakarak on behalf of the co-sharers admitted the alleged facts. In fact, the plaintiffs took permanent settlement of the said pond from Profulla (defendant No. 38) by two registered pattas to the extent of 16 gondas (8 gondas each) and one Dudu Meah took settlement of the remaining 6 gondas of the said pond by another registered patta. Dudu Meah, thereafter, sold his share to the plaintiff No.1 i.e. the present petitioner herein by registered Kabala wherein the defendant No. 2 Fazal Karim alias Fazal Ahamed was an attesting witness. The plaintiffs continued their exclusive possession in the suit pond and its bank. They also constructed a cow shed and planted fruit bearing trees. The plaintiff No. 1 also buried dead body of his wife in the bank of the said pond. As such, the plaintiffs acquired the exclusive title in the suit pond and continuing their possession for more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and also acquired title by adverse possession.

4. The further case of the plaintiffs is that, the defendant No. 37, Monindra Lal Mohajan is a rich and respectable person, the plaintiffs hold high regards for him and then there arose a bad relationship between Dudu Meah and defendant Nos. 14-16 namely, Nirendra Kumar, Pulin Behari, Bankim, son of Nishi Kanta, who with a view to harass Dudu Meah and the plaintiffs created false and collusive kabala in the name of one Abdul Alim, the defendant No 40 without any consideration. Being apprehensive as to the cloud in the title over the suit pond, the plaintiffs went to defendant No. 37, Manindra Lal Mohajan, who advised the plaintiffs to give up some portion of the suit pond in favour of his son, defendant No. 39, Jadab Chandra Mohajan. Monindra Lal Mahajan also advised that the defendant No. 40 Abdul Alim would also transfer his entire share in favour of his son. Thereafter, the defendant No. 39, Jadab Chandra Mohajan would transfer the entire portion of the suit pond in favour of the plaintiffs, otherwise the defendant No. 40 Abdul Alim was not agreeing to transfer his portion of the suit pond. Being satisfied with the advice of Monindra Lal Mohajan the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 40 transferred some portion of their share of the suit land in favour of the defendant No. 39 by registered Kabala. The defendant No. 39 subsequently transferred the entire portion of the suit pond by registered Kabala in favour of the plaintiffs in the benami of Abdus Sattar, son of Ayub Ali (the present petitioner). The plaintiffs have stated that these transactions were merely paper transactions and the same were done for peace and in order to remove cloud over the suit pond. The plaintiffs had been continuously possessing the said pond on payment of rent to the defendant No. 38, Profulla Kumar Mohajan prior to State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation.

5. The case of the plaintiffs is that, the defendant Nos. 1-3 are litigants of worst type and are inimical with the plaintiffs and that is why they have created some false and forged Kabalas in the name of defendant Nos. 1-6 collusively with defendant No. 37 and they also influenced other defendant Nos. 7-10 and threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit pond by cutting trees and catching fish, etc. It has been further alleged by the plaintiffs that the defendant No.37 had only the rent receiving interest, if any, and if any documents are created, those documents would be void and illegal. Having confronted with the aforesaid situation the plaintiffs had no other alternative but to institute a title suit being Title Suit No. 25 of 1965 with a prayer for permanent injunction and the same was withdrawn with a liberty to file a fresh suit and the instant suit was filed with a prayer as stated above.

6. Two separate written statements were filed, one by defendant No. 1 namely, Abdul Karim who is the defendant opposite party No. 1 in this petition and another by defendant No. 19, Dipak Kumar Mohajan (withdrawn from the suit at the appellate stage). Other defendants neither filed any written. statements nor contested the suit. Defendant No. 19 in his written statement has, in fact, narrated the selfsame statements as made by the defendant No. 1 in his written statement and denied the material allegations made in the plaint. However, both the defendant Nos. 1 and 19 have admitted one fact that the suit pond originally belonged to Girish Chandra Mohajan who died leaving four sons and a grandson of a predeceased son. They used to possess the suit pond in ejmali and flatly denied that the suit pond was ever given in exclusive possession of Profulla Kumar Mohajan by amicable arrangement and stated that the defendant Nos. 14-16 and defendant Nos. 13, 17-18 settled 1/5th share of the pond to the defendant No. 40, who sold the same to defendant No. 39. The defendant No. 39, subsequently, sold same share to the son of plaintiff No. 2 The defendant No. 37 sold his 1/5th share of the suit pond to defendant Nos. 1-5 by registered kabalas on different dates and consequently the defendant Nos. 1-5 have been possessing the same. The defendant Nos. 9-36 have also been possessing their shares of the suit pond and the defendants herein above mentioned prayed that the suit be dismissed with costs.

7. The learned Munsif on consideration of the material evidence on record decreed the suit with a finding that though the plaintiffs could not prove mutual arrangement or exclusive possession of the entire tank in favour of Profulla Kumar by cogent evidence, but from the facts evidences and circumstances as noted above I have reason to believe that plffs, proved their continuous possession in the suit land peacefully and adversely against other co-sharers and they acquired good title as exclusive settler from co-sharer. Naturally the plffs, have right to retain their possession even against other co-sharers till it is otherwise declared or decided in a court of law in a partition suit between the co-sharers. The learned Munsif passed the decree declaring that the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit pond entirely and exclusively and their possession thereto be also hereby confirmed, and the defendants be permanently restrained from interfering with the plaintiffs' possession in the suit pond till it is otherwise decided by any court of law.

8. Being aggrieved with the judgment and decree dated 5-1-67 the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 (defendant Nos. 1 and 19) preferred Title Appeal No. 50 of 1967 in the Court of District Judge, Chittagong. On transfer the learned Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, Chittagong heard the appeal and after considering the evidence on record by his judgment and decree dated 27-4-68 allowed the appeal and remanded the case to the trial Court. However, the learned Court of Additional Subordinate Judge, Chittagong permitted defendant No. 19 (opposite party No. 2) to withdraw from the said appeal and directed the trial Court to dispose of the suit in the light of the observation made in his judgment. The relevant portion of the observation in the said order of remand dated 27-4-68 are noted for convenience as under. The trial Court will please frame a specific issue namely, whether pro-defendant No.38 Prafulla got the disputed tank exclusively by virtue of amicable arrangement with his co-sharers or not. The trial Court will please allow the parties to lead fresh evidence, if necessary, on the new issue raised.

9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 27-4-68 allowing the appeal and remanding the case to the trial Court the plaintiffs preferred second Miscellaneous Appeal No.87 of 1968 in the then High Court at Dhaka. The High Court Division by an order dated 12-4-78 disposed of the said appeal with a direction to the lower Appellate Court to dispose of the appeal on merit, if necessary, after reframing issues and taking fresh, further and additional evidence on any issue in the dispute between the parties concerned.

10. On receipt of the records from the High Court Division the learned Subordinate Judge, Patiya did not frame any further issue but permitted the appellant No. 1, Abdul Karim to take evidence of the DWs namely, Abdul Gani and Abul Hossain and allowed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 7-7-86, and set aside the judgment and decree of trial Court dated 5-1-67 without considering the evidence which are already on record.

11. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 7-7-86 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Patiya in Other Appeal No. 50 of 1967 reversing the judgment and decree dated 5-1-67 passed by the 2nd Court of Munsif, Patiya in Title Suit No. 60 of 1965, the plaintiff-petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rule. (The plaintiff No.1 is dead).

12. Mr. Khandaker Mahubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that the learned Appellate Court committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in allowing the appeal without considering the evidence which are already on record. Mr. Khandaker submits that the finding of the learned appellate Court below to the effect that the plaintiffs did not adduce any evidence in support of their case of amicable settlement and exclusive ownership of Profullah is erroneous and not correct because PW 1, Ayub All and PW 2, Amin Sharif have already deposed to the above effect and supported the plaintiffs case and thereby the learned Appellate Court ex facie committed an error of law in not considering the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 which are already on record in deciding the issue of amicable partition in between the co-sharers.

13. Mr. Ahmed submits that the learned trial Court having decreed the suit on the basis of evidence of PWs 1-9 and the Appellate Court below having not considered those evidence on record erred in law in reversing the decision only upon consideration of the evidence of DWs 1 and 2 examined at the appellate stage.

14. Mr. Ahmed submits that in any view of the matter the evidence adduced by the parties in this case, the admitted position being that Prafullah was a sharer to the extent of 1/5th, the Appellate Court below erred in law in dismissing the entire suit. Mr. Khandaker submits that the Appellate Court below has erred in law for non-consideration of the circumstantial evidence in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner that none of the co-sharers in the suit pond excepting Manindra's transferee, the defendant No. 1, is challenging the claim of the plaintiff-petitioner.

15. Mr. Khandaker lastly, submits that the plaintiffs having fully stated in paragraph 9 of the plaint an alternative claim of title by adverse possession followed by similar prayer in paragraph 'Ka' of the prayer portion, and the trial Court having decreed the suit on the basis of adverse possession on consideration of evidence of PWs 1-9, the trial Court was within his jurisdiction to pass such decree, and the Appellate Court having failed to avert that aspect of the judgment of the trial Court, the Appellate Court erred in law in deciding the appeal occasioning failure of justice.

16. Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No. 1), submits that the plaintiffs having admitted that the pond and its bank originally belonged to one Girish Chandra Mohajan and on his death the interest devolved upon his four sons and a grandson of a predeceased son and the plaintiff's having admitted that Monindra on behalf of his three brothers as Karjakarak settled the pond on yearly basis to the plaintiffs and plaintiffs having failed to establish that Prafullah, one of the co-sharers, acquired title and exclusive possession and/or adverse possession by way of amicable settlement amongst the co-sharers, the plaintiffs are not entitled to any declaratory decree and confirmation of possession and permanent injunction against the defendant No. 1

17. Mr. Chowdhury submits that sons of Nishi Chandra Mohajan sold their 1/5th share in the pond to one Abdul Alim, defendant No. 40, who in turn sold the same to one Jadab Chandra Mohajan, son of Monindra Mohajan by registered kabala. At the same time plaintiff No. 2 petitioner also sold a portion of the suit pond to Jadab Chandra Mohajan by registered Kabala. Jadab Chandra Mohajan sold his such acquired share in the pond by registered kabala to one Abdus Sattar in the benami of plaintiff No. 2 petitioner. Therefore, Mr. Chowdhury submits that the petitioner is estopped from challenging the title and possession of defendant No. 1. Mr. Chowdhury lastly, submits that the plaintiffs had no adverse possession over the suit property to the exclusion of other heirs of Girish Chandra Mohajan and that the plaintiffs failed to make out the case of adverse possession. He submits that no evidence was adduced by the plaintiffs to prove their assertion of adverse possession. He submits that the burden of making out ouster is on the person claiming to displace the lawful title of a co-heir by his adverse possession and he has placed reliance on the decisions reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 314.

18. The admitted position is that the High Court Division by its order dated 12-4-79 passed in Second Miscellaneous Appeal No. 87 of 1968 sent back the case to the lower Appellate Court with a direction to decide the case finally on merit, if necessary after re-framing issues and taking fresh, further and additional evidence on any issues in the dispute between the parties concerned. The learned Appellate Court on receipt of the records, accordingly, framed an issue as to whether there had been an amicable settlement amongst the co-sharers of late Girish Chandra Mohajan. The defendant No. 1 (opposite party No. 1) adduced two witnesses at the appellate stage to prove the said issue. DW 1 Abdul Gani who has clearly deposed that Profullah was within the joint mess of Girish Chandra Mohajan after the death of his father Jogesh Chandra Mohajan. DW 1 has also stated that there was partition of landed properties among the co-sharers of Girish Chandra but he could not say as to whether there was any partition deed. He has also stated that the co-sharers used to possess the tanks and ponds separately. The relevant portion with regard to the issue of amicable settlement as deposed by DW 1 is quoted as under:

“ যোগেশ মারা যাওয়ার পরে প্রফুল্ল শিরিশের পরিবারভুক্ত ছিল। গিরিশের ওয়ারিশগণের মধ্যে জমি ভাগ হইয়াছিল, কিন্তু কোন অংশনামা হইয়াছিল কি-না আমি জানি না। জলীয় অংশ পৃথক পৃথক ভাবে দখল করিত।”

19. DW 2. Abul Hossain has stated that except southern corner of the pond Ayub Ali has been possessing the west bank of the pond. He has stated that he has seen Profulla to catch fish out of the suit pond but he said that he cannot say whether any partition deed was made or not. Relevant portion of deposition of DW 2 is quoted as under:

“দক্ষিণ কোনা বাদ দিয়া পুকুরের অন্যান্য পাড় বাদী আইয়ুব আলী দখল করে। পুকুরের পাড়ে মাপ করিয়া কেহ দখল দিয়াছিল কিনা আমি জানি না। প্রফুল্লকে আমি দেখিয়াছি এবং তাহাকে উক্ত পুকুরের মাছ ধরিতে দেখিয়াছি। উক্ত পুকুরের ব্যাপারে কোন অংশ নামা হইয়াছিল কিনা আমি বলিতে পারিব না।”

20. Abdul Gani has also deposed as DW 2 at the trial Court wherein he has admitted in cross-examination that 'about three years back the grave of mother of Ayub was placed at the northern bank of the pond" but he did not say anything with regard to amicable settlement or partition. The plaintiff-petitioner did not produce any witness at the appellate stage. The learned Appellate Court on the basis of the evidence of DWs 1 and 2 taken at the appellate stage disposed of the appeal holding that thee had been no amicable settlement or partition amongst the co-sharers of Girish Chandra Mohajan and therefore, the plaintiffs' declaration with regard to title and confirmation of possession on the basis of registered pattas exhibit 2 and 2(A) cannot be given in favour of the plaintiffs. The Appellate Court observed that the plaintiffs may get at best declaration of the title in respect of 1/5th share of the suit property i.e. 1/5th share of Profullah. The learned Appellate Court further held that since the plaintiffs have been claiming that there had been amicable settlement of the property of Girish Chandra Mohajan and since the plaintiffs failed to prove the said amicable settlement, they are not entitled to the relief as prayed for.

21. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that on the issue of an amicable settlement the Appellate Court has considered only the evidence of DWs 1 and 2, taken at the appellate stage but the Appellate Court clearly failed to consider the evidence on the issues which are already on record. Mr. Khandker submits that PW 1 has stated in-chief that 5 sons settled the suit land to them from year to year basis. Thereafter Profullah had the suit pond in his share and he settled the said pond in favour of them. Relevant portion of deposition of PW 1 is quoted as under:

"The suit land is pond. It belonged to Girish Chandra Mohajan. He died leaving Nishi, Ram Chandra, Mohendra Ch. J ogesh Ch. Manindra. Jogesh died leaving son Profulla. All the 5 sons settled the suit land from year to year on a jama of Rs.8.00 per year about 25/26 years back. We possessed then for 8/11 years on payment of rents to Monindra Mohajan who was Karayakarak of all the 3 brothers. 2 dakhilas are filed. This dakhila was signed and written by Monindra. This is marked Ext. 1. On the 9th year Manindra said that the pond (in suit) fell in the share of ProfulIa by amicable settlement and the rents paid to him. For 2 years we paid rents to him. Then Profulla said that he would settle it permanently. Then my father & myself took settlement of the pond in suit having 8 gandas. The pattas were written by Saleh Ahmed & Oli Mia and executed by Profulla by signing his name himself. These are marked Ext. 2 & 2(a). On that date Profulla also settled 6 gandas of land of suit land. We paid consideration money. The patta in favour of Dudu was written by Saleh Ahmed and executed by Profulla. A consideration money of Rs. 95.00 was paid by him in my presence. This is marked Ext. 2(b). I again purchased the share of Dudu Mia after his possession for 718 years. The kabala was written by Mohendra and executed by Dudu Mia by putting his thumb impression. Imam Baksh wrote his name. I paid the consideration money (This is Ext. 3).

Thus my father & myself possessed the suit pond. My mother died and she was buried at north west bank of the pond. Abdul Karim, Fazal Karim & Afzal Mia, Almas Khatun, Shamsun threatened to dispossess us from suit land. Hence is this case."

22. Mr. Khandaker submits that PW 1 in his cross-examination has stated that the sons of Grish Ch. Mohajan have vast properties but I cannot say if their properties were partitioned. But I have heard that some ponds have been partitioned and some houses have been also partitioned. How long ago this partition took place I cannot say. I heard it from Monindra.

23. PW 2 Amin Sharif has stated in examination in-chief that I know suit land. It belonged to Girish Mohajan at first. Then it devolved upon the plaintiffs on taking settlement from year to year from Girish (wrongly written Girindra) about 26 years back. Amongst 5 sons of Girish, Monindra used to look after the shares of all brothers.

Then Profulla settled the land on behalf of all the brothers by amicable settlement in his share from other brothers to plffs & Dudu Mia. I was an attesting witness of the 2 pattas. The plffs & Dudu Mia gave Nazar Selami to Profulla. Dudu Mia then after 7/8 years sold his share to Ayub Ali. Since then plffs have been possessing. The defdts or anybody did not possess the suit land during last 25/26 years, but the plffs possessed it all along.

24. PW 2, in his cross-examination, has stated that I cannot say if partition of the entire properties of Girish Chandra was made. I hear that there was amicable partition. However he said that he was not present and he said he cannot say if any deed of partition was made. Mr. Khandoker assailed the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court mainly on the ground that the Appellate Court did not consider the evidence of PW s which are already on record to an issue of whether there had been amicable partition of the properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan or not. I find substance in the submission of Mr. Khandoker.

25. DWs 1 and 2 at the Appellate Court have also deposed that the properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan were amicably partitioned but they could not say if there was any partition deed. Similarly, PWs 1 and 2 at the trial Court have deposed that there had been amicable partition of the properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan but they also could not say if there was any partition deed. This shows that there are evidence on record that there had been an amicable partition of the properties of Girish Chandra. But neither the PWs nor the DWs could say if partition deed was drawn up. The attention of Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury was drawn as to whether the Appellate Court considered the evidence of PWs which are already on record in disposing of the appeal, he frankly concedes that the Appellate Court did not consider the evidence of PWs in arriving at a finding as to whether there was any amicable partition of the properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan. But Mr. Chowdhury vehemently argued that Profulla Kumar Mohajan did not exclusively possess the suit pond.

26. Mr. Khondker lastly, submits that none of the co-sharers of Girish Chandra did come to contest the suit except defendant Nos. 1 and 19. Defendant No. 19, with the permission of the court, withdrew from the suit at the appellate stage. Mr. Khondoker submits that the courts below failed to consider the circumstantial evidence especially the Appellate Court in disposing of the appeal.

27. On analysis of the evidence on record and the circumstantial evidence as put forward by the learned Advocate for plaintiff-petitioner I have no hesitation to hold that the Appellate Court has committed an error of law in not considering the evidence of PWs taken at the trial, which are already on record in deciding the issue as to whether there was any amicable partition or not. The then High Court at Dhaka clearly directed the Appellate Court to dispose of the case on merit, if necessary after reforming issue and taking fresh, further additional evidence on any issue in the dispute between the parties concerned. But the Appellate Court misconstrued the direction and did not consider the evidence which are already on record in deciding the appeal. Non consideration of the evidence which are already on record has resulted in an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and accordingly, the judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court is liable to be set aside. I find substance in the submission of Mr. Khondoker Mahbubuddin Ahmed.

28. Mr. Khondoker has next argued alternatively, that the trial Court was fully justified in decreeing the suit on the basis of pleading of adverse possession and a prayer made to the effect, Mr. Khondoker submits that the Appellate Court having failed to avert to that aspect of the judgment of the trial Court has also committed an error of law in deciding the appeal and there has been failure of justice. The Appellate Court in its judgment has stated that since that claim of the plaintiffs are mainly based on pattas settlement obtained from Profulla and since the plaintiffs failed to prove the amicable settlement the plaintiff cannot get declaration in his favour as prayed for on the basis of adverse possession. It is on record that the plaintiffs in their pleading in paragraph 9 of the plaint has set up an alternative claim of title by adverse possession followed by a prayer in para 'Ka' of the prayer portion, and the trial Court decreed the suit on the basis of adverse possession on consideration of evidence of PWs. 1-9.

<u>29. I have given careful consideration of the evidence of PWs as well as DWs. The plaintiffs though have set out in paragraph 9 of the plaint an alternative claim of title on the basis of adverse possession nevertheless the plaintiffs have not led any specific evidence with regard to adverse possession except to say that PWs have claimed to have possessed the suit pond continuously for more than 20/25 years. But there is no evidence that they were possessing openly to the knowledge of the rightful owners. The plaintiffs claim over the suit pond is on the basis of pattas given by Profulla and by purchase from Dudu Mia. Therefore, the case of adverse possession as required under law has not been made out. On this point Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant No. 1. Opposite party has placed reliance on the decision of P Lakshmi Reddy vs. L Lakshmi Reddy reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 314 wherein it has been held that the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that it is in possession adverse to the competitor. It has been further held that it is well settled that in order to establish adverse possession of one co-heir as against another it is not enough to show that one out of them is in sole possession and enjoyment of the profits of the properties. Ouster of the non-possessing co-heir by the co-heir in possession who claims his possession to be adverse, should be made out. The possession of one co-heir is considered in law as possession of all the co-heirs. When one co-heir is found to be in possession of the properties it is presumed to be on the basis of joint title. The co-heir in possession cannot render his possession adverse to the other co-heirs, not in possession, merely by any secret hostile animus on his own part in derogation of the other co-heirs title. It is a settled rule of law that as between co-heirs there must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to constitute ouster. Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury submits that there is no evidence of open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of others. In this particular case he submits that the basis of the claim of the plaintiffs is clearly amicable settlement and taking pattas settlement from one of the co-sharers of Girish Chandra Mohajan. He submits that the result of the case depends on as to whether there has been in fact an amicable partition of properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan. I find force in the submission of Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury. The plaintiffs did not make out a case of adverse possession inasmuch as there is no evidence on record as to publicity and in extent to show that the plaintiffs were possessing adversely against the competitors.</u>

30. The definite case of the plaintiffs is that, ever since their obtaining the patta settlement from Profulla they are in possession of the suit pond. Since I have already held that there are enough evidence on record to come to a finding that there has been amicable partition of the properties of Girish Chandra Mohajan, the settlement obtained by the plaintiffs from Profulla by pattas is valid and legal and the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree as prayed for on the basis of pattas Ext. 2 and 2(A). Besides, the circumstantial evidence is also in favour of the plaintiffs. Nobody contested the appeal except the defendant No.1 No one is coming to contest the revision except the defendant No.1, who alleged to have purchased to the extent of one ganda from Manindra. In that view of the matter I am inclined to hold that the judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court is liable to be set aside and the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree as prayed for on the basis of settlement by registered pattas Exts.2 and 2 (A) and by purchase from Dudu Mia and not by adverse possession.

31. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with no order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 7-7-86 passed by the court of Subordinate Judge, Patiya in Other Appeal No. 50 of 1967 are set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the 2nd Court of Munsif, Patiya Chittagong in Title Suit, No. 60 of 1965 affirmed on reasons set forth hereinabove.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 198 of 1975.
lawyer:
Nurul Huq, Advocate ----- For Appellants.
No one ----- For Respondent.
parties:
Fazlu Molla and others ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Shamsul Hoque Molla ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.:- This appeal at the instance of the defendants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26.4.73 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 58 of 1971 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 14.1.71 passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Gopalgonj in Title Suit No. 135 of 1969.

2. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the deceased Ganzer Molla, father of defendant Nos. 1 to 3 and his wife defendant No.4 filed Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 in the court of the Subordinate Judge against the plaintiff and others. Plaintiff appeared in that suit and filed a written statement but ultimately that suit was compromised out of court between the plaintiff and the aforesaid Ganzer Molla and his wife and that suit was decreed in terms of the petition of compromise or solenama. That solenama provided that the present plaintiff relinquished his claim in respect of 1.04 acres of suit land of that Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 and plaintiffs of that suit agreed to execute and register a kabala in respect of 0.60 acre of their other land as consideration of that Solenama within a month from the date of compromise. Further case of the plaintiff is, that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 took delivery of possession of the said 1.04 acres of land from the present plaintiff but they did not execute and register kabala in favour of the present plaintiff in respect of the aforesaid 0.60 acre of land (suit land of the present suit) in spite of repeated demands of the present plaintiff. Subsequently, said Ganzer Molla died leaving defendants 1 to 4 as his legal heirs. So the plaintiff demanded execution and registration of the kabala from the present defendants on 20th Ashar, 1376 BS for the last time, but his demand having been refused he filed Title Suit No. 135 of 1969 for specific performance for getting a kabala.

3. Defendant No. 1 alone appeared and contested the suit by filing a written statement denying material allegations of the plaint and stating, inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in the present form. Further case of the defendant No. 1 is that the plaintiff obtained the alleged compromise decree in Title Suit No. 179 by practising fraud upon the court. The suit land belonged to Ganzer Molla predecessor of the defendant who possessed the same as his heir. Ganzer Molla and his wife present defendant No. 4, did not file Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 against the present plaintiff and others and there was no reason to file such a suit and also there was no reason on the part of the defendant No. 1 as his first son not to know about that suit. The present plaintiff by false personification through his own man had filed that suit and by practising fraud upon the court obtained a compromise decree on the basis of solenama dated 1.8.66 illegally including the lands which were not subject matter of that suit by forging signature of Ganzer Molla and the present defendant did not dare to file any suit during life time of Ganzer Molla and kept the forged solenama suppressed during life time of Ganzer Molla and filed the suit after his death to injure the defendant.

4. Trial Court dismissed the suit by a judgment dated 14.1.71 and the Court of Appeal below reversed the said judgment and decree by the impugned judgment dated 26.4.73.

5. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submitted that the soleh decree in Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 was not a legal one and as-such court of appeal below acted illegally in passing the decree on the basis of the same. He further submitted that the court of appeal below acted illegally in holding that the suit was maintainable and in reversing the finding of the trial Court in that respect.

It is admitted position that the suit land measuring 0.60 acre was not the subject matter of earlier Title Suit No. 179 of 1965. Trial Court held that the soleh decree passed in Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 is a nullity as the same was obtained by practising fraud upon the court and further held that the suit is not maintainable in its present form.

6. Fraud is a mixed question of fact and law. Court of appeal below on consideration of the evidence came to the finding "I am inclined to believe that solenama filed in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 was genuine and it was filed by Ganzer Molla and his wife respondent No. 4 of this appeal and as such she did not come forward to deny the solenama in question nor does she contest this appeal before this court Having regard to all these facts and circumstances and the evidence on record I find that Ganzer Molla and his wife who is respondent No. 4 in this appeal, filed Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 which suit was compromised in terms of the solenama filed by them with the present plaintiff and by that compromise Ganzer Molla and his wife contracted to transfer the suit land to the present plaintiff.

7. In arriving at the aforesaid finding of fact court of appeal below discussed all the evidence on record, facts and circumstances of the case and that being a finding of fact Mr. Huq finds it difficult to assail the same. Trial Court without assigning any reason held that the suit was not maintainable. But the court of appeal below after considering conflicting decisions of different High Courts of the sub-continent held that the suit was maintainable rejecting contention of the learned Advocate of the defendants that an execution proceeding and not a suit was the appropriate remedy for the plaintiff to enforce the compromise decree in respect of the stipulation to transfer 0.60 acres of lands which was not subject matter of the suit in which the compromise decree in question was passed.

<u>8. We have already noticed that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 179 of 1965 on the basis of a petition of compromise in which the defendant No. 4 of that suit relinquished his right, title and interest in favour of the plaintiffs of that suit in respect of 1.04 acres of the suit land of that suit in consideration of plaintiffs of that suit agreeing to transfer 0.60 areas of their lands which was not the subject matter of that suit in favour of the defendant No. 4 of that suit There is no doubt that the said compromise, decree in respect of 1.04 acres of the suit land was effective part of the decree and can be enforced by putting the decree into execution. Question is whether the stipulation in the said compromise decree in respect of 0.60 acres of land which was not the subject matter of that suit could be enforced by putting the decree into execution. Majority view of the High Courts of the Sub-continent including the Calcutta High Court is that the part of a compromise decree not covered by the frame of the suit i.e. extraneous to the main suit, is not an operative part of such decree and cannot be enforced by putting the decree into execution. Learned Advocate for the appellant failed to point out to any other decision on the question. I, therefore, find nothing wrong in the said finding of the court of appeal below.</u>

<u>9. When contending parties to a suit compromise their dispute in respect of the subject matter of the suit in consideration of something not covered by the subject matter of the suit such consideration forming a stipulation in the petition of compromise cannot be effective part of the compromise decree but such stipulation being part of a valid contract can be enforced by a separate suit though not by putting the decree into execution. (See the case of Rani Hemanta Kumari Vs. Midnapur Zamindari Co. Ltd. 24 CWN 177 (PC) and Md. ldris Mia Vs. Abdul Motaleb, 17, DLR 599.</u>

In the above facts and circumstances and discussions made above I find no merit in the appeal

10. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below is hereby affirmed.

Let the LC records be sent down to the court below expeditiously.

End.
