case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 6th November, 1985 passed by the High Court Division, Sylhet Bench in Second Appeal No.1449 of 1968.)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal, J. : This is a plaintiffs appeal by leave which arises out of the judgment and decree dated 6 November 1985 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Sylhet) in Second Appeal No. 1449 of 1968 setting aside the concurrent decree of the courts below and dismissing the plaintiffs suit, Title Suit No. 89 of 1964.

2. The said suit in the Additional Court of the Assistant Judge. Sylhet Sadar, was one for declaration of title and khas possession in respect of -/4/- annas share (schedule 2) out of schedule 1 land. Admittedly schedule 1 land belonged to Ramanath Ghosh Estate having 1-/12/- annas share and Gobinda Jieu (deity) having-4/- annas share. Plaintiffs case is that he took settlement of the said -/4/- annas share from Jagannath Das Baishnab, shebait of the deity in 1357 BS and went into possession. Admittedly the defendants took settlement of the -/12/- annas share from Ramanath Ghosh Estate in 1321 BS and have been in possession therein since then. Plaintiff alleged that the defendants got the schedule 2 land recorded in their names and dispossessed him forcibly therefrom on 8th Baisakh, 1368 BS =21.4.1961. He filed a criminal case against the defendants in which they filed a farog (rent receipt) fraudulently obtained from the shebait of the Gobinda Jieu and the Criminal Case was dismissed. The Shebait served a notice upon the defendants to take refund of the amount paid by them uponretuming the rent-receipt. The defendants did not take any settlement from the shebait and thus were in forcible possession of the suit land. Hence the suit.

3. Defendants 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the plaintiffs case. Their own case inter alia. is that some of the present defendants and the predecessors of some other defendants took settlement of -/12/- annas share of schedule 1 land from Ramanath Ghosh Estate by executing a registered Kabuliyat dated 24th Jaistha, 1321 BS (certified copy Ext. B) but possessed the entire land of schedule 1 openly and as of right since then by amicable partition among themselves and growing crops etc. and thus they acquired title by adverse possession. Their further case is that the disputed -/4/- annas share originally belonged to one Jagat Chandra Gupta. The shebait of Gobinda Jieu demanded rent from the defendants claiming that he had purchased the share of Jagat Chandra and accordingly they paid rent to the shebait for 1360-67 BS and got a farog (Ext. A). The plaintiff in collusion with the shebait filed the criminal case which was dismissed. They plaintiff was never in possession of the suit land which was all along in the possession of the defendants ever since 1321 BS conferring title to them by adverse possession.

4. The learned Assistant Judge upon a consideration of the evidence and circumstances of the case found title with the plaintiff on the basis of his alleged settlement in 1357 BS from the shebait but it was also found that he had no possession in the suit land ever. that the defendants were in possession of the suit land from before but their possession did not become adverse against Gobinda Jieu, that schedule 1 land was never partitioned between the mirashdars of -/12/- annas share and -/4/- annas share and as such although the suit for declaration of title was maintainable but the prayer for khash possession was not. Accordingly, by judgment and decree dated 19.11.64, the suit was decreed declaring the plaintiff's right, title and interest in the suit land and giving him joint possession therein.

5. On appeal by the defendants, the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Sylhet, by judgment and decree dated 22.2.68, concurred with the findings of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal.

6. It may be observed that the trial Court refused to accept the defendants' case of adverse possession as it was not satisfied on evidence that the shebait knew about their possession (in -/4/- annas) from before and that they possessed the suit land as of right. It was further found that by paying rent to the shebait (by Ext. A) they admitted his interest which disproved their own case. The lower appellate Court made another finding that the defendants' possession in the suit land may be taken to be the constructive possession of the -/4/- annas owners.

7. In the second appeal taken by the defendants, a Single Judge of the High Court Division, as already noticed, by the impugned judgment and decree, set aside those of the courts below, allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit.

8. The High Court Division, inter alia, found that the plaintiff's predecessor had no constructive possession in the suit land and as such the suit is barred by limitation as the plaintiff or his predecessor did not file the suit within 12 years from the date of discontinuance of possession. It was also found that the defendants acquired title by adverse possession of the defendants in the undivided -/4/-annas share (belonging to Gobinda Jieu) was not for themselves but for their own landlords on the doctrine of "the tenant stealing for the landlord" and as such the co-sharer deity was in constructive possession of the suit land through its co-sharer landlords and further in view of the fact that the defendants paid rent to the shebait (PW 4) for 1360 BS to 1367 BS there could not be adverse possession against the deity or its tenant, the plaintiff. In support of this submission, Mr. Khondker relied upon the case of Umarani SarkerVs. Kamala Bala Dassi, 53 CWN 879.

<u>9. The first ground urged by Mr. Khondker as to the application of Article 144 of the Limitation Act instead of Article 142 as applied by the learned Judge of the High Court Division appears to be of little practical consequence inasmuch as it has been found that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession. If this finding remains then the suit will be indisputably barred also under Article 144. Therefore, the main question for consideration is whether the finding as to adverse possession was correct and this brings us to the second ground on which the appeal was mainly pressed. Even so, it may be observed that the question of limitation falls to be decided initially on the plaintiffs own case as set out in the plaint. In the present case, the plaintiff asserted that he was in possession of the suit land upon taking settlement in 1357 BS but was dispossessed by the defendants in 1368 BS and as such Article 142 applies in terms. The courts below, however, disbelieved the plaintiffs case of alleged possession and dispossession but at the same time found his title to the suit land. In such a case, the plaintiff can get recovery of possession only if the title was not lost by adverse possession of the defendants for over twelve years. As the defendants have specifically pleaded adverse possession, the suit will have to be decided on the basis as to when the possession of the defendants became adverse to the plaintiff. In this way, Article 144 gets attracted subsequently although the initial onus was upon the plaintiff to prove his possession within twelve years before the institution of the suit.</u>

10. Coming to the main contention of Mr. Khondker, it may be recalled that the defendants' case is that they started possessing the entire land of schedule 1 (comprising the disputed -/4/- annas share of Gobinda Jieu) openly and as of right, right from their own settlement (of -/12/- annas share) in 1321 BS. The courts below concurrently believed the possession of the defendants but at the same time found that it was not adverse to the deity. This finding has been reversed by the High Court Division. Mr. Khondker contends citing 53 CWN 879 that the defendants by encroaching upon the -/4/- annas share of the deity were possessing the same on behalf of their own landlords on the doctrine referred to above and as such this possession of the said landlords was constructive possession of the other landlord, i.e. Gobinda Jieu. The possession, therefore, cannot become adverse.

<u>11. In the case cited by Mr. Khondker, a Single Judge referred to ILR 10 Cal 820 (1884), Nuddyarchand Vs. Meajan, where Chief Justice Sir Richard Garth observed that there is no doubt whatever that by the English Law, an encroachment made by a tenant upon land adjoining to, or even in the neighborhood of, his holding, is presumed, in the absence of strong evidence to the contrary, to be made for the benefit of the landlord. It was also observed that "And this rule applies to all land so encroached upon, whether the landlord has any interest in it or not." If a tenant during his tenancy encroaches upon the land of a third person, and holds it with his own tenure until the expiration of the tenancy, he is considered to have made the encroachment, not for his own benefit, but for that of his landlord; and if he has acquired a title against the third person by an adverse possession, he has acquired it for his landlord, and not for himself, See Kingsmill Vs. Millard 11 Ex., 313; Andrews Vs. Mailes 2 E & B, 349 and this doctrine appears to have been adopted here in the case of Goroo Doss Roy Vs. Issur Chunder Bose 32 WR 247 as well as in other cases. "Tenant stealing for the landlord" has been held to be the doctrine upon which the principle enunciated is based.</u>

12. It will be seen that the principle is not of an absolute nature and the presumption in favour of the landlord may be displaced by proper evidence and circumstances in a particular case. In 10 Cal 820 the plaintiffs sought to recover possession of the suit land as part of their ancestral taluq under defendant No. 2. Defendant No. 1 contended that plaintiffs had never any possession in the suit land and he (defendant No. 1) had been put into possession by defendant No. 2 who was his Zemindar. The Munsiff found that the land did not belong to the plaintiffs taluq but they had occupied the land for more than twenty years having made encroachment upon the land of defendant No. 2 and thus acquired a valid title. The Subordinate Judge reversed the said decision holding that the plaintiffs' own case having failed they cannot be permitted to turn round and plead adverse possession against their own admitted landlord. The High Court while making reference to the aforesaid principle of English law also observed:

"It is true, that by the English Law, if it could be distinctly proved that the tenant made the encroachment adversely to his landlord, an adverse possession for 12 years might then give the tenant a title by limitation; and probably that would be so in this country."

"The only possible ground, as it seems to us, upon which a person in the plaintiffs position could claim to retain possession of the land so encroached upon, would be, that the landlord had either expressly or impliedly acquiesced in the encroachment; or, in other words, that he had allowed the tenant to add the area encroached upon to his holding."

13. In the case before us the defendants specifically pleaded adverse possession since 1321 BS, that is, they had been on the land for more than 35 years before the alleged settlement of the plaintiff. There is no evidence whatsoever that during this long period any of the landlords, either Ramanath Ghosh Estate or Gobinda Jieu, made any demand or raised any objection with regard to the defendants' possession of the suitland. There is no material or circumstance on record to show that the defendants possessed the suit land in any manner except in assertion of their own right against all others. In view of the findings of fact made even by the courts below, we find it impossible to hold that the defendants were in possession of the suit land on behalf of their landlords. The courts below although found that the defendants were in possession of the suit land from before by growing boro paddy etc, their possession was held to be not adverse mainly because of an erroneous assumption that there ought to have been evidence to show that the shebait knew about their possession from before.

<u>14. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the Secretary of State for India Vs. Debendra Lal Khan 38 CWN 285 pointed out that for adverse possession the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor. It is not necessary that adverse possession should be shown to have been brought to the knowledge of the competitor and that it is sufficient that the possession is overt and without any attempt at concealment so that the person against whom time is running out, if he exercises due vigilance, aware of what is happening. The defendants were possessing the suit land overtly and without any attempt at concealment for over 35 years and the shebait, if vigilant, which, it appears, he was not, ought to have known that time was running cut against him.</u>

<u>15. The allegation that the defendants paid rent to the shebait for 1360-67 BS which according to them was paid under duress makes no difference in determining the question of adverse possession because their possession become adverse in law long before the alleged date of payment of rent. The trial Court itself found that Ext. A (rent receipt in question) was not issued under normal circumstances and there was some foul play over it. Therefore, there cannot be any valid argument against the defendants on the basis of Ext. A.</u>

16. It is clear that the defendants' case of  adverse possession was well-founded and the submission that their possession was the constructive possession of the plaintiffs vendor has no legs to stand upon.

17. The learned Judge of the High Court Division besides 'finding that the defendants acquired title by adverse possession also found that the courts below committed error of law and procedure in finding settlement by the shebait (PW 4) in favour of the plaintiff which has affected the merit of the case, because, the learned Judge says "From a look at the farags Ext 2(a)-2(c) it seems that these farags are written in fresh ink which cast a great doubt as to the genuineness of the alleged settlement, specially when the same shebait granted the farag Ext.4 with respect to the same land to the defendants as well, "It was also held that when the shebait (PW 4) did not or could not prove any legal necessity for permanent settlement of the suit land with the plaintiffs, they did not derive any title thereto even assuming that the deity had any existing right in the land at the time of alleged settlement with the plaintiff. These findings have not been the subject matter of the present appeal as no leave was obtained in that behalf. Be that as it may, there being no substance in the contention raised relating to the finding of adverse possession made by the High Court Division, the appeal cannot succeed in any case.

In the result, therefore, the appeal is dismissed with cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 158 of 1969 arising out of a suit for realisation of compensation for damage to the plaintiffs reputation allegedly caused by the defendant by publication and circulation of a defamatory petition addressed to the three Governor of East Pakistan.

2. The plaintiffs case, in brief, is that the plaintiff was an Advocate of the High Court of East Pakistan as well as the Supreme Court of Pakistan for about 16 years and he is still practising as a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. He has his own residential house at 44, Purana Paltan Road, Dhaka. He is also a senior Lecturer of the Law College, Dacca and previously he served as a part-time lecturer of the Dacca University for about 10 years. He was elected twice as Member of the Dacca University Senate by the registered graduates of the University and at present he is a Member, Faculty of Law of Dacca University for several years. This year also he has been elected as a Member of the Dhaka University Senate by the registered graduates of the Dhaka University, previously he was twice elected as a Regional Secretary of all Pakistan Bar Association for East Pakistan Region. He was also elected as an Assistant Secretary, East Pakistan Bar Association. The plaintiff hails from Village Koundia, PS Kowkhali of Pirojpur Sub-Division of the District of Barisal. His father late Dr. Abdul Karim was a medical practitioner of Kawkhali and a Member of Pirojpur Local Board. He was also a member of the Union Board and Secretary of Kaundia High School for several years. The plaintiffs uncle late Alhaj Mvi. Abdul Aziz was the first graduate of Kawkhali PS. His son Dr. AFM Huq was a Lt. Col. of the Pakistan Army and he is now attached to the Bangladesh Army. The younger brother of the plaintiff namely, Abdul Matin is also a graduate. Mrs. Anwara Akhtar, the plaintiffs wife is a Professor and the Head of the Department of Home Economics of the Eden Girls College, Dacca. The plaintiff has two sons of whom the elder one is Mr. Iqbal Sobhan who secured First Class in MA in Economics and was a member of the Civil Service of Pakistan. After independence he was absorbed in the Bangladesh Civil Service and is now undergoing PHD course in the University of Maryland in USA. The second son of the plaintiff namely Azmal Sobhan is an MBBS of the Dhaka University and is now undergoing higher studies in USA. The Plaintiffs father-in-law late Khan Bahadur A Jalil Khan was a Zamindar of Vikrampur and a Member of the then Bangladesh Civil Service. The plaintiff was also nominated by the Deputy Director of PI Khulna Range as a member of the KG Union High School, Kowkhali from the category of the distinguished persons of the locality. So the plaintiff holds an important position of respect, honors and dignity and he has the reputation of being honest lawyer and a man of independent spirit and integrity in professional, educational and other circles of Dhaka and elsewhere in Bangladesh.

3. The defendants filed a contempt petition against the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal, SDO. Barisal and the plaintiffs younger brother Abdul Matin before the Humble High Court. Dhaka in 1966 making some defamatory allegations against the plaintiff as well.

4. Thereupon plaintiff filed a criminal case in the Court of SDO Dhaka against the defendants u/s. 500 BPC being Case No. 1117A/67 in which the defendants were summoned. Ultimately the defendants apologised to the plaintiff by expressing regret and requested the plaintiff to compound the case to which the plaintiff agreed and the case was accordingly disposed of on 10.8.68 on prayer of both parties. Even after the disposal of that case the defendants who had litigation with the plaintiffs brother Mr. Abdul Matin, continued to bear grudge against the plaintiff and began to defame the plaintiff and his brother at Kowkhali and other places. Ultimately these defendants addressed a petition to the Governor of the then East Pakistan dated 21.10.68 making defamatory allegation against the plaintiff and copies thereof were served on 9 persons namely;

1)	To the Chief Secretary. Govt. of East Pakistan, Dacca.

2)	To the IGP.

3)	To the DIG SD East Pakistan. Malibagh, Dacea.

4)	To DIG. Khulna,

5)	To DC Bakerganj.

6) To the SP of -do-

7) To the SP Dacca.

8)	The District Anti-Corruption Bakerganj.

9)	To the Sub-Divisional Officer, Pirojpur, District- Bakerganj.

5.	In order to lend weight to the said allegations these defendants obtained by fraudulent representation the recommendations of some Basic Democrats on the margin of the said petition and t, sent, the same to the then Governor of East Pakistan. Furthermore they also circulated the said petition to the IGP, East Pak. and caused an enquiry into the allegations contained in the petition through his departmental officer and ultimately the SDPO, Pirojpur held an enquiry at Kawkhali in presence of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 on 2.5.69 and submitted a report to the IGP, East Pakistan, Dhaka in May, 1969. The statements and allegations made in that petition are absolutely false and malicious and they are highly defamatory and as such harmed the plaintiffs fame and reputation and lowered him in the estimation of the people. The plaintiff has been badly defamed by the statements contained in paragraphs 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18 and part of paragraph 19 of the petition which have been quoted in the schedule appended to the plaint. The plaintiff has also suffered consequential mental agony. The plaintiff has therefore claimed Taka 10,500.00 as compensation for the damage to the reputation caused by the defendants and prays for a decree for that amount.

6. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statements. The defence case is as follows:

7. The defendants are permanent residents of Kawkhali in the District of Barisal. They purchased a property at Amrajuri Mouza of Kawkhali PS in a certificate sale and they got possession of a portion of the said property, while the remaining portion was under requisition by the Govt. Then at the request of these defendants the said property was de-requisitioned but even after that defendants did not get possession because the original allotted namely the Circle Officer, Development, was to be given an alternative accommodation. Thereafter all on a sudden the SDO, Pirojpur went to the suit property taking some police force and gave possession of that property to M/s. Karim Rice Mill of which the plaintiff and his brother Abdul Matin were the owners. Thereupon these defendants approached the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal. Then they filed a Officer, Writ Petition before the then Hon'ble High Court. Dhaka and the said case went upto the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in which the defendants got decision in their favour. The plaintiff filed a sale set aside case in the name of the certificate debtor which went upto the Board of Revenue. This plaintiff moved the appeal before the Board of Revenue which was dismissed. Even after that due to ill luck these defendants did not get possession of the said property. Not only that the plaintiff filed a suit being TS No. 110/68 by his uncle Abdul Malek in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Pirojpur against these defendants for the selfsame property of Amrajuri. Out of that suit Mr. Abdul Malek filed Civil Revision No. 990/68 in the Hon'ble High Court, Dhaka at the instance of this plaintiff which is still pending. Furthermore that Abdul Malek filed another suit being TS No. 378/68 in the 3rd Court of Munsif at Dhaka against these defendants and the said suit was looked after and conducted by this puff. Thus the plaintiff started many other litigations, both civil and criminal-against these defendants with a view to harass the latter. It is true that this plaintiff started a criminal case u/s 500 BPC against these defendants which was ultimately withdrawn; but it is not at all a fact that these defendants apologised to the plaintiff or expressed any regret in that criminal case. Besides all these litigations these defendants had many other confrontations with the plaintiff at Kowkhali of which the remarkable one took place on 3.10.68. On that day the plaintiff threatened the defendants with consequences by starting different litigations. The next incident took place on 20.10.68 when the defendant No. 2 was residing at Tripti Hotel at Dhaka. On that day 4 policemen, two in uniform and the two in plain dress went to that Hotel in the evening and enquired about defendant No. 2 when this defendant No. 2 was away from the Hotel. About an hour after that these policemen again went to that Hotel when the defendant No. 2 was there. Defendant No. 2 in the meantime got a scent of conspiracy being hatched up against him. He also recognised. Mr. Israil, an Inspector of Police who happens to be a close relation of the plaintiff as one of the member of the police team. The defendant No. 2 thereupon reported the arrival of the police to the other inmates of the Hotel who locked him up in a room from outside. The police again enquired about this defendant and then went away. Thereafter the defendant No. 2 left the Hotel then and there and went straight to Kawkhali via Barisal and got this alleged petition drafted which was recommended by an MPA and several Chairmen and Members of the Union Council and addressed the same to the Governor. These statements made in that petition are all true and were not made out of any malice nor with any motive to defame the plaintiff. As a matter of fact these were made in good faith for bringing the facts to the notice of the authorities for the sole purpose of their safety and protection. It is not at all a fact that the defendants at all circulated any copy of that petition at Kowkhali or anywhere else. The plaintiff has not at all been defamed and he has not sustained any damage whatsoever by that petition. So he is not entitled to any compensation as claimed in the suit.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record both oral and documentary dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by that the plaintiff preferred this appeal before this Court.

9. The material point for determination in this appeal is whether by the publication and circulation of the letter Ext. 3, the plaintiffs reputation has suffered in the estimation of general public and on that account he is entitled to compensation for damages.

10. It is admitted that exhibit 3, the impugned petition was written by the defendants and sent to the then Governor of East Pakistan. It is also admitted that the copy of Exhibit 3 was also circulated to the Chief Secretary, Govt. of East Pakistan, Dhaka, to the IGP, to the DIG SB East Pakistan, Malibagh, Dhaka, to the DIG Khulna, to the DC Bakerganj, to the SP of Bakerganj, Dist. Anti-Corruption Office, Bakerganj and to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Pirojpur, District-Bakerganj. The plaintiff's contention is that by circulation of this defamatory petition to all these authorities the plaintiff's reputation has seriously suffered, and these statements were made by the defendants with an intention to defame the plaintiff in the estimation of public in his locality and to the people in general. As against this, the defendants' contention is that all these statements made in the petition are true and those were not aimed either to defame the plaintiff nor with any malicious motive.

11. Before going into the merits of the case, we will refer to the relevant offending paragraphs of the letter Ext. 3 as has been mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. The schedule of the plaint reads as follows:

Schedule

"Extract from the petition under the signature of the defendants addressed to the Governor, East Pakistan with copies forwarded to others.

(i) In paragraph 12 of the petition the following words:

"That Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan falsely started GR Case No. 117 of 1967 under section 500 PPC against him before the learned SDO (s) Dacca and ultimately the case has been withdrawn by him in the month of August, 1968".

(ii) In paragraph 13,

"That Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan threatened us with dire consequences at Kowkhali on 5.10.68 alleging that he will finish us by starting false case against us under section 395 PPC and under the provisions of the DPR either by themselves or by the party men."

(iii) In paragraph 14.

"That the said Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan also lodged a false GD Entry at Kowkhali PS against us".

(iv) In paragraph 15,

"That Inspector of Police Dhaka is closely related to Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan and while on 20.10.68 I, Parimal Kumar Dey, was staying at Dhaka I got a scent at the instance of Advocate Abdus Sobhan, the said Inspector is moving to involve me in a Criminal case whether under the provisions of the DPR or PPC or Sea Customs Act or Foreign Exchange Regulation Act or Smuggling Act".

(v) In paragraph 17.

"That we have land dispute with Advocate Abdus Sobhan and it is quite impossible on our part to follow even the intrigues and machinations adopted by them against us."

(vi) In paragraph 18.

"That Advocate Abdus Sobhan is moving heaven and earth against us and he and his other relations are trying to stop our movement towards Dhaka so that our cases go uncared for

(vii) "That we apprehend serious type of troubles from the side of Advocate Abdus Sobhan."

(viii) Concluding paragraph.

"From the imminent troubles created by the said Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan."

12. Mr. Abdus Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing before us submits that the findings of the Trial Court that the statements made in Exhibit 3 are true is contrary to the evidence on record and the Trial Court without assessing the evidence both oral and documentary in its proper perspective has come to findings as to the truth of the allegations on pure surmises and conjectures.

13. The learned Advocate further submits that all the statements made in exhibit 3 arc false and concocted and those were made with a malice just to humiliate the plaintiff in the estimation of the people of the locality in particular and all the people in general. He further submits that the publication and circulation of this petition to all important functionaries of the Govt. including the then Governor of Province clearly shows that the defendants deliberately wanted to injure the reputation of the plaintiff in the estimation of right thinking members of the society.

14. We will presently refer to the oral and documentary evidences of record to see the truth or otherwise of the statements made in the petition itself.

15. The plaintiff in this case examined 7 witnesses and the defendants examined 8 witnesses. Apart from this oral evidence some documents were filed in this case.

16. PW 1 Abdus Sobhan is the plaintiff in this case. He testified that he is a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and comes of a very respectable family from the District of Bakerganj. The plaintiffs father was a medical practitioner and his wife is also a Professor and all his sons are highly educated and well settled in life. This witness testified that he filed a petition under section 500 BPC in the Court of SDO, Dhaka against the defendants and on the date of final hearing the defendants expressed regret in writing and withdrew the allegation for which he compromised the case. Exhibit 1 is the petition of compromise and Exhibit 2 is the order passed in that case. From Exhibit 2 it appears that the parties compromised the case outside the Court and the accused were acquitted. This witness further testified that Exhibit 3 was sent to all relevant authorities to the Government just to injure him in the estimation of public. He further stated that false, baseless and malicious statements were made and circulated out of grudge against him. In cross-examination he admitted that one Mr. Abdul Malek filed Title Suit No. 110 of 1965 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Pirojpur against these defendants. He also stated that he did not remember if he got Title Suit No. 378 of 1968 filed by his Junior Abdul Razzaq in the local 3rd Court of Munsif, Dhaka. He further stated that it is false that he tried to bound down the defendants under section 107 CrPC. This witness also stated in cross-examination that he has no dispute with this defendant over the Rice Mill or over the property on which the mill was situated. The plaintiff deposed that he filed the money suit claiming Tk. 10,500.00 as damages as the plaintiffs reputation suffered due to publication and circulation of this defamatory petition.

PW 2 Khan Bahadur Naziruddin Ahmed, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh proved exhibits 1 and 2 and testified that the case was withdrawn as the matter was compromised. PW 3 Md. Sarwar Miah, a retired Senior Forest Ranger who comes from the same village of the plaintiff, deposed that the plaintiff, is a very reputed and influential person at Barisal and Dhaka and in first part of 1969 this witness came to know at Kaukhali that the defendants filed an application ·to the Governor against the plaintiff. This witness stated that Abdul Majid Mridha, the Chairman of Kowkhali Union read the petition exhibit 3 before him. This witness was very much aggrieved to see that the plaintiffs reputation is being lowered in such a way in his own village. In cross-examination this witness admitted that plaintiffs brother Abdul Matin is the owner of Karim Rice Mill. PW 4 Abdul Mannan Mia, a retired clerk of the Barisal Civil Court also testified that in the later part of 1968 he went to the SDO's office at Pirojpur and heard that some clerks were discussing about the petition filed by the defendants against the plaintiff. This witness also himself read the petition and had a very bad impression about the plaintiff and found that the plaintiff has been harassed in this way. PW 5 Joynal Abedin also heard about the petition from the dispensary of Doctor Dhirendra Babu and heard about the contents of the petition. This witness is known to both the plaintiff and the defendants. PW 6 Md. Motiur Rahman, a Director, Physical Education, Dhaka University testified that he knows the plaintiff for about 25 years as the plaintiff is a very reputed man being an Advocate, member of Dhaka University Senate. He also testified that this plaintiff comes from a good family and has got great respect in his locality and Dhaka. PW 7 KB Abdur Rashed, a retired Deputy Director of Public Instruction also testified that the plaintiff was known to him for 15-16 years and plaintiffs brother was Deputy Magistrate and the plaintiff is an Advocate in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, This is all the oral evidence adduced in the case by the plaintiff.

17. DW 1 Parimal Kumar Dey is the defendant No. 2 and a permanent resident of the Kaukhali and co-villager of the plaintiff. He stated that they purchased the property at Amrajari, Mouza of Kaukhali PS in 1964. They got possession in some portion of the plot and some portion was under requisition and they could not get possession. Even after de-requisition they did not get possession of the plot and possession was given to Karim Rice Mill, the owner of which Rice Mill is the brother of the plaintiff. He also testified that the plaintiff filed a case in the name of judgment-debtor. This witness admitted about the filing of the case under section 500 BPC by the plaintiff. He admitted that they filed this petition Exhibit 3 to the Governor and sent copies thereof to the different law enforcing agencies of the country. He also testified that on 20.10.68 when he was residing at Tripti Hotel at Dhaka one Md. Israil, Inspector of Police, DAB came to arrest him who happens to be a close relation to the plaintiff. He admitted that Abdul Malek filed Title Suit No. 378 of 1968 against him. This witness stated in cross-examination that he had no knowledge as to whether a criminal case under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was started on the basis of GD, Entry against Mr. Amir Hossain and Ali Hossain and they were bound down in that proceeding.

18. DW 2 Ranjit Kumar Roy, DW 3 Ramendra Ranjan Chowdhury, DW 4 MA Nabi and DW 5 Abdur Rahim have only testified with regard to the fact that on 20.10.68 DW 1. Parimal Kumar was a resident in Tripti Hotel at Dhaka. These witnesses have only stated that police came in search of DW 1 and they having not found him went away. DW 6 Amir Hossain is a resident of Dasherkathi under Kaukhali Police Station. He testified that Abdul Matin is the brother of the plaintiff and Abdul Malek is the uncle of the plaintiff. This witness admitted that he was involved in several cases. This witness admitted in cross-examination that the plaintiff did not file any case against Minhajuddin but his brother filed that case. He admitted that the plaintiff did not file any case against Munsur Ali. This witness stated that the plaintiff had litigation against Harolal Kundu. He also admitted that he had no knowledge as to whether the plaintiff filed any case against the defendants. DW 7 Abdul Latif Howlader testified that about 5 years ago the plaintiff and his brother Abdul Matin threatened Parimal with litigation in his presence. In cross-examination he stated that when he went to get paddy husked in the latter part of Kartic about 5-1/2 years ago standing on the road he heard about the threat given by the plaintiff. DW 8 Taheruddin testified that the plaintiff has no good reputation in our locality. In cross-examination this witness admitted that he is a cultivator and he admitted that he stayed in the same hotel where the defendants were putting up.

19. Now in the light of the evidence on record as has been discussed above, we are to see whether the findings of the Trial Court that the statements made in these paragraphs are true is correct or not. From the oral evidence of PWs 1, 2 and DW 1 and Exhibits 1 and 2 it is found that the case No. 117/67 under section 500 BPC was withdrawn as defendants expressed regret and withdrawn the allegation and the case was compromised and withdrawn accordingly. So the statement in paragraph 12 of the petition that Advocate Mr. Abdus Sobhan falsely started this case is not correct. In paragraph 13 of the petition it has been stated that Advocate Abdus Sobhan threatened on 5.10.68 that he would start a false case under section 395 BPC, and under provision of the DPR either by themselves or by the party men. With regard to this statement nothing has been specifically said by DW 1 and other witnesses. Thus the defendants could not adduce any evidence with regard to the statements in paragraph 13 that the plaintiff told DW 1 that we would start case against him. In paragraph 14, it is stated that Advocate Abdus Sobhan lodged a GD Entry at Kowkhali PS against the defendants. A reference to exhibit 10 series show that the case was filed by Md. Abdul Matin, the brother of the plaintiff against one Mir Amir Hossain and Syed All Hossain and not against this defendant. From Exhibit 10(B and C) it also appears that on enquiry the police found truth in the allegation against the persons and bound them for good behaviour and bond was furnished by Amir Hossain under section 107 of the CrPC. Thus the GD. Entry was not filed by Advocate Abdus Subhan but it was filed by one Abdul Matin who happens to be a brother of the plaintiff. Thus, the defendant made a false statement in paragraph 14.

<u>20. In paragraph 15 of Exhibit 3, the defendant stated that Inspector of Police Dhaka is related to Advocate Abdus Sobhan and the defendant No. 2 got a scent that the said Inspector is moving to involve this defendant in a criminal case at the instance of the plaintiff Advocate Abdus Sobhan either in the DPR or PPC or Sea Customs Act or Foreign Exchange Regulation Act or Smuggling Act. This statement is too vague because it is only the suspicion of the defendant No. 2 that the said Inspector is moving at the instance of the plaintiff Advocate Abdus Sobhan. The name of the said Police Inspector is not given in the written statement. From the evidence of DWs 2, 3, 4 and 5 we only find that on 20.10.68 one Police Inspector came, to Tripti hotel at Dhaka and inquired about defendant No. 2. In paragraph 17, the positive statement is that Advocate Abdus Sobhan had land dispute with the defendants and it is impossible on his part to follow even the intrigues and machinations adopted by them against the defendants. In fact the defendant could not adduce any evidence either oral or documentary to show that the plaintiff had any civil litigation with the defendants. Of course, the defendants adduced evidence to the effect that the plaintiffs brother and uncle had litigations with the defendants. In paragraph 18 they have stated that the plaintiff is moving heaven and earth against them and their relations and arc trying to stop their movements towards Dhaka so that their cases go uncared for. This statement is indeed very vague and the defendants could not adduce any evidence to show that there is any basis for such statement as made in the petition which circulated to the Governor and other relevant hi officials of the Government. In the said paragraph they also stated that they apprehend serious trouble from the side of the plaintiff in present and future.</u>

21. Thus on a careful consideration of the materials on record we find that the statements made in paragraphs 12, 13 and 14 are incorrect statements made by the defendants just to malign the plaintiff. With regard to the incident of 20.10.68 at Tripti Hotel at Dhaka, the evidence is that one Police Inspector came in the Hotel and beyond that there is nothing on record. Thus the story of the alleged incident on 20.10.68 may be true but there is nothing on record to infer that the Inspector came at the instance and behest of the plaintiff. In such circumstances the publication of this statement is surely unfounded and made with a motive. The other offending statements of paragraphs 17 and 18 are that the plaintiff is trying to obstruct the defendants in their legal pursuit, and also starting false case against them and creating present and future trouble for them. There is nothing on record in support of these statements. These allegations are also too vague and lack in any particulars.

<u>22. It is the established principle of law that truth is a complete defence to a civil action for libel. On a careful consideration of the entire evidence on record we have found earlier that the offending statements are true and those statements have been made, published and circulated with a malice or improper motive. It is on record that the plaintiff is a very respectable man in the social and his wife and children are highly educated and well-placed in society. The plaintiff himself is a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and by such publication and circulation of false and defamatory statements the plaintiffs reputation has definitely been injured in the estimation of right thinking people in society. Further from the evidence on record it has been found that the letter exhibit 3 was widely circulated in Dhaka and within the District of Barisal for which the plaintiff's reputation was definitely lowered in the estimation of his known-circle and to the members of the society in general. We also fail to understand why the defendant sent the letter to the then Governor of East Pakistan and other important functionaries of the Govt. It is difficult to hold what these authorities had got anything to do with these allegations as made in the petition. Wide publication and circulation of this letter definitely establishes malicious and improper motive of the defendants.</u>

23. Thus on a careful consideration of the materials on record we find that the statements made in the offending paragraphs were made in bad faith 1 and with a malice to humiliate and malign the plaintiff in the estimation of others. The learned Trial Judge without considering the positive evidence on-record on pure surmises and conjectures have found that the offending statements in the petition, exhibit 3 are true. There may be litigation with the plaintiffs brother and uncle but for that such defamatory statements cannot be made in the application against the plaintiff himself and by publication and circulation of that to the Governor and other important functionaries of the Government the plaintiffs prestige and reputation has surely been injured. Thus, the findings arrived at by the Trial Judge in the present case is against the evidence on record and the Trial Judge has failed to decide this case on proper interpretation on law and fact involved in this case. Consequently, we set aside the judgment of the trial Court and decree the suit. In the facts and circumstances of the case a decree for Taka 5,000.00 (Taka five thousand) only will meet the ends of justice and will vindicate the grievance of the plaintiff. Accordingly the suit is decreed to the extent of Tk. 5,000.00 (Tk. five thousand) only as damages.

In the result, the appeal is allowed. Since there is no appearance we do not award any costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arising out of an order of the appellate Court made on March 17,1986 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 254 of 1982 from an order of the executing Court dated April 22, 1982 gives rise to an important question of law for consideration. The question is whether the lower appellate Court was legally competent to direct the Executing Court to proceed with an Execution Case which was disposed of by the Executing Court by the order under appeal on the ground that the decree was fully satisfied as one of the decree-holders got delivery of possession of the disputed building on the reasoning that no appeal lies from such order of the Executing Court.

2. Mr. SR Karmaker contends that in view of provision of section 47 CPC the appeal being incompetent the impugned order of the appellate Court was without jurisdiction and the remedy of the opposite parties lies in a properly constituted separate suit and not in the execution case under Order 21 rule, 15 CPC as the dispute between the decree-holders was not a question between the parties to the suit as contemplated in section 47 CPC. His second contention was that the decree having been fully satisfied by delivery of possession of the disputed building to the petitioner the execution case was rightly disposed of on the ground of satisfaction of the decree as the delivery of possession to the petitioner was for the benefit of all the several joint decree-holders-opposite parties. Mr. Karmaker places the relevant laws and cites a number of decisions in support of his contentions which will be referred to at the relevant place in this judgment.

3. In repelling the contentions of Mr. Karmaker, Mr. Md. Nurul Huq submits that the appeal at the instance of the opposite parties was competent and the decree not being satisfied in terms of the order of the Court but beyond that in collusion with the judgment-debtor Saleha Khatun there was no satisfaction of the decree in law the Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 before the Subordinate Judge was competent to determine the dispute between the petitioner and the opposite-parties-decree-holders and no separate suit is necessary as suggested by Mr. Karmaker. He has also invited my attention to several decisions in support of his contentions.

4. To answer the points mooted at the bar it is necessary to state the relevant facts of the case. The opposite parties and the petitioner who are full brothers instituted Title Suit No. 101 of 1966 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka against sole defendant Salcha Khatun, the predecessor of the opposite parties No. 3 to 3(b), for specific performance of contract in respect of the disputed two storyed building on the basis of a registered deed of reconveyance executed on April 2, 1956. On transfer to the Court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 147 of 1968. On April 21, 1981 the suit was decreed ex pane and the defendant was directed to execute and register the deed of sale in favour of the plaintiffs on receipt of Tk. 8,275.00 within 60 days. The petitioner deposited the money on May 15, 1981 on behalf of the decree-holders. The decree-holders-opposite parties also by depositing the said amount on July 17, 1981 started Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 on behalf of all the joint decree holders under Order XXI rule 15 CPC. The Court on July 27, 1981 on the prayer of opposite parties directed the judgment-debtor Salcha Khatun not to deliver the possession of the building to anybody other than the decree-holders. But inspite of the said order Salcha Khatun executed a deed of sale in respect of the building on commission obtaining the balance consideration money from the petitioner on 27.7.1981 and delivered possession of the building to the petitioner alone. Thereafter the executing Court on 22.4.1982 disposed of the execution case holding that the decree is fully satisfied and to proceed with the execution case will be abuse of the process of the Court.

5. In the above background we are to see whether the appeal before lower appellate Court was incompetent and it acted without jurisdiction in setting aside the order of the executing Court and in directing it to proceed with the Executing case No. 14 of 1981. This requires consideration of the provision of section 47 CPC as well as Order 21 rule 15 CPC and the decisions cited at the Bar. Before embarking upon a discussion on the decisions cited at the Bar I shall better proceed first to examine the relevant provision of section 47 CPC and Order 21 rule 15 CPC. Sub-section (I) of section 47 reads:

"All questions arising between the parties to the suit in which the decree was passed, or their representative, and relating to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree, shall be determined by the Court executing the decree and not by a separate suit."

Order 21, rule 15 reads:

"(1) Where a decree has been passed jointly in favour of more persons than one, any one or more of such person may unless the decree imposes any condition to the contrary, apply for the execution of the whole decree for the benefit of them all, or, where any of them has died, for the benefit of the survivors and the legal representatives of the deceased.

(2) Where the Court sees sufficient cause for allowing the decree to be executed on an application made under this rule, it shall make such order as it deems necessary for protecting the interests of the persons who have not joined in the application."

<u>6. Mr. Karmaker relying upon section 47 submits that the expression "the parties to the suit" used in section 47 means either the defendant or the plaintiff and not, as in the present case, the plaintiffs inter se i.e. to say in this case the decree-holders and the present dispute being a dispute between the decree-holders inter se relating to the satisfaction of the decree the same is to be decided only in a properly constituted separate suit and not in Execution Proceeding under Order 21, rule 15 CPC as the expression "parties to the suit" does not contemplate decree-holders inter se the appeal was incompetent. He relied upon the case of Munshi Rai Vs. Rap Narain and others, AIR 1927 Pat, 288 wherein it has been held that where a question arises between the decree-holders with regard to payment of compensation to a decree-holder who purchased certain property in auction in execution of a decree obtained by all the decree-holders such question is not between the parties to the suit but is a question between the decree-holders as such the order made by the Court for payment of compensation to the purchasing decree-holders on setting aside the sale on payment of the decretal amount by the judgment debtor is not an order under section 47 CPC and therefore no appeal lies from such order. He also cited the decision in the case of Bans Rai Singh Vs. Krishna Chandra AIR 1981 All. 280 wherein a Single Judge held that dispute between the decree-. holders inter se and question between them do not fall under section 47 and is foreign to the scope of section 47 CPC. The decisions cited by Mr. Karmaker are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case before me. In none of the decisions the decree was satisfied in violation of the Order of injunction issued by the Court. Where the decree is satisfied in violation of the order of the executing court during pendency of the Execution case, as in the present case, it seems to me that such satisfaction of the decree being violative of the order of the court cannot be construed to be a satisfaction of the decree pursuant to the Court's order. In the instant case during pendency of the Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 the judgment-debtor Saicha Khatun delivered possession of the building on receipt of the consideration money from the petitioner and the petitioner after obtaining the delivery of possession gave an undertaking to the effect that Saleha Khatun shall not be liable to the decree-holders present opposite parties and he himself shall be held responsible in the event of any objection to be raised by them with regard to the satisfaction of the decree. Inviting my attention to such undertaking Mr. Karmaker contends that the petitioner is bound by such undertaking and would be responsible for satisfaction of the decree and the petitioner having obtained the delivery of the building for the benefit of other decree-holders the decree is fully satisfied and the order impugned before me has no legal foundation as the appeal before the lower appellate Court was incompetent and the Executing Court correctly disposed of the execution case on the ground that the decree has been fully satisfied. The contention does not impress me as the conduct of the petitioner also betrays a total lack of his willingness to part with the respective shares of the decree-holders opposite-parties till today. Not only the petitioner got delivery of possession of the building against the order of the Court but his conduct in not handing over possession of the building to the opposite parties No. 1 and 2 does not call for disposal of the execution case by the executing Court.</u>

<u>7. Now the question remains to be resolved is whether the appeal before the Additional District Judge in the instant case was incompetent in view of the expression "parties to the suit" used in section 47 CPC. It is difficult for me to put such a narrow construction to words "the parties to the suit" as suggested by Mr. Karmaker relying on the decisions cited by him referred to above only to mean either the plaintiff or the defendant. The words "parties to the suit" are of wide connotation and it also means, in my opinion, either the plaintiffs inter se or the defendants inter se as well. I am fortified in this view by the decision in the case of Valchand Gulabchand Shah Vs. Manekbai Hirachand Shah and others, 1953 Born. 127 relied by Mr. Huq wherein it has been held that in a fit case the Court may allow other decree-holders to intervene in pending execution if it is not properly conducted. In that case it has been, after reviewing a large number of decisions of different High Courts held that payment to one of the several joint decree-holders cannot be recognised as a payment to all unless he is authorised to receive such payment on behalf of all and does not amount to 'pro tan to satisfaction even to the extent of what is regarded to be the share in the decree of the decree-holder who received payment. It was further held therein that it is not correct to say that the remaining decree-holders can maintain the 'darkhast' only to the extent of their own shares in the decree but the remaining decree-holders are entitled to execute the whole decree. Therefore, on the strength of this decision, I hold that even where the dispute regarding discharge, satisfaction and execution of a decree arises between the decree-holders inter se the dispute can be determined by the executing court and no separate suit is necessary. In one of the earliest decisions in the case of Moti Ram Vs. Nannu Prashad, 26 All. 335 Aikman, J. took the similar view. It was held that one of the two or more joint decree-holders is not competent without having been authorised by others to certify the satisfaction of the decree by payment out of court the entire decree. This case is somewhat similar to the instant case. In the instant case before me the opposite parties did not authorise the petitioner to certify satisfaction of the decree by delivery of possession of the building. In view of my discussion above and in the light of the aforesaid principles of law laid down in Valchand Gulabchand Shaha and Moti Ram referred to above I am of the opinion that where other joint decree holders do not authorise the decree holder who receives the delivery of possession of the decretal building the decree can not be said to have been satisfied and the execution case at the instance of the other decree holders can be proceeded with according to law and the other joint decree-holders need not file a separate suit. As the dispute in the instant case relates to satisfaction of the decree although the dispute is between the decree-holders inter se, I am of the opinion that there was no satisfaction of the decree as the certificate by the petitioner of the satisfaction of the decree out of Court was not valid satisfaction as the same was done not in terms of the Court's order, rather in violation of the order of injunction and the dispute in the instant case as to satisfaction of the decree being a question between the decree-holders is to be determined by the Executing Court and the appeal before the Additional District judge was competent and the impugned order was not made without jurisdiction as suggested by Mr. Karmaker. So far as the filing of separate suit is concerned I am also of the view that the satisfaction of the decree was not in compliance with the order of the court and being out of the Court in collusion with the judgment debtor without there being any authority given to the petitioner by the opposite parties Nos.1 and 2 to take delivery of possession of the building the other joint-decree holders should not be compelled to institute a separate suit unnecessarily as suggested by Mr. Karmaker which I think rather would be abuse of the process of the Court and the question regarding satisfaction of the decree in the present case must be decided in the Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 as the question between the decree-holder relates to execution, discharge and satisfaction of the decree falls within the purview of section 47 CPC.</u>

For the reasons stated above, I find no reason to interfere with the order of the appellate Court dated 17.3.1986. Accordingly, I direct the executing Court to proceed with the Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 according to law.

In the result, the Rule is discharged. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
