case_source: (From, the judgment and decree dated 5.4.1984 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench, in First Appeals Nos. 90 of 1979 and 46 of 1980 respectively.)
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J: These two appeals by special leave, at the instance of the plaintiffs, have arisen out of a judgment and decree dated 5 April 1984 of the High Court Division (Comilla Bench) modifying the judgment and decree dated 31 March 1979 of the Subordinate Judge, Noakhali, in Title Suit No. 417 of 1978.

2. Plaintiffs-appellants filed the said suit for declaration of their title to the suit land as they found their title clouded by a Notice dated 18 April 1978 served upon them by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Feni, treating the suit land as Vested and Non- Resident Property and asking them to surrender it. Their simple case was that the suit land was not an enemy or vested property and as such the Notice for surrendering it was illegal and void.

3. The suit land originally belonged to one Shashi Bhusan Mujumdcr, on whose death in or about the year 1943, his six sons including Hemendra Kumar Majumder inherited it along with other properties of Shashi Bhusan. After the death of Shashi Bhusan the six brothers amicably partitioned all the inherited properties lying in different places; the suit land at Feni fell exclusively to the share of Hemendra; the property at Narayanganj fell to the share of Dhirendra, the eldest of the brothers, while the property in Calcutta fell to the share of remaining four brothers, namely, Mohendra, Narendra, Sat yendra and Rabindra. Hemendra by four registered sale deeds, transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs who went into possession thereof; but the Sub-Divisional Officer illegally served the notice treating it as enemy and vested property. Hence they filed the suit against the Sub-Divisional Officer (defendant No.4.) Additional Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Custodian of Vested Property (defendant No.3), Deputy Custodian of Vested Property (defendant No. 2) and the Government of Bangladesh (defendant No. 1) seeking declaration of their title to the suit land.

4. The suit was contested by two sets of defendants, one by the Government officials including the Additional Deputy Commissioner and one by the added defendants Nos. 5-11 who claimed to have taken lease of the suit land from the Vested Property Authorities. The common defence is that all the six sons of Shashi Bhusan, the original owner of the land, had migrated to India immediately after the Partition of the country in 1947 and they were Indian nationals when the Indo-Pak war of 1965 broke out in consequence of which the suit land became enemy property by operation of law and as such it was rightly treated as enemy and vested property and the Sub-divisional Officer's notice for taking over possession of the land was perfectly lawful. The plaintiffs' claim of amicable partition among the six sons of Shashi Bhusan was denied and it was challenged as a device to save the land from the mischief of law. It was also denied that Shashi Bhusan had left any property anywhere except the suit land at Feni. The plaintiffs' sale-deeds purportedly executed by Hemendra were also challenged as fraudulent transactions without any consideration in that Hemendra was not in Bangladesh at the purported time of execution and registration of the sale-deeds.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of evidence, both oral and documentary including a photostat copy of a declaration dated 2 April 1963 made by the four sons of Shashi Bhushan living in Calcutta (Ext, 16) and the judgment of a previous suit in respect of the amicable partition of the same land (Ext. 7d), found that there was an amicable partition by which the suit land fell exclusively to the share of Hemendra who was all along in this country and that the transfers made by him to the plaintiffs were genuine; on those findings the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in full. Both the sets of defendants challenged this judgment before the High Court Division-the Government and its officials by First Appeal No. 90 of 1979- and Defendant Nos. 5-11 by First Appeal No. 46 of 1980. The learned Judges on re-assessment of the evidence held that the main documents in support of the amicable partition namely the declaration (Ext. 16) and the judgment of the previous suit (Ext. 7d) are not admissible in evidence or at least they got no probative value; and as to the nationality of the sons of the late Shashi Bhushan, the learned Judges found that except Hemendra all other sons of Shashi Bhusan were Indian Nationals from before 1965 Indo-Pak War and as such the suit rand to the extent of their share, that is, 5/6, was enemy and vested property and on those findings modified the trial court's judgment and decreed the suit to the extent of 1/6 only. Plaintiffs 'felt aggrieved thereby and filed these appeals by special leave which was granted by us to consider whether the learned Judges were justified in discarding Ext. 16, the photostat copy of a purported declaration and the judgment, Ext. 7 (d) of a previous suit.

6. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that both the photostat copy, Ext. 16 and the previous judgment Ext. 7(d) are not only admissible but also they have got evidentiary value, and that these documents, considered along with the oral evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 are sufficient to establish the claim of amicable partition among the sons of Shashi Bhusan long before 1965. Ext. 7(d) is a certified copy of a judgment dated 31-1-70 in Title Appeal No. 169 of 1965 which arose from Title Suit No. 126 of 1962 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali. That suit was filed by one Golam Hossain (who is P.W.2 in the present suit) against one Mukhlesur Rahman and others impleading all the six sons of Shashi Bhushan as Proforma-defendants Nos. 4-9; pro-forma-defendant No.9 was Hernendra and pro-forma-defendant No.8 was his brother Dhirendra. Facts of that case are that Hernendra Kumar, while he was in exclusive possession of' the suit land at Feni on the basis of an amicable partition, inducted Muklesur Rahman as a monthly tenant in a hut on a part of the suit land; on the ground of default of payment of rent Hemendra filed S.C.C. Suit No. 153 of 1960 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Feni, against Mukhlesur Rahman and obtained a decree for ejectment. But Mukhlesur Rahman did not vacate the hut. Hemendra then transferred pucca structures on the suit land to Golam Hossain, as mentioned above, by a registered kabala dated 26 October 1961 claiming exclusive right and possession on the basis of the amicable partition. Golam Hossain then filed Title Suit No. 126 of 1962 against Mukhlesur Rahman impleading all the sons of Shashi Bhusan. Two of them namely, Hemendra and Dhirendra deposed in that case as P.Ws. 1 and 2 admitting the amicable partition. The trial Court did not accept the claim of amicable partition and decreed the suit to the extent of 1/6 share that is, in respect of Hemendra's share only. But on appeal, the Additional District Judge, Noakhali, by his judgment, Ext.7(d) decreed the suit in full on a finding that there was an amicable partition by which the suit land at Feni fell exclusively to Hemendra's share. It is this judgment which is before us for consideration whether it is admissible under ss.13 and 43 of the Evidence Act and may be considered as evidence of the alleged amicable partition.

7. Judgments, orders or decrees are relevant under ss. 40, 41, 42, 43 and 44 of the Evidence Act. "Relevant" means and relates to, admissibility only. The question as to the evidentiary value of a judgment which is relevant is different from the question whether the judgment is admissible in evidence, because it may be relevant, but its evidentiary value may be different in different cases; in some cases the evidentiary value is small and in other cases it may be conclusive evidence against the person who was party to the previous suit in which the judgment was passed. Under s. 40 a previous judgment, order or decree, is relevant to bar a second suit, that is, when such a judgment operates as res judicata under s. 11 Civil P.C. Under s.41 a final judgment, order or decree of a competent court in the exercise of probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction, is not only relevant but also is conclusive both against the parties thereto as well as against the rest of the world, that is, it is a judgment in rem as distinguished from a judgment in personam. Under s.42 a judgment is relevant if it relates to any matter of public nature but it is not a conclusive proof of the fact it states. None of these sections, 40, 41 and 42, obviously is attracted to the instant case. It is section 43 which may be attracted to the instant case. It reads thus:

"4. Judgments etc. other than those mentioned in sections 40 to 42; when relevant. Judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in sections 40, 41 and 42, are irrelevant, unless the existence of such judgment, order or decree, is a fact in issue, or is relevant under some other provision of this Act."

8. Mr. Pal contends that the judgment (Ext. 7d) in the previous suit is quite relevant in the instant case as the question whether there was an amicable partition among the sons of Shashi Bhusan in respect of the suit land is a material question for consideration in both the suits. Though the learned Judges of the High Court Division expressed grave doubt as to its very admissibility, Mr. Ranadhir Sen, learned Counsel for respondents No.5, does not dispute that this judgment, Ext. 7(d), is relevant in the present suit; but he contends that its evidentiary value is practically nil in that it is relevant only to show that a judgment like this is in existence and nothing more. He contends that though an amicable partition among the sons of Shashi Bhusan is a common question in the two suits, but the questions have been decided in the two suits on different facts and circumstances and in different contexts, and though, in the previous suit, sons of Shashi Bhusan were parties, they are not so in the instant suit. Mr. Pal has, however, contended that a judgment whether inter parts or not, may be conclusive evidence against all persons of its own existence, date and legal effect, as distinguished from the accuracy of the decision rendered. In support of this contention he has referred to a number of decisions including a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in Malik Din v, Mohammad Aslam, 21 DLR SC 94, Relevant portion of that judgment is quoted below:

"Judgments, whether inter parties or not, are conclusive evidence for and against all persons whether parties, privies, or strangers of its own existence, date and legal effect, as distinguished from the accuracy of the decision rendered. In other words, the law attributes unerring verity to the substantive as opposed to the judicial portions of the record. But where the judgment is inter parties even recitals in such a judgment are admissible. A previous judgment is admissible also to prove statement or admission or an acknowledgment made by a party or the predecessor-in-interest of a party, in his pleadings in a previous litigation. Similarly, a judgment narrating the substance of the pleadings of the parties to a litigation is admissible to establish the allegations made by them on that occasion."

In that case the plaintiff denied that the defendant had obtained an order of mutation from the Revenue Officer, but he was confronted with an order of the Collector which showed that in his appeal before the Collector in connection with an earlier mutation proceedings, he did not challenge the fact turn of mutation but had attacked the mutation on the ground that its basis-a gift-was void. The order of the Collector in the previous proceedings was held not only admissible in evidence for proving the fact about mutation, but also it was old to be binding upon him as his statement in own pleadings in the previous litigation.

9. Other cases referred to by Mr. Pal in this connection are Tepu Khan v. Rajani Mohan Das, 2 CWN, 501; Govinda Narayan Singh v. Shamlal Singh, 58 Indian Appeals, 125; Maharaja Sir Kesho Prosad Singh v. Bahuria Mt. Bhagjogna Kuer and others, AIR 1937 PC 69. In the last mentioned case the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council observed:

"A judgment is not admissible as evidence against one which is a stranger to the suit. But the judgment in a prior suit together with the plaint which preceded it and the steps in execution which followed it are evidence of an assertion by the holder of a judgment of the right which he claims to acquire and are then admissible in evidence of his right. Such judgment is of great evidence even against third parties."

10. Mr. Pal has next submitted that s. 43 should be read with s.l3 of the Evidence Act for appreciating the circumstances in which a judgment, though not inter parts, may be considered for existence of any right or custom. S. 13 provides that where the question is as to the existence of any right or custom, certain facts are relevant, such as any 'transaction' by which the right or custom in question was created, claimed, modified, recognised, asserted or denied, and 'particular instances' in which the right or custom claimed, recognised or asserted. Mr. Pal, relying on an observation of the Allahabad High Court made in Collector of Gorakhpur v. Palakdhari Singh (1889) All. 1, F B. stated that the former judgments and decrees were not themselves a transaction or an instance within the meaning of section 13; but the suit in which they were made was a transaction or an instance in which the defendant's right of possession was claimed and recognised and that to establish that such transaction or instance took place they were the best evidence. The learned Judges of the High Court Division did not straightaway reject the previous judgment Ext. 7(d) as inadmissible but they were of the view that the probative value of the judgment "is very small", firstly, because this judgment reversed that of the trial Court where the plaintiffs' title to the extent of only 1/6 share was declared, and secondly, this judgment itself is under appeal in Second Appeal No. 58 of 1972. With respect, we find that neither of these two reasons for deprecating the evidentiary value of Ext.7(d) is tenable. For, there hardly any distinction may be made between a judgment of affirmation and that of reversal, and secondly, the result of the second appeal which arose from the judgment in question is also not a matter for consideration at the time its admissibility and evidentiary value come up for consideration. However, it is now found that the second appeal as referred to was dismissed and the judgment, Ext.7(d) was upheld in due course was by a learned Single Judge who is a party to the impugned judgment before us in these appeals.

11. In the previous judgment the present respondents were not parties, obviously because they came to the scene much later in consequence of the operation of the Enemy Property law. But the persons interested in the suit land namely, Hemendra and his brothers were parties. Be that as it may, the judgment Ext. 7(d) is not interparts, and ordinarily a judgment cannot be used as evidence against a person who is a stranger thereto. But the judgment in a prior suit together with the plaint and other steps taken in connection therewith is evidence of an assertion by the, holder of the judgment of the right which he claims to acquire and is then admissible in evidence of his right. Such right is of great evidence even against third parties, as has been held by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council already referred to above. The simple fact is that the amicable partition of the same property of late Shashi Bhusan was the subject-matter in both the suits and as such the previous judgment showing the amicable partition is certainly an evidence in the present suit and it may be considered along with other evidence in the subsequent suit. Evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 goes to establish Hemendra's exclusive title by an amicable partition long before the Indo-Pak War of 1965. P.W.2, already mentioned before, is Golam Hossain who was plaintiff of the previous suit claiming a part of the suit land on the basis of purchase from Hemendra by a registered kabala of 1961. The basis of that registered kabala was the same partition of Shashi Bhusan's property; he has supported the present plaintiffs' claim of partition. P.W.1 is one of the plaintiffs-appellants; he has deposed from his own knowledge about the partition. Their oral evidence has been rejected by the learned Judges, as according to them, they arc "thoroughly incompetent" in that they were not present at the time of partition. The partition, it may be remembered, took place some time in 1946, after the death of Shashi Bhusan. These P.Ws. came to the scene much later. They may not have been present during the talk of partition but they cannot be said to be incompetent. They have come from the same locality having particular knowledge about the property of which they subsequently purchased. The claim of amicable partition was made even before Golam Hossain's purchase in 1961, for in a much earlier suit, S.C.C. Suit No. 153 of 1960, Hemendra had put up the same claim on the basis of the amicable partition and became successful. In the light of these facts and circumstances, we are of the view that the previous judgment Ext.7(d) was not given the consideration it deserves by the learned Judges whose decision therefore cannot be sustainable both in fact and law.

12. Much arguments have been led on Ext.16, the photostat copy of a declaration purportedly made by four brothers of Hemendra who resided in Calcutta. It says that they declared before the Pakistan High Commissioner at Calcutta that there was an amicable partition among them and their other brothers by which the property at Feni fell to the share of Hemendra. When the photostat copy was filed as evidence before the Court no objection was raised as to its admissibility without proof. But subsequently its admissibility was challenged on the ground that the original was not produced nor any reason for non-production was given. The learned Judges have observed that "Ext. 16 was simply produced before the Court and marked an exhibit; it is not such a document which could be received in evidence without formal proof; therefore, we are clearly of the opinion that secondary evidence e.g. photostat copy, which is not even proved legally, could not be admissible in evidence.

<u>13. Mr. Pal has contended that the objection  as to formal proof of Ext. 16 was to be taken at the earliest point of time, that is, when it was sought to be admitted but its admissibility not having been objected to, the defendants arc debarred from raising this objection now. In support of this contention he has relied upon a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in Abdullah and others V. Abdul Karim and others, 20 DLR SC 205 where it has been observed.</u>

<u>"The Code of Civil Procedure provides for the admission of documents and it is now well settled that if objection to the formal proof of a document has not been taken at the earliest point of time it cannot be taken subsequently and certainly not in appeal."</u>

<u>Mr. Ranadhir Sen, hardly finds anything to dispute this proposition of law as to admissibility of a document, but he contends that this principle is not applicable to the case of a document which is per se inadmissible and that in the instant case no explanation was given why the original was not produced. Mr. Sen has pointed out that it is not known who actually produced it before court, particularly when no witness has been examined on this point excepting that this document was filed by the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>14. Secondary evidence of a document is admissible in the cases specifically mentioned in s. 65 of the Evidence Act and if the original is not available, reason for non-availability must be given. It appears that at the time the photostat copy was filed no objection was taken as to its formal proof. The declaration though made in 1963 was not referred to in the previous judgment Ext.7(d) dated 31 January 1970. The learned Judges discarded it for another reason which, according to them, is that its contents are materially inconsistent with the plaint case. The learned Judges did not, however, point at any inconsistent statement between the two documents. Be that as it may, the question as to merit of this document, Ext. 16, will arise only if it is found to be admissible in evidence without formal proof. We think that though objection was not raised when it was produced, the party producing it was not exempted from explaining in the course of recording evidence why its original was not produced. Even assuming this is not admissible in evidence, the appellants case of amicable partition stands independent of Ext. 16 as other evidence and circumstances including the previous judgment are quite sufficient to prove it. An amicable partition like this between brothers-co-sharers need not be effected by a registered instrument, as Mr. Pal has rightly referred to the decision in the case of Nani Bai V. Gita Bai, AIR 1958 SC 70.</u>

15. In the result, both the appeals are allowed with costs. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the trial Court is restored.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Ansar Ali J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the defendant No. 2 appellant is directed against the judgment and order dated 19th February, 1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1 st Court and Commercial Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 52 of 1987/Other Suit No. 2 of 1992 restraining the defendant appellant from proceeding with the Execution Case No.10 of 1992 pending in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong. Short facts relevant from the disposal of the aforesaid appeal are, that the defendant-appellant instituted a suit being SCC Suit No. 33 of 1983 for eviction of the defendants i.e. the present respondent, and another from the suit premises alleging, inter alia, that defendant No.1 in the SCC suit was a monthly tenant under the plaintiff who habitually defaulted in payment of monthly rents and illegally sub-let some portion of the suit-premises to defendant No.2 of the said suit. Both the defendants of that suit filed separate written statements to contest the same. Defendant No.1 alleged that he was not at all a tenant under the plaintiff and that he was not a defaulter and defendant No.2 alleged that he was not at all a sub-tenant in the suit premises as he purchased the suit premises by a registered deed and has been in possession of the same as a legal owner; hence the suit for eviction was not maintainable against him without a prayer for declaration of title and recovery of possession. The learned SCC Judge at the conclusion of the trial found that the defendant No.1 was a monthly tenant under the plaintiff and a habitual defaulter and that defendant No. 2 was an illegal sub-tenant in the suit-premises and accordingly, decreed the SCC suit for eviction by his judgment and decree dated 14-5-86. Being aggrieved by the same, both the defendants came by way of revision in this Court in Civil Revision No. 233 of 1986 and a Bench of this Court after hearing both the sides was pleased to discharge the Rule and uphold the judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge by the judgment and order dated 25-11-91. Thereafter the defendant No. 2 filed a Leave Petition before the Appellate Division of this Court being Misc. Petition No. 3 of 1993 but the same was also dismissed by their Lordships on 23-2-1993 as not pressed. Meanwhile the decree-holder plaintiff in the SCC Suit put the decree into execution by starting SCC Execution Case No. 10 of 1992 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong. But before the conclusion of the SCC proceeding by a final decision of the highest court, the defendant No. 2 himself instituted a suit being Other Suit No. 52 of 1987 in respect of the suit-premises against the decree holder plaintiff of the SCC suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 1st Commercial Court, Chittagong praying for declaration of his title and confirmation of possession in the suit-premises. The suit on transfer was however renumbered as Other Suit No.2 of 1992 and the defendant of the said other suit filed written statement to contest the same. On the prayer of the plaintiff of the subsequent suit, the learned Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court No. 1 was pleased to direct both the parties to maintain status quo in respect of possession, but in spite of the said order of status quo, it was alleged that the decree holder of the SCC suit through the Execution case being SCC Execution Case No. 10 of 1992 was trying to evict the plaintiff of the subsequent suit and judgment-debtor defendant No. 2 of the SCC suit from the suit-premises. Hence, the plaintiff of the subsequent suit filed an application before the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge and 1st Commercial Court, Chittagong praying for a temporary injunction restraining the decree-holder of the SCC suit and defendant in the subsequent other suit from proceeding with the aforesaid Execution case. The learned Subordinate Judge accordingly granted temporary injunction to the above effect vide order dated 19-2-1995.

2. Being aggrieved by the same, the decree holder of the SCC suit and defendant in the subsequent suit has preferred the present 1st Miscellaneous Appeal in this Court.

3. Mr. SK Sinha with Mr. AK Ahmadul Hasan and Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, Advocates appeared for the defendant-appellant and Mr. Abu Nayeem with Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocates appeared for the plaintiff-respondent.

<u>4. Mr. Sinha, the learned advocate for the appellant, has assailed the impugned judgment and order on various grounds. His first contention is that defendant No. 2 of the SCC suit and plaintiff of the subsequent suit has been found to be an illegal sub-tenant in the suit-premises by the learned SCC Court and the decision of the SCC Judge has been upheld by the apex court of this country and as such he is a trespasser in the suit-premises and has no locus standi to file any application for injunction. His further submission is that the plaintiff of the SCC suit i.e. the present defendant-appellant, has obtained a decree in his favour as far back as in the year 1986 which has been upheld by the highest Court of the country and thereafter for the execution of the said decree, he started the Execution Case in the year 1992 but he could not get the decree duly executed and enjoy the fruits of the same as yet and hence there is no justification in passing the impugned order of injunction by the learned Subordinate Judge depriving him of the enjoyment of the fruits of the decree. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned order is not at all justified in an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the CPC as the execution of valid decree by the decree-holder cannot give rise to an injury to the judgment-debtor as contemplated under rules 1 and 2 of the said Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure and unless such injury is shown, no temporary injunction can be granted. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Firm Ishardes Devi Chand and another vs. RB Prakash Chand and another reported in AIR 1969 (SC) 938 and he also relied on some other decisions in this connection in the case of Abdul Hamid Khan and others vs. Tridip Kumar Chanda and another reported in AIR 1953 (Assam) 104 and in the case of Hemanta Kumar vs. Ayodhya Prasad reported in AIR 1957 Madhya Bharat 95, and another in the case of Rutan Chand Gai Gopal and others vs. Mian Saifuddin and others reported in AIR 1961 (JK) 29, and as to want of locus standi to get relief of temporary injunction by a trespasser, the learned Advocate for the appellant has referred to some decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 20 (Belayet Hossain vs. Nurul Alam Mir and others) and 10 DLR 193 (Chand Mohamood Mondal vs. Fayezuddin Ahmed and others). Lastly, Mr. Sinha has contended that the Court while passing an order of injunction acts as a court of equity and it cannot knowingly pass an infructuous order of injunction. According to him, by the impugned order, the defendant appellant has been restrained from proceeding with the execution case pending in a different court but no order of injunction or stay has been passed against the proceeding of the said Execution case of that Court but the impugned order of injunction has been passed only against defendant-appellant in a different suit i.e. the subsequent suit of the plaintiff respondent. Now, according to him, if the defendant-appellant even docs not proceed with the SCC execution case pending in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong, in view of the impugned order, there is no legal bar for the Executing court to proceed with the Execution case in absence of the decree-holder-defendant appellant and, as such, the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is, in fact, an infructuous order which the Court was not competent to pass. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the appellant has referred to a decision in the case of Monohar Lal Chopra vs. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 527.</u>

<u>5. Mr. Abu Nayeem with Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed the learned Advocates appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submit that the plaintiff of the present suit cannot be termed as trespasser in the suit-premises as his consistent claim is that he purchased the suit-premises in his possession from the real owner and he has valid right, title and possession in the same and he is or was never a tenant or sub-tenant in the suit-premises at all as alleged and that in the SCC suit the question of title could not be gone into and properly decided and hence he has instituted the present suit in the year 1987 before the decree in the SCC suit was passed and, as such, without final determination of the question of his title in the said suit, the plaintiff-respondent can be termed as a trespasser in the suit-premises and therefore the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant on this point cannot be accepted and the decision referred to in that connection by the learned Advocate for the appellant has no application to this case. Next, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the respondent that it is not disputed that the defendant-appellant has obtained a decree in the SCC suit for eviction of the defendants and for compensation and the same has been upheld by the highest court of the country but the law did not permit the SCC Judge to conclusively decide the question of title of the parties in the suit-premises which question was kept open for a decision of an appropriate civil Court and now the defendant of the SCC suit and plaintiff of the present suit has prayed for declaration of his title and confirmation of his possession in the suit-premises by his title suit which has already become ripe for final hearing and on the prayer of the plaintiff of this suit, there has been an order of status quo directed against both the parties in respect of the suit-premises but in spite of that, the decree-holder of the SCC suit, the present defendant-appellant, has been trying hard to proceed with the execution case for eviction of the present plaintiff and another from the suit-premises. In the above circumstances, the plaintiff however filed an application praying for temporary injunction restraining defendant-appellant from proceeding with the SCC execution case to prevent multiplicity of litigation and in the interest of justice and the learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the sides was pleased to pass the impugned order of injunction against defendant-appellant for the ends of justice, presumably under section 151 of the CPC, though not specifically mentioned in the order. Mr. Nayeem emphatically contends that the impugned order is not an order passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the CPC in which case an injury as contemplated in rule 2 of the said Order must be proved before an order of temporary injunction is passed, but the case is different here. In fact, the relief of injunction was sought for under the inherent jurisdiction of the court and the same was accordingly granted for the ends of justice. Hence, the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant have no manner of application to the impugned order passed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection the learned Advocate further submits that under this section for prevention of the abuse of the process of court or for the ends of justice, the Court possesses inherent power to restrain any party from proceeding with the suit or proceeding pending in a different court provided the facts and circumstances of the case warrant exercise of such power. In support of his contention he has also relied on some decisions namely, AIR 1962 (SC) 527 (Monohar Lal Chopra vs. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hirelal), AIR 1961 Kerala 178 (Shama Amma vs. Venkappa Bhutta and ors), AIR 1955(Kundapanemi Ragh Vaiah and others vs. Inonva Lakshmina Royana and another), AIR 1950 Madras 219 (Ahmed Abdul Sukkor vs. Uallabhade, Kanji Firm). He further contends that staying any proceeding or granting any order of temporary injunction during the pendency of a suit or proceeding is a discretion of the Court concerned which of course has to be exercised judiciously and carefully and stay can be granted for a reasonable period for the suit to be disposed of. In support of his contentions, he has relied on the decisions in the case of Mannujan Begum vs. A Samad Mollah and others reported in 29 DLR (SC) 282 and in the case of Soleman Miah and others vs. lshaque Ali being dead his heirs and othen reported in 41 DLR (AD) 104. He has also relied on a decision in this connection in the case of A Barek Miah and others vs. ABM Serajul Islam reported in 20 DLR 501 to show that even if an application for temporary injunction is made under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, yet the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of any process of the court, may however pass an order of injunction in exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It has been observed inter alia by their Lordships in the decision reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 527 as follows in para 18.</u>

<u>"That the courts have inherent jurisdiction to issue temporary injunction in circumstances not covered by Order XXXIX or by any rules under the Code. It is well settled that the provisions of the Code are not exhaustive."</u>

<u>Again in para 43, it has been held that:</u>

<u>Inherent jurisdiction of the court to make orders ex debito justitiae is undoubtedly affirmed by Section 151 of the Code, but that jurisdiction cannot be exercised so as to nullify the provisions of the Code.</u>

<u>Mr. Nayeem further contends that there were genuine attempts from the side of the plaintiffs to get the present suit heard and disposed of as quickly as possible and towards that, the date of peremptory hearing of the suit was even shifted from 19-4-95 to 19-3-95 at the instance of the present plaintiff but on the prayer of the defendants adjournment was granted and as a result the suit could not be heard and disposed of on that date and the next date was again fixed on 19-4-95 but again on the prayer of the defendants, hearing of the suit has been adjourned and the date has been fixed on 8-5-95 for hearing; hence in the above circumstances, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent submits that in any view of the matter, the impugned order should not be interfered with which has been rightly passed by the learned Subordinate Judge for the ends of justice in exercise of the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further contends that the impugned order is quite valid and effective and there is no scope of its being infructuous and hence the same should be upheld.</u>

<u>6. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and considered the above submissions and perused the impugned order and the decisions and the relevant laws referred to by both the sides and we are of the view in consideration of the same that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly passed the impugned order in the facts and circumstances of the case and we find no reason to interfere with the same at this stage when the suit has already been finally fixed for hearing. Of course, we feel that the decree-holder of a suit should not be deprived from the enjoyment of the fruits of his decree for indefinite or unlimited period. But in a matter like present one where the question of title in the suit-premises is yet to be finally decided by a competent civil Court we think for the ends of justice, the decree-holder of the SCC suit has no alternative but to wait for the decision on question of title in the suit premises to be determined in the present suit which is already fixed for hearing and may be disposed of within a short time. We therefore find no justification in disturbing or interfering with the impugned order of injunction which should continue till disposal of the suit in the interest of justice.</u>

7. For the reasons stated above and in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions made at the bar, we find no illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the learned Court below. The appeal is therefore dismissed without any order as to costs. We, of course, direct the court below to hear and dispose of the suit within a month from the date of receipt of this order without granting any unnecessary adjournment and if the suit cannot be finally disposed of within the above period for any fault of the plaintiff, the order of injunction shall stand vacated after the period fixed for disposal of the suit. In view of the above decision, the connected application is however rejected.

Communicate this order to the court below at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Nurul Haque Bhuiyan J: This appeal by added defendant No. 3 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 8.2.74 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Money Suit No. 3 of 1969 and arises out of a suit for realisation of Tk. 19050.12 paisa with interest at the rate of 9% till realisation.

2. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiff is a banking company and it has a branch at Ajmiriganj, District Sylhet, now district Habiganj. The defendant No.1 was the acting Head Cashier of the said branch and was in charge of the cash kept in the branch. It was a part of his duty to keep the cash, enter it in the Vault Register and also to have the key of the vault in order to open the vault and take out the cash when needed. On inspection check on 14.7.66 by the Bhairab branch Manager it was found that there was a cash shortage of Tk. 19050.12 paisa as per books of entry on 12.7.66 for which the defendant No. 1 is solely responsible. The defendant No. 2 is an insurance company with whom by policy No. MCS/MISC-0223 (a)/63 FG-27 all shortages of cash due to defalcation is covered up to the limit of Tk. 10,00,000/- for which full premium has been paid and the defendant No. 2 is thus bound to make good the loss in case of such defalcation of money of the plaintiff. The said defalcation amount has not been paid by the defendant No. 1 in spite of repeated demands and hence the suit.

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the defendant No.1 on promotion joined at the Ajmiriganj branch on 18.6.66 and at the time of his joining he pressed the then Manager Abdul Awal Mia and the then Cashier-in-charge Bashir for physical verification of the chest and of all duplicate keys of the operations but the Manager and the Cashier concerned did not give any reply regarding preservation of the duplicate keys concerned of the four (4) operations for taking and keeping the cash in the iron safe. The Manager gave vague replies and asked the defendant No. 1 not to bother about the duplicate keys and he verbally told on false pretext that the duplicate keys were lying in the Bhairab branch of the bank. As a matter of fact the defendant No. 1 did not know where the duplicate keys were kept. As per Rules of the Bank at the time of making over and taking over charge the duplicate keys must be tested on withdrawal from the custodian on with whom it is kept and it must be verified and tested and then sealed in a cover in presence of the Manager and the Cashier and other staff and then it is to be kept in joint custody in a parent branch of the said bank or any other nearest schedule bank under a sealed cover in safe custody containing signatures of the Cashier and the Manager in order to avoid any fraud or deception by entering in relevant registers and the mainten an Cease of such a register namely, duplicate key register is a mandatory one. The Manager Abdul Awal Mia did not show any key register in this connection to the defendant No. 1 nor the Manager gave any opportunity to defendant No.1 to verify the duplicate keys of the operations. The defendant No.1 tried to refer the matter regaling the duplicate keys and maintenance of relevant register to the Principal Office, Dhaka but the Manager threatened the defendant No.1 and out of fear he could not refer the matter and this defendant believes that the Manager had certain hyprocisy in the matter. After the incident e.g. the defalcation the Manager opened a new key register. The defendant No.1 and the said Manager were then residing on the 2nd floor of the same building where the Bank was situated. On the night following the day of 12.7.66 at about 11-00 PM the defendant No.1 found the Manager puzzled in the verandah of the residence and also found him whispering with some unknown persons inside the room which was just adjacent to the room of the defendant No.1. On the next day on 13.7.66 in the morning when defendant No.1 became ready to resume his duty he found some police personnel moving hither and thither near the bank building and on enquiry they told the defendant No.1 that the Manager Abdul Awal Mia lodged First Information Report to the Police Station alleging that this defendant No. 1 removed a cash of Tk. 19000/- with the help of his brother who came to Ajmiriganj some days earlier. But as a matter of fact the brother of defendant No.1 had left Ajmiriganj on 9th of July at 8-00 AM. The police thoroughly checked the Bank quarter and the person of the defendant No.1 at about 9-00 AM on 13.7.66 but they did not find any amount of the alleged shortage or duplicate key whatsoever outside or inside of the quarter. On 14.7.66 Nurul Islam Bhuiyan came to Ajmiriganj and ordered defendant No. 1 to hand over charge to Kazi Abul Khair, Assistant Cashier by his order No.3 dated 14.7.66 which was without jurisdiction, illegal and malafide. Nurul Islam Bhuiyan along with Abdul Awal Mia and some unknown persons with the help of the police forced the defendant No. 1 to sign a written statement against the will of the defendant No. 1 and this defendant out of fear of his life and criminal assault handed over the charge and signed the written statement. At that time a key out of 4 keys in the custody of Manager was discovered by Nurul Islam Bhuiyan on the floor of strong room and the same was seized by the Officer-in-charge of the thana. The key was thrown by Nurul Islam Bhuiyan to take a plea to put the blame on this defendant. The defendant No. 1 was forwarded to the Court of SDO, Habiganj on 16.7.66 and on his release on bail from the Court he went to resume his duty but he was not allowed to join his duty. In spite of many representations to the Principal Office the principal office did not take any action again, the Manager as the Manager had got some high official relations in the bank. The Deputy Director, Anti-Corruption Department, Chittagong Division made Abdul Awal Mia an accused in the criminal case but due to illegal influence of the relations he was not charge-sheeted in the criminal case but the defendant No. 1 was made a scape-goat in the matter to shield the guilt of the Manager. The Manager Abdul Awal Mia with the help of the duplicate keys in collusion with the guard and also with the Bhairab Branch of the bank and other local unknown persons defalcated the alleged amount during the absence of the defendant No.1. This defendant No. 1 never defalcated the amount of Tk. 19050.12 paisa or any other amount while he was on duty as acting Head Cashier in the Ajmiriganj Branch and as such the question of payment of the amount by him does not arise. It is absolutely false and malicious to say that the defendant No. 1 is responsible for the alleged shortage. The charge of defalcation was fabricated against this defendant No.1 in order to shield the Manager Abdul Awal Mia. The defendant No.1 and the Manager Abdul Awal Mia after closing the banking transaction on 12.7.66 by performing all the formalities such as making entries in the Vault Register, Cash Analysis Book, Balance Book, Cashier's Receipt Book, Cashier's Payment book and Manager's Cash Scroll Book and then physically verifying the Cash Book, signed the relevant registers and then the cash including the Cashier's hand balance was kept in the iron safe by the Manager and the defendant No.1 jointly. Thereafter they closed the strong room and the key of the door was duly checked by the guard concerned under the instruction of the Manager. There were four joint operations for taking and keeping the money, namely (1) Strong Room for which two separate locks are maintained and key of one of which lies with the Manager and another with the Cashier for joint operation, (ii) Collapsible gate for which two separate keys are maintained for joint control and one key lies with the Manager and the other with the Cashier, (iii) the iron safe for which also two separate keys are maintained — one by Manager and the other by Cashier and (iv) finally and lastly, is the money drawer for which also two separate keys are maintained by the Manager and the Cashier. All the duplicate keys used in all these 4 operations are to be kept in the safe custody of a nearest parent Branch of the same bank or any other bank under a scaled cover. As a result of these joint operations no one can reach the money drawer singly without the help of the other . This defendant has all the reasons to believe that the said Manager with the help of duplicate keys in his custody about which this defendant was kept in dark and in collusion with the guard defalcated the said amount.

4. The defendant No. 2 the Bangladesh Insurance filed a written statement stating that this defendant would not contest the suit and would abide by the result of the suit.

5. The defendant No. 3 who was subsequently added as a party to the suit by order No. 18 dated 10.6.70 filed a separate written statement denying all the averments made in the written statement by the defendant No.1. His case is that plaintiff Bank decided to open a branch at Ajmiriganj and sent him there with appointment as Manager designate for the said branch in May, 1966. The branch was opened with the steel almirah for safe custody of the money in the strong room. The cover door of the strong room had 2 locks with key of one lock with each of the defendant Nos. 1 and 3. The green door had 2 locks with key of one lock with each of the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and the body lock of the steel Almirah had two keys one with each of the defendants No. 1 and 3 and the cash was being withdrawn and kept by opening and closing the locks jointly by them. Each such key had its duplicate and the keys were kept within this steel almirah. Bashir Uddin Ahmed, Assistant Cashier-in-charge was replaced by the defendant No. 1 as Assistant Cashier in charge when the latter joined the Ajmiriganj Branch on 22.6.66 and started working. For want of keys the key safe could not be used and the keys of the key safe were supplied to the Branch on 30.7.66. The defendant No. 3 repeatedly requested the Principal Office and the intermediary Bhairab Branch of the Bank to take delivery of the surplus cash, but no arrangement was made. The 4 operations system or the defendant No. 1's demand for physical verification and safe preservation of the duplicate keys as alleged by the defendant No. 1 in his written statement were absolutely false. The keys of the key safe and other money safe, steel almirah and their keys were not reaching the Branch; so the key register was not opened or maintained at the relevant time. On 12.7.66 the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 to start with the business of the day opened the lock of the cover door and grill door and then locks of the steel almirah where the money was kept. The defendant No. 1 then bought out cash, Cash Books, Vault Register, Cash Analysis Book and Cash Balance Book from within the almirah. Armed Guard Abu Taher was present there. The defendant No. 3 who had been suffering from dysentery from 2/3 days before suddenly felt a motion and for that hurrying up his duties of closing die door of the almirah, grill door and cover door rushed to the privy leaving instructions to the defendant No. 1 that he would sign vault register after return from the privy. On his return he found that the defendant No.1 had started business transaction. On being asked the defendant No. 1 told that everything was all right. The defendant No. 3 on bonafide belief and good faith and also on account of pressure of official works proceeded with his duties. At the end of the working day when the defendant No.1 produced before him the Cash Balance Book and other registers including the Vault Register showing a Cash Balance of Tk. 1,23,595/83 paisa and began insisting for his signatures with unusual haste and this defendant put his signatures with a mind to verify the cash afterwards. The restless conduct of the defendant No. 1 at that time raised suspicion in the mind of the defendant No. 3. The defendant No. 3 and armed guard Abu Taher verified the cash of the Cash Balance Book and found a shortage of Tk. 19000.00 A statement showing the shortage of the amount of Tk. 19000.00 by denomination of currency notes was obtained by the defendant No. 3. Before signing the Cash Balance Book and other books of the records the defendant No. 3 could not check and verify the physical position of cash due to the clever tactics adopted by the defendant No. 1 and after closing of the business transaction the defendant No. 1 did not hand over the cash to the defendant No. 3. Nurul Islam Bhuiyan came on 14.7.66 for inquiry and on his verification of Cashier's hand balance a further shortage of Tk. 50.12 paisa was found. The defendant No. 3 informed the Officer-in-Charge Ajmiriganj police station and also telegraphically informed the Principal Office, Dhaka on 12.7.66 regarding the shortage of the cash and for sending an investigating Officer immediately mentioning that the strong room remained open. This defendant No. 3 also informed Dr. Kripendra Barman, A Rob Patwari andmany others about the incident on 12.7.66. The defendant No. 3 along with the staff went to the Thana on 12.7.66 and informed the Officer-in-Charge, Ajmiriganj PS about the occurrence verbally and lodged FIR on 13.7.66. The OC Ajmiriganj went to the Bank on 13.7.66 at about 9-00 AM and tried to count the cash but the defendant No. 1 did not allow. The officer-in-charge therefore sealed the door of the record room within which the strong room is situated. On interrogation by the Officer-in-Charge the defendant No. 1 told that the missing cash was stolen by a thief by breaking the door of the strong room. Before arrival of the OC, Circle Officer (Dev), Thana Agricultural Officer, Malu Mia, son of the owner of the building and leading businessman viz. Siraj Mia visited the Bank. On interrogation by the Circle Officer (Dev), the defendant No. 1 in presence of the gentlemen said that the matter was simple and could be amicably settled up if it had not been published or circulated by the defendant No. 3. He again said that he made over the money to the defendant No. 3 on 12.7.66 against payment of a Bank draft and that the draft would be given afterwards. From the report of Nurul Islam Bhuiyan the Investigating Officer of the Bank to the Officer on Special Duty of the Bank dated 16.7.66 it would appear that the defendant No. 3 did not know how the shortfall was made. The defendant No. 1 told Nurul Islam Bhuiyan on the same date that on 12.7.66 during the transaction hour the defendant No. 3 took a sum of Tk. 19000.00 from him for making payment to a constituent giving an understanding that the cheque for the amount would be given afterwards but the defendant No. 3 later on did not give him the cheque and the defendant No. 1 waited till 5 PM and closed the cash keeping the amount short in the vault. The defendant No. 1 made many other contradictory and false statements both orally and in writing to the plaintiff Bank and from all these the Investigating Officer and the Bank were satisfied that the defendant No. 1 used to reside in the western room of the 2nd floor of the building and the defendant No. 3 used to reside in the middle room of that floor. 2/3 days before the occurrence defendant No. 1 wanted to shift to the room of defendant No. 3 on the allegation that he was not feeling comfortable to live in the western room and the defendant No. 3 allowed the defendant No. 1 to live in his room. The defendant No. 3 used to keep his keys under his bed. The defendant No. 1 stole one key of the defendant No. 3 and managed to place the same on the floor of the strong room which was discovered by the I0 during the investigation. After discovery of the shortage amount of Tk. 19000.00 in the afternoon of 12.7.66 the defendant No. 3 wanted to cheek the remaining Cashier's hand balance but the defendant No. 1 hurriedly closed the Steel Almirah and the grill door and left for up-stairs. The defendant No. 3 did not close the cover door and he with his staff ran to Ajmiriganj Police Station for lodging the complaint about the incident. One Bazlur Rahman, brother of defendant No. 1 and one Abdul Hakim, sister's husband of defendant No. 1 came to Ajmiriganj on 9.7.66 to meet the defendant No. 1. Abdul Hakim left the place on the same day, but Bazlur Rahman continued to stay at Ajmiriganj and left the place on the evening of 12.7.66 the day of occurrence. The said Abdul Hakim mysteriously arrived at Ajmiriganj just after defendant No. 1 was arrested by Police on 14.7.66 and demanded to take away the belonging of defendant No. 1. The movements of the relatives of the defendant No. 1 as stated above were very much suspicious. The defendant No. 1 during the absence of defendant No. 3 on call of nature committed theft of Tk. 19050.12 paisa from the cash and passed on the money through his brother Bazlur Rahman during the banking transaction hour. The defendant No. 3 was falsely implicated in the suit and the suit is barred by limitation against this defendant. The Cashier, the defendant No. 1, was the main custodian of the cash and was personally responsible to make good any loss, defalcation or shortage of cash. The defendant No. 3, the Manager had only a supervisory duty over the defendant No. 1 and not over the cash and hence the defendant No. 3 cannot be held liable for any defalcation of shortage of the cash. The plaintiff found the defendant No. 1 guilty and dismissed him from service and also proceeded against him in criminal case. The plaintiff was aware of the character and conduct of the defendant No. 1 who caused shortfalls and defalcation in his service earlier. The plaintiff should not have added this defendant No. 3 in this suit which is liable to be dismissed against him with costs.

6. At the trial the learned Subordinate Judge framed the following issues :

"1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form ?

2. Is the suit bad for non-joinder and misjoinder of parties ?

3. Is the suit barred by limitation ?

4. Was there a defalcation as alleged in the plaint, and if so, who is responsible and liable for the alleged defalcation ?

5. To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled ?"

7. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on contest with cost against the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 respectively and ex parte against defendant No. 2 with direction that the plaintiff would get a decree for Tk. 19050.12 paisa plus cost thereof against the defendants. The findings that the suit was not barred by limitation, that both the defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 3 were jointly and equally liable for the defalcation and that the plaintiff should first try to realise the amount from both the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 3 to the extent of 50% each and in case of failure the entire decretal amount might be realised from the defendant No. 2, the Bangladesh Insurance who did not contest the suit and agreed to abide by the result of the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge dated 8.2.74 the added defendant No. 3 preferred this appeal to this Court.

8. BK Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant No. 3 appellant, has not argued the appeal on merit but he has argued the appeal only on point of law. His first submission is that the learned Subordinate Judge had erred in not holding that the suit is not barred against the defendant No. 3 under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 22(1) of the Limitation Act as the cause of action for the suit arose on 12.7.66 and the defendant No. 3 was added as party in the suit on 10.6.70. In support of his submission he has relied on the case of Messers Chand Oil Mills Vs. Haji M Muhammad Zakaria & Co. & 2 others, PLD 1958 Kar. 510. His second submission is that even after the addition of defendant No. 3 as party in the suit the plaint was not amended as per Order 1 rule10 (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and no allegation of defalcation was made and no relief was prayed for against the defendant No. 3 but on the other hand, the plaintiff claimed in paragraph No. 4 of the plaint that the defendant No. 1 and not defendant No. 3 was responsible for the defalcation and as such the issue No. 4, namely," was there a defalcation as alleged in the plaint, and if so, who is responsible and liable for the alleged defalcation ?" cannot include defendant No. 3 and the decree passed against defendant No. 3 is not sustainable in law. In support of this submission he had relied on the case of Md. Ibrahim Vs. Md. Alauddin and others, 27 DLR 413 and the case of Ranjit Kumar Rakshit Vs. Sudhir Kumar Chowdhury, 38 DLR 39.

9. In reply Mr. S H Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent No. 1, has submitted that under clause (b) of rule 4 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Subordinate Judge is justified in decreeing the suit against the added defendant No. 3 even in the absence of amendment of the plaint as it is found by the learned Subordinate Judge on evidence that the added defendant No. 3 is liable for the defalcation. He has next submitted that the addition of defendant No. 3 as party in the suit will take effect from the date of filing of the suit and therefore the suit is not barred against him under section 22(1) of the Limitation Act. He has further submitted that in view of the plaintiff's prayer (D) e.g." such other relief or relief, may be granted as the plaintiff may be entitled in law and equity", the Court is competent to pronounce judgment against the added defendant No. 3 on the evidence.

10. In PLD 1958 Kar 510 it has been held :

"A suit against a party joined at a later stage can be deemed to have been filed on the date when he was so made a party to the suit. Where such date fell beyond the period of limitation allowed by the Limitation Act, the suit was time barred against such party."

In the instant case the cause of action arose admittedly on 12.7.66 and the suit was filed on 11.7.69 within three years but the defendant No. 3 was added on 10.6.70 by Order No. 18 of the Trial Court. Order 1 rule 10 (5) provides as follows:

"5. Subject to the provisions of the (Limitation Act, IX of 1908). Section 22, the proceedings as against any person added as defendant shall be deemed to have begun only on the service of the summons."

Section 22(1) of the Limitation Act provides as follows:

"22(1) Where, after the institution of a suit, a new plaintiff or defendant is substituted or added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party."

Under section 22(1) of the Limitation Act the present suit will be deemed to have been instituted on 10.6.70 so far as the added defendant No. 3 is concerned as he was added as a party in the suit on 13.6.70. But before 10.6.70 the 3 years' limitation for filling the suit had expired and therefore the suit was barred against defendant No. 3 and this is exactly the view taken in the case reported in PI,D 1958 Kar. 510 and to which we fully agree.

11. Admittedly even after the addition of defendant No. 3 as party in the suit the plaint was not amended as required under Order 1, rule 10, Sub-rule (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows:

"Where a defendant is added, the plaint shall, unless the Court otherwise directs, be amended in such manner as may be necessary, and amended copies of the summons and of the plaint shall be served on the new defendant and, if the Court thinks fit, on the original defendant."

<u>12. Order 1, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, relied upon on behalf of respondent No. 1, runs as follows:</u>

<u>"4 Court may give judgment for or against one or more of joint parties. Judgment may be given without any amendment-</u>

<u>(a) for such one or more of the plaintiffs as may be found to be entitled to relief, for such relief as he or they may be entitled to :</u>

<u>(b) against such one or more of the defendants as may be found to be liable, according to their respective liabilities."</u>

<u>The plaintiff has claimed in paragraph 4 of his plaint that only defendant No. 1 and not defendant No. 3 was responsible for the alleged defalcation and no relief whatsoever was prayed for by the plaintiff against the added defendant No. 3 nor any allegation of defalcation was made against the added defendant. After the addition of defendant No. 3 as a party in the suit the plaintiff did not amend the plaint as required under Order 1 rule 10 sub-rule (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure making any allegation against the added defendant No. 3 as to defalcation. In such circumstances we hold the view that in determination of the question of fact namely, defalcation of the amount of Taka 19,050.12 the parties should not be allowed to lead evidence against the added defendant No. 3 and the issue No. 4 as quoted above cannot and will not include defendant No. 3 as a person to be responsible or liable for the alleged defalcation. In the absence of pleadings against the added defendant No. 3 the learned Subordinate Judge cannot allow the parties to lead evidence in the absence of pleading against the added defendant No. 3 and the learned Subordinate Judge has obviously erred in allowing the parties to lead evidence against the added defendant No. 3 and therefore the decree passed by him against added defendant No. 3 is not sustainable. This view finds support in decisions reported in 27 DLR 413 and in 38 DI,R 39. In 27 DLR 413 it.was held :</u>

<u>"In determination of question of facts the parties should not be allowed to lead evidence without proper pleadings. It is no longer a mere technicality that material facts should be specifically pleaded and omission to do so would certainly deprive the other side of an opportunity to meet the allegation. This salutary provision of law is designed as a safeguard so that one cannot be taken by surprise by the other side at the time of trial".</u>

<u>In the case reported in 38 DLR 39 the Trial Court allowed the plaintiff to introduce a new story (in his deposition and by production of documents) without amending the plaint. In these circumstances it was held in this case that such introduction of new story without amendment of the plaint was not permissible.</u>

13. The Order 1, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure relied upon on behalf of respondent No. 1 refers to plaintiff or defendant who is already in the suit and not to an added defendant who was added after the period of limitation from the cause of action. Prayer (D) in the plaint as quoted above cannot override the provision of Order 1, rule 10, sub-rule (5) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. None of the submissions of the learned Advocate for respondent No. 1 therefore has, stance but the submissions of the learned advocate for the defendant No. 3 appellant are of substance.

15. In the circumstance, it is found that the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge suffer from error and illegality calling for interference.

In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is dismissed on contest against the added defendant No. 3 without cost.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated 26.7.83 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Civil Order No. 234 of 1983.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.-This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order passed by a single judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 234 of 1983 summarily dismissing the application.

2. Plaintiff-appellant and the predecessor of respondents 3 to 6 instituted Title Suit No. 263 of 1975 in the First Court of Munsif, Gopalganj for a declaration that order of mutation dated 10.5.1975 was null and void and not binding upon them.

3. When the suit was thus pending it is alleged that the plaintiff intended for making a prayer for temporary injunction against the defendants restraining them from cutting away the paddy and for that purpose their lawyer obtained left hand thumb impression on some bank cartridge papers. But subsequently it was found that a false and bogus solenama was created for compromising the suit and the same was filed in the Court. The plaintiff challenged this solenama as fictitious and false for which a miscellaneous case was started being Misc. Case No. 71 of 1980.

4. Evidence was led by both the sides and the learned Munsif found that the solenama was not genuine and accordingly rejected it with a direction that the original suit be proceeded with. The learned Munsif found that in the so-called solenama nothing was mentioned about any consideration but in the evidence the defendants took the stand that they paid Tk; 5,000/- as consideration of the compromise. This story was disbelieved by the trial court.

5. On appeal by the defendants the Appellate Court below noticed that the evidence was given as to the genuineness of the solenama and the plaintiff failed to substantiate their case that they intended to file a petition for injunction. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Court below disbelieved the story of the plaintiff that the blank papers were converted fraudulently into a compromise petition. As to the consideration of Tk. 5,000/- it was noticed that though the consideration was not mentioned in the solenama itself but evidence was given as to the payment and the discrepancy with respect to denomination of notes for which the alleged payment was made "can be disregarded as minor one." In this view of the matter, the appeal was allowed and the solenama was treated as part of the decree.

6. In Civil Revision the matter came before the learned Single Judge and the learned Judge considered that the appellate court below arrived at a finding as to the passing of the consideration which need not be disturbed. Then posed the crucial question as to whether the interest of the minor plaintiffs had been protected in the solenama or not. It was noticed that the solenama contained signatures of all the plaintiffs. It was observed:

"There was no allegation at any stage of the Miscellaneous case that the interest of the minor plaintiffs were not protected in the solenama in question. In that view of the matter the plea appears to be it belated one." The revisional application was dismissed summarily.

<u>7. Leave was granted to consider the question whether alleged solenama could be treated as a part of the decree when there was no permission from the Court for compromising the suit on behalf of the minors as required by rule 7 of Order 32 of the Code of Civil procedure.</u>

8. At the time of hearing of the appeal the appellant submitted in person that he was unable to engage a Counsel be. came of his poverty. He is a rickshawala but he prayed for justice. Mr , Abdul Malek a Senior Advocate voluntarily offered his service to appear and conduct the case on behalf of the appellant and also as amicus curiae.

9. Mr. Abdul Malek fairly placed the facts of the case and then placed the scheme of Order 32 of the Civil Procedure Code and pointed out that when the mother was acting as next friend in the suit of the plaintiff Rule 6 clearly prohibits acceptance of any money for compromise of any suit without the leave of the court. The learned counsel submitted that the payment of Tk, 5,000/- was disbelieved by the trial Court and the discrepancy in the evidence as to the payment was ignored by the appellate court below, the High Court Division simply overlooked the point. Mr. Abdul Malek pointed out in the setting of Rule 6 the case of the defendants does not stand scrutiny that they had made any payment and the worse situation comes when Rule 7 in the mandatory term prohibits compromise without leave of tile Court which must be expressly recorded in the proceeding and in the absence of such compromise shall be voidable against all the persons and void against the minor.

<u>10. Reading the Provisions of Rules 6 and 7 of Order 32 there is no hesitation in saying that the High Court Division and the Appellate Court below erred in law in accepting such compromise and treating the fame as a part of the decree which is in violation of the Rules 6 and 7 of Order 32. The allegation of the plaintiffs was that the blank pacers were converted fraudulently into a compromise petition when thumb impressions were given on blank papers for filing an injunction petition. Be that as it may, taking the compromise petition on its face the least can be said that such compromise petition in a suit in which a plaintiff is minor cannot be compromised without leave of the Court. So far the minors are concerned it is void; as for the mother it is voidable. In this view of matter when both the mother and the minor plaintiffs disown such compromise petition, the only conclusion that can be made is that the trial Court was correct in rejecting the compromise and the High Court Division and the appellate Court erred in law in accepting the same.</u>

11. Before parting with the case it must be mentioned that the Court appreciated the gesture of Mr. Abdul Malek, who in painstaking manner submitted the case in full perspective and assisted the Court in coming to the conclusion in accordance with law. The Court records its appreciation for the free service rendered by Mr. Abdul Malek.

12. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed. The orders of the High Court Division and the appellate Court below are set aside and that of the trial Court is restored. The original suit will now proceed expeditiously from the stage where it was left. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
