vs. 
Hriday Ranjan Das being dead his heirs: Bimal Kanti Das and others ------Respondents:
case_source: From the judgment and order dated 7-6-84 passed by the High court Division, Chittagong, in Second Appeal No.456 of 1968.
full_judgment:
SHAHABUDDIN AHMED, J:- This is a plaintiffs appeal she won on merits in both the trial court and the lower appellate Court, but in second appeal she lost as the High Court Division found her suit barred by the principle of res judicata. Impugned decision of the High Court Division is in the judgment and decree dated 7 June 1984 in S.A. No. 456 of 1984, Chittagong Bench. Circumstances that led to this appeal are given in the following paragraphs.

2. The land in suit comprising plots Nos. 1958 and 1965 originally belonged to two brothers, Jaghabandhu and Hara Govinda to secure a loan they mortgaged it by a simple mortgage deed dated 15 November 1911 to Siristidhar, Thereafter they kot-mortgaged this land, by two registered mortgage-deeds dated 16-4-1916, to Pran Krishna who went into possession. Sristidhar filed Mortgage Suit No. 502 of 1921 against Jagabandhu and the heirs of Hard Govinda, got a decree and in execution of the decree, in Mortgage Execution Case No. 1615 of 1921, he himself purchased the land on 20 January 1922 and got delivery of possession through court on 28 June 1923. But as he did not implead in his Mortgag Suit the second mortgagee in possession, namely, Pran Krishna, it is alleged, Sristidhar was going to initiate legal action against Pran Krishna to recover possession, but Pran Krishna amicably settled the matter and delivered possession to him. Thus getting possession Sristidhar sold the land to Akhil and Hara Das by a Kabala dated 25 February 1924; Akhil and Haradas then sold the land to Chandra Bala (the plaintiff) by a kabala dated 8 October 1926.

3. Hriday Ranjan Das, son of Jagabandhu, filed two Redemption suits-Suits Nos. 13 and 14 of 1952 against the heirs of Pran Krishna impleading Chandra Bala as one of the defendants. In these two suits Chndra Bala filed an application to be transposed on the side of the plaintiff (Hriday) but her application was rejected; both the suits were decreed on contest on 23 June 1955. Chandra Bala, alleging that she was not bound by the decree in the Redemption suits, filed the instant suit, Other Suit No. 88 of 1957, in the First Court of Munsif, Satkania, for declaration of her title to the suit land and confirmation of possession in 2nd/3rd share and recovery of possession in the remaining 1/3rd share of the suit land on the basis of her equity of redemption.

4. Defendant No. 1 (Hriday) contcsted the suit denying title and possession of Chandra Bala contending that she got no title to-the land and that her right of redemption, if any, was barred by limitation and, above all her suit itself was barred by the principle of res-judicata in view of the decision against her in the two Redemption Suits; he also alleged that Chandra Bala was setup by her brother Khemesh who had unsuccessfully contested the Redemption Suits as defendant No.3,

<u>5. The trial Court by judgment dated 27 August 1959 decreed the suit holding that the suit was not barred by limitation or by res judicata and that the plaintiff was in possession as Sristidhar and had obtained possession amicably from Pran Krishna Defendant No.1 preferred an appeal, Other Appeal No. 463 of 1959 which, after going through two rounds, was finally disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Chittagong .by his judgment dated 31 March 1967. By this judgment the trial Court's decision was confirmed with a modification that instead of confirmation of possession the plaintiff would recover possession. Defendant No. 1 preferred a second appeal as already mentioned- S.A. No. 456 of 1984 which the learned Single Judge allowed by judgment dated 7 June 1984: the learned Single Judge, on setting aside the judgments of the courts below, dismissed the suit on a finding that the suit was hit by res judicata in view of the decision the two Redemption Suits. Against this decision leave was granted by us to consider the question whether the principle of res judicata was applied by the High Court Division on proper appreciation of facts and correct interpretation of law involved in this ease.</u>

6. Facts of the case thougha little complicated, are not seriously disputed except in the case of possession, and as such it is a case mainly involving questions of law. The original parties in the case have been changed. Chandra Bala died whereupon her heirs have been substituted; they are now appellants before us. Hriday Ranjan Das, defendant No. 1. (son of Jagabandhu, one of the two brothers who bad created the mortgage) is also dead and his heirs are on record by substitution; they arc contesting this appeal. There is no dispute that Sristidhar the first mortgagee instituted Mortgage Suit No. 502 of 1921, obtained a decree and in execution of the decree purchased the land on 20 January 1922 and got delivery of possession through court on 28 June 1923. But he could not get actual possession of the land as the puisne mortgagee, Pran Krishna, was admittedly in possession. Pran Krishna was not made a party by Srisudhar in his Mortgage suit. Plaintiff, Chandra Bala claimed that Sristidhar was going to take legal action to recover possession from Pran Krishna whereupon the latter amicably gave up possession. This claim has been found to be totally baseless by the learned Subordinate Judge who, in Title Appeal No. 463 of 1959, modified the trial Court's decision In respect of possession holding that Chandra Bala was not in possession; that is why the trial Court's decree for confirmation of possession -was modified directing recovery of possession. That Sristidhar did not go into possession gets support from transferes of the land in. quick succession he transferred to Akhil and Haradas on 25-2-1924 and they also transferred it to Chandra Bala on 8-10-26. Now the position is that the first mortgagee claiming under a simple mortgage got a decree in the mortgage suit without impleading the second mortgagee in possession and that neither the first mortgagee auction purchaser nor his successive transferees, such as Akhil and Haradas and thereafter Chandra Bala, took any legal action for recogery of possession or to be redeemed by the second mortgagee on payment of the mortgage money till Chandra Balathe third trasnferee, filed the instant suit in 1957- 35 years after the decree in the mortgage suit for declaration of her title and confirmation of possession on the basis of equity of redemption. But before that her claim to equity of redemption was held barred in the two redemption Suits which she contested but did not take any step to challenge the decision against her. Her contention is that as the suits were dismissed against her she had no occasion to go further in appeal against the adverse finding in those suits it is to be scan how far this proposition can be accepted.

<u>7. Mr. S.R. Pal learned Counsel for the appellants has referred to section 91 of the Transfer of Property Act and he made a lengthy submission as to rights and interests of a mortgagee-auction-purchaser on a suit for enforcement of mortgage. He has contended that when a prior mortgagee brings the mortgage property to sale and himself purchases if he acquires the equity of redemption. He has explained that the auction-purchaser of a mortgage-property acquires all the eights and interests of the mortgagor as they stood when the mortgage was created as against an auction-purchaser in any other case who purchascs the judgment debtor's rights and interests as they exist at the time of the sale. Mr. Pal has also submitted that after the equity of redemption has passed out of the mortgage to the mortgagee purchaser, there can be no question of revival of such right in the mortgagor when the puisne mortgagee attempts to redeem the prior mortgagee. In support of this proposition of law he has referred to a number of decisions including a decision of the Kerala High Court in the case of Kurumpakochika v. Narayana Pillai. AIR 1959 (Ker) 56. We have hardly any dispute about the correctness of this proposition of law but in the instant case it is to be seen how far this proposition can help the appellants; heirs of Chandra Bala, who had no doubt stepped into the shoes of the first mortgagee auction-puchaser. The question whether the equity of redemption was revived in the mortgagor was relevant in the Redemption suit Nos. 13 and 14 the decree in those suits has not been reversed and as such it stands.</u>

<u>In this appeal arising out of a separate suit the question is whether this suit is barred by res judicata. The first, mortgagee it should be remembered, filed the mortgage suit without impleading the second martgagce in possession and ultimately purchased the land. The pertinent question is what he actually acquired thereby? According to Nasim Ali J, of the Calcutta High Court, he acquired nothing, as the ownership of he equity of redemption was wholly unrepresented in his suit. The learned judge elucidated the law as to right of such a purchaser in a Letters Patent appeal. "Dhapubhai Mini v. Chandra Nath 42 CWN 721 in the following words:</u>

<u>"A simple mortgage is a contract creating a personal obligation to repay the loan. It also operates as a conveyance of an interest in the property mortgaged. The interest which passes to the mortgagee is not the ownership of the properly which, not with standing the mortgage remains in the mortgagor together with the right of redemption. The mortgagor, parts only with the right of sale and nothing more.. An action to enforce mortgage is not properly constituted unless any person who has an interest either in the security or in the right of redemption is joined as a party (Ord. 34, rule 1 C.P.C.)...If however the equity of redemption is wholly unrepresented in the action the purchaser of the mortgage sale acquires nothing. He does not get the right of redemption which includes the right to possess the mortgage properly ... Plaintiff in the present case cannot fall back on the mortgage admittedly the right to enforce the mortgage was barred by limitation before the institution of the present suit. She cannot therefore compel the defendants No. 1 to 4 to redeem her."</u>

8. Facts of that case are that defendants 5 and 6 mortgaged their land (schedule 1) to the plaintiff by a simple mortgage deed dated 17 January 1917. Plaintiff by filing a Mortgage suit and obtaining a decree purchased the land on 26 August 1930 and got delivery of possession through court. In 1935 defendants Nos. 14 erected a building in one part of the land (schedule II) claiming to be lessees in possession under lease deed dated 15 December 1920 executed by defendants 5 and 6but those defendants. 1-4 were not made parties in the Mortgage suit when the plaintiff filed another suit on 25 December 1935 to recover possession from defendants 1-4, they contended that they were not bound by the decrees in the Mortgage suit. Finally their contention was upheld in the Letters Patent Appeal, recovery of possession from them was. refused and the plaintiffs claim to be redeemed by them was also found barred by limitation under Article 132. Limitation Act. In two other suits of this nature, this principle of law was followed. In Guru Prasa Sukul v. Tarini Chandra Debnath, 42 CWN 1065. the first mortgage-auction-purchasers right LO be redeemed by the second mortgage was held barred by limitation in Bipra Charan v. Rupeswari Das, 57 CWN, 707, the mortgagor's right to be redeemed by the lessee in possession was refused as it was barred by limitation. This principle of law has been applied by the learned Munsfi who decreed the two Redemption suits on consideration of the facts given below:

9. Chandra Bala was defendant No. 10 in Redemption. Suit No. 13 and defendant No. 14 in Redemption Suit No. 14. The Judgment in those two suits, Ext. B, shows that Chandra Bala had first disputed the right of redemption claimed by the plaintiff of those suits, namely mortgagor's son and then she switched on to her claim to the right of redemption and made an application to be transposed to the side of the plaintiff. The learned Munsif on discussing the evidence observed:

"I have shown that there is no evidence that Sristidhar got possession of the plots Nos. 1958-1965 or that he compelled Duuas (second mortgagee's family ) to redeem his or that Dutta redeemed the simple mortgage, It is unbelievable that Duttas gave up possession of, the said plots who were not parties in the suit filed by Sristidhar, As such the proper remedy of Sristidhar or his transferees was to sue for sale against the persons left out when he could compel them to redeem if the mortgage was legally enforceable, that is, it was not barred by limitation. As the mortgage of Sristidhar became barred by limitation, he, or Akhil or Chandra Bala, can have no, right of possession of those plots. The idea of Chandra Bala now trying to become a plaintiffis to revive a right which she has lost on the bar of limitation, Obviously Chandra Bala wants to redeem, to have a chance of claiming he title in the plots 1958-1965 which she could not do as in transferee from prior mortgagee auction purchaser and she cannot be given a barred right which is otherwise barred by limitation."

<u>10. In this appeal, we are not to see if that judgment is correct, but we are to see whether the adverse finding in that judgment of the two previous suit operates as res judicata in the instant suit. Mr. Pal has contended that it will not operate as res judicate in that those two suits were dismissed so far as defendant Chandra Bala was concerned and that as there was no occasion for her'  to challenge those findings in appeal this finding cannot be accepted as final to operate 1S res judicata. In support of this contention he has relied upon a number of cases. The first case he has referred to is Midnapore Zamindary Co. v. Naresh Chandra Roy, AIR 1922 PC 241. In that case a landlord sued his tenant for khas possession but the tenant took the aplca of occupancy right. In a previous suit by the landlord's father against the tenant the same pica of his occupancy right was taken along with a plea that the suit was not maintainable being 'premature'. The plea of occupancy right was rejected, but the other plea that the, suit was premature and therefore not maintainable was accepted and the suit was dismissed. In the subsequent suit the question arose whether the decision in the earlier suit that the tenant had no occupancy right would be a res judicata. The matter ultimately went to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council where their Lordships held:</u>

<u>"Their Lordships do not consider that this will be found an actual plea of res judicata, for the defendants having succeeded on the other plea, had no occasion to go further as to the finding against them."</u>

11. The next case cued by Mr. Pal is Abhay Ram v. Jhanda, AIR 1929 (All) 910. In that case  the question that arose was whether a finding in the previous suit which was dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff had no right to "continue the suit could operate as res judicata in favour of sons of the plaintiff in the subsequent suit. It was held that the finding being not "conclusive" could not be u res judicata in the subsequent suit, Sulaiman J., as his Lordship then was, observed that "Il finding cannot be conclusive against a party if the decree is not based upon it but is made in spite of it. Such a finding against the plaintiff cannot found a plea of res judicata when they succeed on other pleas and have no occasion to go further, as to the finding against them." The next casecited by Mr. Pal is "Thakur Magundeo v. Thakur Mahadeo Singh," 18 ILR Cal. 647. It was also a suit for ejectment of a tenant from a land carted by the landlord as" "majhes land," ordinarily cultivated by the landlord himself or by thicadar. In a previous suit the tenant  had pleaded his right of occupancy. The Court rejected the tenant's plea and found that the land was 'Majhes land', but dismissed the suit on the ground that no valid notice to quit was served upon the, tenant. In the subsequent suit the decision as to the character of the land, whether the tenant had occupancy right or the landlord held it as majhes land, was not held to be res judicata.

12. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel for the respondents, while accepting the general proposition of law that when a suit is dismissed the adverse finding in the decree against the defendant will not ordinarily operate as res judicata, has contended that this proposition has no unvicrsl application for, he argues, when such a decision forms the fundamental part of the decree then it will operate as res judicata, no matter the suit has been dismissed against the defendant. In supprt of this contention the learned Counsel has relied upon a number of decisions.

13. In the case of Chockalingam v. Sccthai Acha, AIR 1927 PC 252, the plaintiff in a previous suit sought a declaration against defendant No. 1 that a sale-deed executed in his favour was invalid; the other defendants were transferees from defendant No.1; the suit was dismissed against all the defendants with a finding that the sale-deed was valid as between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. The plaintiff filed an appeal against the other defendants who were subsequent transferees of defendant No.1, but without making defendant No.1 as respondent in the appeal, It was held that " owing to the failure to make the defendant 1, a respondent, there was no appeal [rom this finding, which had consequently become res judicata as between the plaintiff and the first defendant, and must also be regarded as res judicata against the  respondents, who claimed through the first defendant, In the case of Sham Nath Madan v . Mohammad Abdullah, AIR 1967 IJ & K ) 65 a question arose whether an adverse finding against the defendant in previous suit which was dismissed would operate as res judicata in .1 subsequent suit between the same parties. It was held:

"It is true that generally an adverse finding against a defendant inn decree for dismissal of the suit would not operate as res judicata, but it is equally well settled that where such an adverse finding forms a fundamental part of the decree itself it operates as res judicata in spite of the fact that the decree is one of dismissal."

In the case of Murad Biswas v. Basti Mondal, AIR 1929 Cal.449, a suit was filed by landlord for ejectment of his under-raiyat. The defendant pleaded that he was a co-sharer and not a raiyat. The court rejected this plea holding the defendant to be an under-raiyat, but nevertheless, dismissed the suit on the ground that no notice to quit was served upon him by the landlord. In a subsequent suit between the same parties the plea that the defendant was a co-sharer and not an under raiyat was raised. The question was whether the suit was barred by res judicata in view of the finding in the previous suit and it was answered in the affirmative on the ground that the suit was not dismissed on a preliminary point but it was decided conclusively and as such the subsequent suit was hit by res judicata.

<u>14. On consideration of these two lines of decisions we rind hardly any conflict on the fundamental point. General principle is that an adverse finding against a defendant when the suit is dismissed is nut res judicata in a subsequent suit interpartics. But if the adverse finding is actually the decision of the suit and it forms a fundamental part of the decree, then it will operate as res judicata. Adverse finding against the defendant, if made incidentally or when it was not necessary for disposal of the suit or made in an interlocutory order, will not operate as res judicata. But in this case, Mr. Pal docs not say that the decision against Chandra Bala was made incidentally, unnecessarily or in any interlocutory order. His only argument is that the previous suits having been dismissed Chandra Bala had no scope to file appeal against the dedision. We do not think that Chandra Bala had no remedy against the decision against her, for when her application for transposition to become a co-plaintiff in those Suits was dismissed, she could have challenged it by appeal or by revisional application. She also could have filed a cross appeal when another contesting defendant (defendant No. 3) filed an appeal being S.A. No. 139 of 1957- against the decree, A copy of Memorandum of that Appeal has been produced before us by the learned Counsel for the respondent at the time of hearing of this appeal; no-reference to it was made before the courts below. Nevertheless, independent of this Memorandum of Appeal, it can be safely held that an adverse finding in any judgment of a suit dismissed, particularly when it is a conclusive decision in the suit, can be challenged in higher forums. Decision in the redemption suits was on the same issue which is the issue in the subsequent suit and as such, it is res judicate. It may be mentioned that a decision may be res judicata against co-defendants as well if there was conflict between them as held by the Privy Council in Munni Bibi v. Tirloki Nath, 53 ILR PC 103 and Kishun Prasad v. Durga Prashad. AIR 1931 PC. 231. On this analogy also the decision against Chandra Bala, in EXt. B, will operate as res judicata. We therefore, find that the High Court Division correctly applied the principle of res judicata and dismissed the suit.</u>

15. In the result the appeal is dismissed without however any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and decree dated 30th March, 1983 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka Bench, in Second Appeal No. 454 of 1974.
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman, J. This appeal by leave is at the instance of defendant Nos. 2 and 5.

2. Respondent No. 1, Hari Mohan Das, filed Title Suit No. 45 of 1972 in the 1st Court of Munsif Madaripur for specific performance of the contract, the defendants alleged to have entered with him on 10th Shraban 1375 B.S. corresponding to 29.7.1968 for sale of 0.32 acre of the suit land, in presence of P.W. 2 Abdur Rab Howladar, P.W. 3 Asmat Ali Mia and P.W.4 Mani Mohan Roy and others. On the disclosure of defendant No.1 Radhika Jiban Sil that a stamp paper and cartridge papers, purchased earlier on 17th February, 1967, were available for writing the documents the scribe Asmat Ali wrote the agreement to sell at the direction of the defendants. Defendants 1-3 signed the document and defendant Nos. 5 and G put their left thumb impressions on receiving Rs, 4,000/- from the plaintiff. Defendant No. 5 put the left thumb impression on her behalf, and en behalf of her minor son defendant No. 4. The plaintiff also purchased the defendants' huts on the suit land and was residing there. He also mode new huts there. As there was some legal difficulty in executing the kabala, the vendors being the members of the Minority Community, it was decided that they would execute the necessary document when that difficulty would be over. After putting the plaintiff in possession of the case land the defendants went to West Bengal. The plaintiff left the suit land when the Pakistani Army started operation in March, 1971 and returned borne after liberation of the country on 16th December, 1971. The defendants also came back from West Bengal. The plaintiff requested them to execute the kabala, but they refused to comply with his request. On humanitarian ground Mr. M. A. Razzaque, the local Com manlier of the Mukti Banini, allowed the defendants to live temporarily on the suit land by erecting a hut.

3. Defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 contested the suit. They denied the execution or any contract in favour of the plaintiff. Their case is that the homestead 00 the southern half share of the suit plot, measuring 0'78 acre, belonged to Mani Mohan Sil and Radaika Mohan Sit and the northern half share measuring 0'39 acre, belonged to Rudha Charan Sil and Puma Cuandra Sil were recorded in respect of their share. As Radha Charan Sil and Puma Chandra Sil left for India their share was declared as enemy property. From the share of defendant No. 1 and his brother 0'07 acre in the western side of the suit plot was acquired by Madaripur Municipality. Mani Mohan Sil died about 8/9 years back leaving behind. three sons, defendant Nos. 2-4, and one widow, defendant No. 5. Defendant No. 6 was the mother of defendant No. 1 Defendant Nos. 1 and 6 left for India about one and half year after the Indo-Pakistan  war in 1965. Their share was declared as enemy property. At the time of his migration to India defendant No. 1 Radhika Mohan Sil (now deceased) sold his hut on the suit land to the contesting defendants for Rs. 300/-. He handed over a blank stamp paper Rs, 1/8 and a demy paper, purchased by him on 11th February, 1967, with his signature on them as a token of the sale of the hut to defendants Nos. 2-5, In Shraban, 1375 B S. defendant Nos 2-5 sold that but to the plaintiff for Rs, 400/ and handed over the said blank stamp paper after putting their signatures thereon. The defendants feared that by using that stamp paper the plaintiff fabricated a forged document.

4. After considering that P. Ws. 2, 3 and 4 supported the plaintiff’s case and that defendants Nos. 1, 3 and 6 did not come to contest that case the trial Court decreed the suit.

5. The appellate Court, however, reversed the decision of the trial Court and dismissed the suit on the following findings: that the plaintiff examining himself as P.W. 1. could not give the knatian or plot number, or the area of the suit; land, nor he could give the year of his purchase! that he could not say when he went into possession of the suit land; that he admitted that he had no bank balance and cash money and be had no paper to show the payment (If Rs, 4,000/- to the defendants except the agreement to sell; that he also admitted that the defendants were living on the disputed land; that neither Abdur Razzaque nor anyone else was examined to say that the defendants were allowed to reside in the suit hand in the manner stated in the plaint; that the plaintiff's story that the defendants left the suit land immediately after the execution of the bainapatra on 29th July. 1963 was falsified by his own admission that he took lease of the suit land in the name of his wife after the same was treated as enemy property; that the petition for lease was filed on 1st September, 1968 i.e. nearly a month after the execution of the disputed bainapatra and that it was not probable that the suit land was declared as enemy property within a month after the execution of the bainapatra; that after the death of his wife the plaintiff took lease of the suit land in his own name; that he played hide and seek by not dis- closing the bainapatra in the applications for lease (Ext. C and C(1) nor about the lease in the plaint; that the Refugee Registration . Cards Ext. D series indicated that defendants crossed the East Pakistan border on 2 15t October, 1971 and that the plaintiff failed to point out that the defendants resided in any other places than the suit plot before leaving this country in 1971; that none of the P.Ws. could say the date or year of the alleged talk of sale; that the P.Ws. did not appear to be clean people as P.W. 2 falsely stated that he received summons from a peon, and P.Ws. 3 and 4, professional scribes, failed to corroborate each other; that in view of D.W. 1's unchallenged assertion that defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 6 were in India and the plaintiff's own admission that defendants Nos. 1 and 6 left for India and they were Dot in this country the trial Court erred in holding that defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 6 virtually admitted the plaintiff s claim by not appearing and contesting tile case; and that the suit was bad for defect of parties as admittedly the interest of defendant Nos. 1 and 6 was declared as an enemy property but the custodian of the enemy property was not impleaded in this case.

6. In second appeal the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division restored the judgment and decree of the trial Court and set aside those of the appellate Court after noting the following four faults there: (i) that the appellate Court's finding that the suit was bad for defect of parties was misconceived as no Objection was taken in this regard and, furthermore, the Government was impeded as a defendant under President Order No. 142 of 1972; (ii) that the inference made by the appellate court from Ext. C and C(1) was not maintainable as the claim for specific performance of contract was Dot inconsistent with the recitals in Ext. C and C(1) and that there was no scope for construing any admission by the plaintiff that the suit land was enemy property; (iii) that the observation of the appellate Court that P.Ws. were not clean people was Dot supported by the materials on record; (iv) and that though Abdur Razzaque., the Commander of the Mukti Bahini was dead, the appellate court erroneously took exception for not examining him as a witness.

<u>7. Leave was granted to consider whether the Learned Single Judge of the High Court Division exceeded his jurisdiction in second appeal in disturbing the finding of fact as to the genuineness of the disputed agreement to sell.</u>

<u>8. The plaintiff- respondent contends as the appellate Court's decision was based on suppositions without a correct construction of the evidence on record the High Court Division correctly interfered in the matter. In support of his contention reliance is placed on Mr. Altafur Rahman Vs. Tamijur Rahman, 30 DLR (SC) 236. Erfan Ali vs. Joynal Abedin 35 DLR (AD) 216-1983 BLD (AD) 342 and Sk. Abdul Latif and another Vs. Abdul Malek Kazi, 38 DLR (AD) 22.</u>

<u>The case reported in 30 DLR (SC) 236 arose out of a suit for setting aside a kabala executed by a Pardanasheen lady. Ignoring the unchallenged essential evidence of genealogy, given by P.W. 1, assuming corroborative evidence as substantive evidence and relying on D.W.T who was found by the trial court hesitating while deposing the lower appellate court reversed the finding of the trial Court that the questioned document was fraudulent and without consideration. The High Court interfered with that finding and decided the issues itself after resorting to section 103 of the Code. In upholding that decision it was held that the function of the High Court in a second appeal is not the mere correction of error of a legal proposition. or pointing out the true procedure but also to determine properly issues of fact after making the correct exposition of law, if such determination is essential for disposal of the appeal. Subject to this narrow jurisdiction of interference, the finding of fact of the first appellate court 'is conclusive and binding upon the High Court."</u>

<u>In 35 DLR (AD) 216 this court upheld the High Court Division's interference in second appeal with the lower appellate court's fin- ding of fact as to a tenancy, arrived at after excluding from its consideration the plaintiff's document of title and a long series of rent-receipts.</u>

<u>In 38 DLR (AD) 22 it is held that the second appellate court may reassess the evidence and come to its own finding where the appellate Court reversed the trial Court's finding of fact without taking any notice of a material document on record.</u>

9. In the instant case defect of party was not made an issue. The appellate Court does not appear to have dismissed the suit on that count. though it accepted the defendants" contention advanced at the time of the hearing of the appeal.' From the appellate Court's judgment it appears that the learned Judge knew that Abdur Razzaque was dead at the time of the trial but he inadvertently referred to him in considering the plaintiff's failure to examine anyone else in support of his case that the defendants were allowed by Abdur Razzaque to live on the land temporarily. Apart from the two slight mistakes the judgment of the appellate Court does not suffer from any legal infirmity. The plaintiff claimed to have entered into a contract for purchase of the suit land on 29-7-1968, but he himself subsequently applied for lease of the same land before the S.D.O., Madaripur. Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings). In the plaint he could explain his stand, but he did not do so. In his lease-application he was also silent about his contract. The Appellate Court rightly drew an inference adverse to the plaintiff, The defendants were admittedly in possession of the suit-land. It was explained in the plaint that they were allowed to live there by Abdur Razzaque, the Commander of the Mukti Bahini, As Abdur Razzaque was Dot alive at the time of the trial the plaintiff ought to have examined some one else to support his explanation, but he did not do that. The Appellate Court rightly inferred that defendants" possession in the suit-land remained unexplained. The Appellate Court's finding that PWs. were not clean people was a legal inference from the false and untrue statements of the witnesses.

10. In this case the plaintiff himself could not give the material facts relating to the disputed contract, the year of the alleged contract, the description or the quantum of the suit-land. He also failed to explain the defendants possession in the suit-land.

11. It was settled long ago in Najar Chandra Pal Vs. Sukur Sk. AIR 1918 PC 92 that the High Court should not interfere with the finding of fact on the ground that upon the documents and evidence placed before the lower Court the High Court would have come to a different conclusion.

<u>12. It appears that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division without going into the heart of the matter, namely the genuineness of the disputed contract, objected to some of the findings of the Appellate Court which did not produce any error or defect in the decision of the case upon the merits.</u>

13. In view of the above, we allow this appeal. The impugned judgment and decree are set aside and those of the lower Appellate Court affirmed. There will, however, be no order as to cost. The application for substitution is rejected.

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and decree dated 15-3-83 passed by the High Court Division. Comilla Bench, in SA No. 394 of 1967.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J : This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench in Second Appeal No. 394 of 1967.

2. Respondent 1-8 instituted Title Suit No. 174 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Moulvibazar, against the predecessor of the appellants as defendant No. 49 and others praying for declaration of their title in the suit land and for khas possession of their share on partition.

3. Main contesting defendant in the suit was defendant No. 49, who by filing a separate written statement contended that the first schedule of land of the written-statement was owned by him by virtue of purchase from one Mukhyadamoyee and others, and since purchase he is in possession thereof by paying rent to the landlords. He further contended that the second schedule of the land of the written-statement was taken by settlement from Taranl, plaintiff No. 6 on the basis of such purchase and settlement he is in possession of the suit land. Subsequently, plaintiff No. 1 demanded rent from this defendant on behalf of plaintiff No. 6 and on refusal to that the suit has been instituted out of grudge.

The trial court observed:

"PW 1 the plaintiff No. 1 has clearly stated in cross-examination that the defendants alleged first schedule land of WS does not appertain to the disputed lands."

Accordingly it excluded the first schedule land by observing:

"Thus this land claimed by the defendant No. 49 goes out of the consideration for the present suit land as the plaintiff have no claim for this."

4. The learned Munsif, however, rejected the claim of settlement in so far as the second schedule is concerned. The learned Munsif, however, while drawing up the decree did not leave out the first schedule land of the written statement of defendant No. 49, from the suit land to be partitioned. The Pleader Commissioner was appointed for the purpose of effecting partition who did not leave out the first schedule land of the written-statement of defendant No. 49, from partition and allotted it to the saham of the plaintiffs and the final decree was made accordingly on 20-7-63.

5. Defendant No. 49 preferred Title Appeal No. 438 of 1963 from the said final decree. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge while noticing the objection of defendant No. 49 observed that the preliminary decree had made the entitle suit land liable to partition and no appeal was taken against the preliminary decree in respect of the claim of defendant No. 49 regarding first schedule land of the written statement. It was observed:

"So no action can be taken not at this stage which may in any way affect the preliminary decree. A judgment cannot be interpreted to mean something other than what has been clearly decreed by the court. The final decree was in terms of the preliminary decree. So, I find no scope for interference with the final decree."

In this view of the matter, the appeal was dismissed.

6. In second appeal, the High Court Division took the same view by observing:

"This prayer cannot be granted at this stage unless the preliminary decree is set aside. In the preliminary decree the entire suit land was decree to be partitioned among the co-sharers. No appeal was referred against the preliminary decree. Hence there is no point in remanding the case for relayment of the kabala of the defendant after nearly 20 years.

In this view of the matter, the second appeal was dismissed.

7. Leave was granted to consider the question, in the context that the property in schedule I of the written-statement did not appertain to the lands in suit since the plaintiff had not claimed for the same, but through mistake the said first schedule land was not excluded from the preliminary decree for partition and the Pleader Commissioner allotted the said land to the plaintiff and the final decree was passed thereon. The contention of the learned Counsel was that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the preliminary decree cannot be corrected and modified in the appeal against the final decree.

8. Mr MH Khandker Learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants, pointed out that the Appellate Court below had erroneously taken the view of the law when it said that a judgment cannot be interpreted to mean something other than what has been clearly decreed by the court Mr. Khandker argued forcefully that this is a wrong view of the law and placed reliance on section 2 and Order 20 and rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. Mr. BN Chowdhury, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, argued on section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submitted that the courts below have correctly refused to amend the decree since no appeal had been filed against the preliminary decree.

Since an important question of law has been raised we allowed the learned Advocate to address the Court fully as it was a case of first impression.

10. Section 2(2) defines "decree Means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regards to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final, "The explanation adds: "A decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of. It is final when such adjudication completely disposes of the suit. It may be partly preliminary and partly final."

11. Order 20 deals with judgment and decree. Rule 6 (1) provides: "The decree shall agree with the judgment; it shall contain the number of the suit, the names and descriptions of the parties, and particulars of the claim, and shall specify clearly the relief granted or other determination of the suit."

12. Mr MH Khondker argued that the Appellate Court below was palpably wrong when it said, a judgment cannot be interpreted to mean something other than what has been clearly decreed by the court." There is no hesitation in saying that the Appellate Court below erroneously interpreted the law and the law is that the decree shall agree with the judgment. It has been noticed by both the Appellate Court and the High Court Division that the learned Munsif excluded the first schedule land of the Written statement from the suit and therefore, by no stretch of imagination it could be said that such land is liable to be partitioned when the trial court in its judgment excluded the land from the purview of the suit itself. It needs little imagination to say that this must have been the result of mistake. If it is a case of mistake, as it has been accepted by the courts below, then the only question is whether such mistake could not be rectified by taking resort to the provision of section 151 or 152 CPC. The Appellate Court below and the High Court Division found the impediment in doing so, because of presence of section 97 CPC section 97 reads as follows:

"Where any party aggrieved by a preliminary decree passed after the commencement of this Code does not appeal from such decree, it shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final decree."

13. Mr BN Chowdhury, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, contended that since the appellants did not file any appeal against the preliminary decree he is now precluded from disputing its correctness, Reliance was placed on the decision reported in AIR 1961 (SC) 790,42 IA 91, AIR 1965 (SC) 1325. The latter decision however explains the scope and ambit of section 97 CPC and the other two decisions laid down the proposition that when no appeal is filed against preliminary decree, the same cannot be challenged after the final decree. These two decisions have no manner of application in the facts of the present case.

14. The Code defines decree in section 2(2) which conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit. The trial court expressly excluded the first schedule land of the written-statement, in as much as, the plaintiff has no claim for this. It observed:

"Thus this land claimed by the defdt No. 49 goes out of the consideration for the present suit and as the plaintiffs have no claim for this."

This was also noticed by the Appellate Court "because the plaintiff did not claim it. Even then the Courts below have found it difficult to accede to the prayer of the appellants. This first schedule land of written statement was never in controversy in the suit and the mistake crept in while drawing up the decree.

15. The question is whether the decree could be amended even now. As far back in 1882 the Court of Appeal in English in In re Swire Mellor vs Swire reported in LR 1885 (CD) 239 this point was considered. Gotton L, J. observed;

"The Court will not allowed order to stand which does not express what the Court intended an order containing a declaration on a point which was not before the Court at all."

In that case, the question was whether certain property was included in the decree. The Court allowed the amendment by saying:

"Therefore, in my opinion. We ought to strike out from the order as passed and entered the words. "and proceeds of investment of profits" and also the reference to the collieries in which the testator was not interested at the time of his death, as they relate to what was no part of the matter then before us, and therefore, do not express our judgment."

Accordingly the decree was amended. The Court further noticed; we are not now making a new order on the appeal, but simply amending the record because it does not correctly state what the order of the Court was."

16. A similar question came before the House of Lords in the case of Henry William Hatton v Hugh Harris reported in 1892 LR (AC) 547. It was argued that forty years have passed since the decree came, after such a lapse of time the decree must stand, whether it be right or wrong; it cannot be touched now. This contention was repelled and Lord McNaughton observed:

'I am of the opinion that there is a mistake in the decree of 1853, occasioned by an accidental omission and that mistake ought to have been corrected as a matter of course."

Report was taken to the provision of general Order of 1843 which provides that any clerical mistake in a decree or any error arising from an accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected on an application and accordingly in that case the decree was corrected, "because that mistake ought to have been corrected as a matter of course."

17. In Seth Manakchand vs Chaube Manoharlal and another reported in 48 CWN 435 the Privy Council considered the question and observed:

"The question was what the decree meant and in interpreting the decree no document was so directly in point as the judgment. Where the judgment expressly said that the appellant's interests were not affected, it was a mistake in method to read the general words of the decree as covering those very interests by reference to the mortgage deed and erroneous to direct execution of the decree passed in the absence of the Appellant, so as to affect his interest.

In that case the question was whether the respondents are entitled to recover possession from the appellant for four annas share in a village called Chip bad. The Privy Council considered that the appellant was no party to the proceedings as he claimed paramount title. It was viewed that a party who is dismissed from the suit on the ground that he has no concern with it, he is no longer a party to the suit and he is not bound by the decree. The Privy Council, therefore, held that the order to eject the appellant was irregular and unjustified, inasmuch as, his interests were not affected and it was a mere mistake in drawing up the decree.

<u>18. In RMKRM Somasundaram Chetty vs MRMVL Subramaninam Chetty reported in AIR 1926 (PC) 136 the Privy Council re-iterated the principle as follows:</u>

<u>"The only cases in which the Court can interfere after the passing and entering of the judgment are (1) where there has been an accident or slip in the judgment as drawn up, in which case the Court has power to rectify it; and (2) where the Court itself finds the judgment as drawn up does not correctly state what the Court actually decided and intended."</u>

<u>19. Coming to the Indian subcontinent in the case of CK Mukhopadya vs SMB Debi reported in AIR 1924 (Cal) 895 it will be seen that the Calcutta High Court took consistent view that the Court by taking resort to section 152 CPC can amend decree to conform to the judgment at any time and there is no time limit to such amendment. In that case in a partition suit Commissioner was appointed for allotting the shares. The dispute was between defendant No.8 who was a petitioner and defendant No. 7, the opposite-party. The two plots allotted to those defendants were contiguous. It was agreed that defendant No. 8, the petitioner, should give a road over his plot No. 8 to defendant No. 7 and in exchange got a 2 feet wide strip of land east to west being the northern portion of plot No. 7. Ali these terms were embodied in the judgment. The decree, however though it mentioned that a way will be kept over plot 8 for access to plot No. 7 from the north, did not mention the 2 cubits wide strip of land to be allotted to defendant No. 8 The defendant No. 8 accordingly applied to have that clause inserted in the decree and to make it conform to the judgment. The Division Bench after reviewing the decisions noticed that the preponderance of opinion in the sub-continent and also in English is that it is the duty of the Court to amend the decree when it is brought to its notice that it does not agree with the judgment. The necessary amendments were made in that case.</u>

<u>20. Even a decree was amended after determination of the appeal to the Privy Council. In Ahidhar Ghosh vs Secretary of the state reported in 36 CWN 605 the Calcutta High Court noticed that the judgment of the High Court had been affirmed by the Privy Council and after the disposal of the Privy Council the appellant for the first time discovered that in the High Court decree against him the item of court fees paid by the other side on their memorandum of appeal to the High Court had been included twice in the costs. Rankin, CJ considered the question that "the memorandum of appeal of the High Court had been included twice over in the decree drawn up and signed by the judges of the High Court. The said mistake being discovered at this stage had not been made one of the grounds of the appeal to the Privy Council." The Court found precedent for such amendment by correcting the mistake and found that in a previous appeal before the Privy Council a mistake was detected after its disposal and that mistake was rectified by the Calcutta High Court and accordingly, the Court ordered:</u>

<u>"Let the decree of this Court be amended by correcting the mistake as prayed for in the petition".</u>

21. In Khandesh Laxmi Villas Millis Co. Ltd vs Graduate Coal Concern Jalgaon reported in 59 ILR (Bombay) 158 a decree was amended by the trial Court under section 152 so as to bring the name of the applicant upon the decree as judgment debtor. It was contended that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to amend the final decree at this stage of the proceeding since he was functus officio. The Bombay High Court repelled the contention and upheld the order of the trial Court for amending the decree "in such a way as to bring it into conformity with the meaning of the Court which ordered the decree to be passed."

<u>22. It is necessary to multiply instance when the various High Courts of India had taken uniform view that the Court can always amend the decree if there is a mistake that had crept in for bringing the decree in conformity with the judgment.</u>

<u>23. In CP No. 180 of 1974 Mahabubul Huq vs Abdul Huq this Court approved the order of the learned Munsif when he vacated his earlier order when the mistake that occurred due to the lapse of the dealing assistant. The High Court affirmed the order as having been made under section 152 CPC and this Court observed "the impugned order was passed in the ends of justice so that the defendants should not be made to suffer for no fault of their own. The impugned order merely restores the matter to where it was before the order No. 3 was passed due to the fault of the Court."</u>

<u>24. Applying these principles we have no hesitation that it was a clear case of mistake which had crept in drawing up the decree when the judgment of the trial Court expressly excluded the first schedule of the written statement belonging to defendant No. 49, who is the appellant before us. That property was never in "controversy in the suit" and the plaintiffs did not claim that property. When this is the position then a clear case of mistake is made out and keeping in mind the consistent judicial pronouncement since 1882 we have no hesitation in saying that the decree is liable to be amended by excluding the first schedule of the written-statement of the appellant by taking resort to the provision of section 152 CPC.</u>

<u>25. Section 97 CPC has no manner of application in the facts of this case. We are respectfully in agreement with the Supreme Court of India when it said in Chittoari Subbanna vs Kudappa Subbanna and others reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 1325 (1332) that the object of section 97 is that questions which had been urged by the parties and decided by the Court at the stage of the preliminary decree will not be open for agitation at the stage of the preparation of the final decree and would be taken as finally decided if no appeal had been preferred against the preliminary decree. In the present case, as has been noticed that schedule-l of the written statement was expressly excluded from the adjudication and therefore, it could not be a matter which was decided by the Court at the stage of preliminary decree. As such section 97 has no application.</u>

26. Accordingly, we allow this appeal and set aside the judgments of the Courts below and direct the trial Court to amend the decree so as to bring it in conformity with the judgment by excluding first schedule land of the written-statement of the appellant, who figured as defendant No. 49 in the partition suit.

In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

Rokanuddin Mahmud with Murad Reza, Advocates ------- For the Petitioner.

parties:

full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Chowdhury, J. : This rule arises out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against an order dated 2.9.90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Money Suit No. 32 of 1990. decreeing the suit in part on admission made by the defendant-petitioner in his pleading in suit.

2. Facts leading to this in short is that, MM Aziz as plaintiff filed a suit being Money Suit No. 32 of 1990 in the court of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong for realisation of Tk. 11,44,254.00 against defendant-petitioner namely M/s. A Elahee & Co represented by its proprietor Md. Ishaque, 366, Strand Road, Majhirghat, Chittagong on the allegation that defendant-petitioner M/s A Elahee & Co. who was engaged by the Government to carry Urea of Fertilizer Factory Ltd. to the jetty and other places by road/railways engaged the plaintiff vide letter dated 16.8.89 for supplying trucks and labourers for such carriage and for loading and unloading of Urea Fertilizer from the godown to the jetty side. The plaintiff started carrying urea on and from 16.8.89 and delivered the said to the jetty. The defendant namely M/s A Elahee & Co. after two months engaged one Jahirul Alam to look after his work. The plaintiff carried 23.173 tons of urea from the godown to the jetty which were thereafter carried by river boats by Progati Paribahan and 29847 tons of urea were carried from the godown to the jetty by defendant direct there from by road/railway. The plaintiff submitted 10 bills for Tk. 15.44,254.00 out of which defendant Co. paid in Tk. 2,00,000.00 on 27.1.90, Tk. 1,00,000.00 on 22.2.90 and Tk. 1,00,000.00 on 19.3.90 a total payment of Tk. 4,00,000.00. The carrying work was completed on 1.1.90. The defendant submitted his last and final bill but he did not pay the plaintiffs hill in spite of repeated request. Hence the suit.

3. After institution of the suit, the plaintiff filed an application under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure for attachment of Tk. 11,64,254.00 from the bills of the defendant Co. under process with the Government namely, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, accrued and due to the defendant Co. for the carriage of this urea though carrying through defendant No. 1.

4. That application was contested by the defendant company where it had been alleged that the application for attachment is not maintainable and that the plaintiff had already received payment of Tk. 4,50,000.00 at the rate of Tk. 20.00 for the carriage per ton and having received the aforesaid payment, the plaintiff is now making a claim to be paid at the rate of Tk. 30.00 and Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation is to pay the defendants Bill of Tk. 21 lacs including the deposit of Tk. 2 lacs which amount is much greater sum than the claim of the plaintiff and hence the order of attachment before judgment will cause irreparable loss and injury of the defendant Company.

5. The learned Subordinate judge by his order dated 21.5.90 ordered attachment of Tk. 11,64,254.00 out of the bills of the defendant, pending payment in the hands of BADC before judgment An application for vacating the attachment before judgment on furnishing security for the equivalent amount was filed by defendant in court. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, rejected the application vide his order dated 4.6.90 holding that the defendant had not specified the security he was willing to offer. Another application was filed offering a landed property situated in Chittagong City as a security and prayer was made for release from the attachment before judgment the bill amount of Tk. 11,64,254.00. With the said application the plaintiff filed a written objection to the said prayer of the defendant dated 15.5.90. This was rejected with the order that the defendant may provide cash security if so advised. Again, an application was filed for release of the attachment order by furnishing bank guarantee for Tk. 11,64,254.00 as security for the claim of the plaintiff in the suit.

6. The plaintiff filed an objection to the prayer of the defendant for release of the attachment order and the plaintiff filed an application under Order 12 rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for part decree for Tk. 5,90,540.00 on the basis of the admission of the defendant in their pleadings.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge upon hearing the parties passed an order on 2.9.90 holding that the defendant may provide the bank guarantee as prayed for but ordered partial decree for an amount of Tk. 5,90,540.00 on the basis of admission in the pleadings of the defendant asking the defendant to realise the decretal amount within 15 days and further ordered the defendant to furnish the bank guarantee for the rest. Against which this revisional application was moved and the rule obtained. At the time of issuance of the rule the operation of the order was stayed by this Court which is now heard and disposed of by this judgment.

8. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel appearing in support of the rule for the petitioner having taken us through the impugned judgment and the other related papers in original from the records of the Money Suit submitted that the learned court below erred in law in holding that the defendant Company has made an admission in their pleadings in Court for the application to be allowed under Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure in view of the fact that no written objection was submitted by the defendant company in that suit at the time when the order decreeing the suit in part was passed.

<u>9. It has been submitted that Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure provided that any party may, at any stage of suit, where admissions of fact have been made, either on the pleadings, or otherwise, apply to the Court for such judgment or order as upon such admission he may be entitled to, without waiting for the determination of any other question between the parties; and the Court may upon such application make such order, or give such judgment, as the Court may think just. It is the contention of the learned Counsel that under Order 12, rule 6 of the said order the admission need be made on the pleadings of the parties or otherwise and even if it is to be argued that there is some admissions made by the defendant in their written objection filed against an order of attachment, is not an admission in their pleadings because under Order 6, rule 1 "pleading" means only plaint or written statement and in the written statement of the defendant Company there having existed no admission and at the time of passing of the decree there having existed no written statement, the court misdirected itself in passing the order on the ground that the defendant admitted the claim partially in their pleadings, It has been further submitted that the applicability of the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be limited to the provision of Order 12 only. He has further submitted that in the written statement there was categorical denial made by the defendant Company as to any admission made by their Manager, Mrinal Kanti Dhar in written objection and he could not do so as he was not authorised to make any such admission and if he admits any the defendant Company is not bound by such admission. That being the position and the admission having been challenged subsequently in the written statement by the defendant Company and defendant Company having disowned the previous written objection filed by Mrinal Kanti Dhar on behalf of the Company, written objection filed by Mrinal Kanti Dhar on behalf of the Company while asking for vacating the attachment order, it could not be said that there was an unqualified admission made by defendant Company for it to be construed as an admission under Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and even if there was an admission it was not unconditional as there also it was urged that the suit is not maintainable and there is no claim that can be decreed. That cannot be an admission to attract the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention he has relied upon the decisions reported in PLD 1966 (Karachi) 75, PLD 1952 (Dhaka), 137 and 25 DLR page 418.</u>

10. Mr. M Fazlul Karim, the learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff opposite party in the Rule, submitted that the admission that was made was unconditional and, in fact, it was made even by the proprietor of the company himself subsequent to the written statement of the Manager of the Company, dated 15.5.90 and the subsequent admission was made by the proprietor in his application dated 4.6.90 and Mr. Karim referred to the said application in original, as on record. It is his submission that in the instant case, the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable and the Court has rightly passed the order causing no error or illegality or causing any injustice because the plaintiff in fact claimed much more than what is partially decreed and if the decree in part is allowed and eventually the court does not allow the claim of the plaintiff in full the defendant Company will suffer no loss but, on the other hand, the plaintiff who, according to the learned Advocate while carrying the fertilizer by his trucks and employed labourers had borrowed substantial amount from the market, if not paid immediately would be in very great difficulty but the defendant Company being very rich may pay Tk. 5,90,540.00 as a part decree. It will not affect them at all because on their own admission bills to an amount of Tk. 21.00 lacs are pending to be paid to the defendant Company by the BADC which is expected to be paid soon but the plaintiff has nothing to fall upon to repay the loan already incurred in the market.

<u>11. In the instant case, the point to be decided is whether the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case for the Court to pass a decree in part on admission on pleadings of the parties in a suit. Order 12, rule 6 provided that admission made by the parties is to be admission made in pleadings or otherwise. Order 6, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure defines pleading to be the plaint or written statement. Written statement is not the same thing as written objection because Order 6 rule 1 does not include written objection to be a pleading. Written objection filed in an interlocutory matter during the proceeding would not be a part of the pleadings of the parties in the suit as such but we are of the view that if there is an admission in the said written objection it would certainly be regarded as an admission "otherwise" as appearing in rule 6.</u>

12. From a reading of the documents on record and also from the impugned judgment it is seen that there is an admission. It was first made by defendant No. 1, the Company, the principal defendant and who would be made liable to pay the decretal amount as in the plaint, in the written objection filed against the order of attachment before judgment. It was for vacating the order after the ad-interim order has been passed. From a reading of the said written statement dated 15.5.90 it is seen that there it has been stated by Mrinal Kanti Dhar, who described himself to be the Manager of the Company of defendant No. 1, that in fact the plaintiff had carried 53020 tons of fertilizers in their trucks @ Tk.20% per ton and therefore, would be entitled to an amount to Tk. 10,40,540.00 and not Tk. 15,44,254.00 as claimed in the plaint. It has been stated in that written statement that the plaintiff was paid not Tk. 4,00,000.00 but was paid Tk. 4,50,000.00 and by deducting that amount from the total amount of Tk. 10,40,540.00 the plaintiff will get the balance of Tk. 5,90,540.00 and the defendant No. 1 is always willing to pay the said amount and it is denied that the defendant No. 1 is never interested to pay the balance or any amount and it has been further stated in paragraph 13 of the written objection that the plaintiff would get in total Tk. 5,90,540.00 after deducting Tk. 4,50,000.00, already paid out of the total amount of Tk. 10,40,540.00 and the defendant No.1 is always ready to pay and ready to pay "right now" through the court and, therefore, the attachment order of the bills of defendant company lying with the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation to the extent of Tk. 21,00,000/= need be vacated otherwise they will suffer irreparable loss. This written objection was affirmed by Mrinal Kanti Dey claiming himself to be the Manager of the Company stating also that the owner Md. Ishaque being bed ridden due to illness, he is affirming his affidavit as their Manager and he is affirming this affidavit because he is the Manager of the Company and conversant with the facts and circumstances of the case and that the statement made therein are true to his knowledge and belief. From a reading of this, it appears that the said admission, though admitting a lesser amount than claimed by the plaintiff in the suit, is not a qualified admission on any averment that the suit itself is not maintainable or the suit is premature or that the court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, though part of the claim is admitted. It is a clear admission and very defensive in nature and appears to have been made in the interest of the company. This petition for vacating the ad-interim attachment was rejected by the Court. Thereafter another application has been filed before the said court on 4.6.90 after the final order of attachment dated 21.5.90 and this time this application was affirmed by the proprietor of the Company namely, Md. Ishaque, himself to allow the defendant company to furnish Bank guarantee and to vacate the attachment order. It stated in paragraph 5 that the defendant No.1 is willing to submit bank guarantee to the extent of Tk. 11,64,254.00, the money claimed by the plaintiff in the Money Suit though they did not accept that the said amount is due and it is stated immediately thereafter that according to the statement of the said defendant No. I, the plaintiff will get only Tk. 5,90,540.00 from defendant No.1. Yet the defendant No. 1 is willing to submit bank guarantee for an amount of Tk. 11,64,254.00 and the order of attachment may be vacated. That was also rejected by the court below. But from the said written objection dated 4.6.90 it is seen that the said application has been affirmed by Md. Ishaque himself stating that the statements made therein arc true to his knowledge and belief. He was duly identified before the court by Mr. Abu Zafar his advocate. That being the position it could not be said that Mrinal Kanti Dey, the Manager of defendant No. 1 had been gained over in making the previous admission and it would be rather material contradiction to submit, as in the written statement signed by the same person namely, Mr. Md. Ishaque, that Mrinal Kanti Dey has been influenced by the plaintiff to make admission of Tk. 5,90,254.00 and the written objection submitted by Mrinal Kanti Dey making any such admission to any amount of Tk. 5,90,254.00 is a total lie and unauthorised and it is also a material contradiction to make a statement subsequently by Mr. Md. Ishaque that the plaintiff will get nothing from him because in the written objection filed by him in court and affirmed by him also in court on 4.6.90 under his own signature he made an admission to the effect that though the plaintiff will get from him Tk. 4,90,540.00 yet he is willing to submit a bank guarantee for the amount of Tk. 11,44,254.00. The contention of the learned Advocate to the effect that the admission was not unconditional or unequivocal has also no basis at all.

<u>13. This admission, however, is not in any written statement as stated herein before but we find that it is an admission made before the court otherwise. This question of admission "otherwise" had also been examined by the courts in England and reference may be made to the case of Ellis Vs. Allen (1914) Chancery Division, 904. Rule 6 of Order 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure as applicable in this country corresponds to rule 6, Order 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure as is in India and corresponds to rules 6, Order 32 of the Supreme Court Rule (English) now rule 3 of Order 27. They appear to be legislations in parimateria and are all identically worded.</u>

14. In that case of the Chancery Division under report, Rule 6 of Order 32 of the Supreme Court Rule of England, which is similarly worded as in rule 6, Order 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the expression "or otherwise" came for consideration to substantiate the view that "otherwise" would also include even a letter written by the Solicitor of the defendant in the suit filed by the landlord for eviction for breach of a covenant of the contract, admitting breach of the covenant of the contract. The letter written by the Solicitor of the lessee to plaintiff Solicitor was not in any way related to any pleadings in court yet it was used as an admission under rule 6 Order 32 for decreeing the suit on the basis of such admission. Sargant, J. in delivering the judgment for the Chancery Division rejected the argument that the rule is confined to admissions made in the pleadings only and confined to rules 1 to rule 4 of the same Order, which rules 1 to 4 are also the same as in our Code of Civil Procedure, having found that the admission has been made "otherwise"

15. In the case of Shikhar Chand Vs. Mst. Bari Bai, reported in AIR 1974 (Madhya Pradesh), 75 a Division Bench of the said Court quoting with approval the decision in Ellis Vs. Allen (1914) (Chancery Division), 904 observed thus:

"Rule 6 Order 12, in my opinion, must bear the same construction as was put upon the corresponding English rule by Sargant, J. The words either on the pleadings or "otherwise" in rule 6 enable us not only to see the admission made in pleadings or under rules 1 to 4 of the same Order but also admissions made else-where during the trial. We are, therefore, entitled to see the appellants reply dated 10th March, 1959 to the application for appointment of receiver as also their reply dated 29th June 1970 to the plaintiffs' application for judgment on admission."

16. We are in respectful agreement with the observations as made above which is in complete accord with the view we have taken to the effect that the expression "or otherwise" as under rule 6 of Order 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure would empower the court to see the admission made else-where in the proceeding during the trial and should not be confined only to written statement. It can also be in a written objection filed against the order of ad-interim attachment before the judgment and also in the application made for vacating the final attachment order.

17. In the case of Kassamali Alibhoy Vs. Shaikh Abdul Satiar, reported in PLD 1966 (WP), Karachi, 75, it has been held that for a judgment on admission the admission must be unqualified and unconditional and when factually the admission is accompanied by a qualification that the suit itself is not maintainable or that the claim suffers from a legal difficulty, it cannot be said that the admission is unqualified and it was held that when such a legal defence is raised, its consideration must wait until the suit itself comes to be tried and the court cannot in such a case proceed under Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and pass a judgment upon such admission.

18. In the case of Wazedunnessa Khatun Vs. Daliluddin and others reported in 25 DLR 418 the same principle was reiterated to the effect that admission of the defendant must be positive, clear and unequivocal and the said admission cannot be split up. Thus, if there is an admission and in the other para there is a denial it cannot be said that there is an unequivocal admission and where there is an admission but it has been pleaded that the suit is not itself maintainable, then also no decree can be passed on such admission.

19. There is no dispute with the principles enunciated in the case under report but they are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as in the instant case in the first written objection filed on 15.5.90, a clear admission has been made to the effect that the plaintiff after deduction is entitled only to an amount of Tk. 5,90,850.00 and they are willing to pay and willing to pay immediately through the court which was again reiterated by the proprietor himself, though in the written statement quite sometime after it has been submitted by the proprietor himself that it is the plaintiff who is demanding Tk. 5,90,850.00 though it was not due to him and as a matter of fact nothing is due to them and in fact the plaintiff has been over paid after disowning the admission made by his Manager in an application dated 15.5.90 but without withdrawing his own statement on admission made by him in Court on solemn affirmation dated 4.6.90. This written statement has been filed long after the court passed the decree in part. The court passed the decree in part on admission and at the time of passing of the decree on admission no such objection has been taken by the lawyer in court at the hearing that the admission made before by the owner himself or his Manager had no authority and when the court passed the decree on admission the written statement had not been submitted.

<u>20. In the instant case we find that the order was passed by the Court decreeing the suit in part on admission and on unequivocal admission and passed when the denial, as made in the subsequent written statement, was not there before the Court nor any such denial was taken before the court. The decree on admission was passed, in our view, in accordance with law causing no error or illegality for this court to interfere in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.</u>

21. In the result, this Rule is discharged with the observation that the decretal amount is directed to be paid by the defendant No. 1 within 3(three) months from date and the rest of the amount in the suit be covered by the bank guarantee as ordered by the court below and the bank guarantee be continued till the matter is finally decided.

Let the suit proceed in accordance with law. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs.

Send down the LC records at once.

End.
