full_judgment:
This Second Appeal at the instance of the defendant appellant arises out of the judgment and decree dated 29th April, 1967 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Partition Appeal No. 271 of 1965 affirming those dated 30th July, 1965 passed by the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Cox's Bazar in Partition Suit No. 106 of 1960, decreeing the suit of the plaintiff.

2.  The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for partition of the suit-lands and for allotment of Saham in respect of his share on declaration of his title thereto. Plaintiffs case, briefly, was that the 1st schedule land of the plaint which includes the 2nd schedule-land belonged to the present defendant No. 1 Abdur Rahman and defendant No. 2 Md. Ilias jointly in equal shares which were recorded in the RS Khatian accordingly; that defendant No. 3 Jobeda Khatoon who is the divorced wife of defendant No. 1 Abdur Rahman obtained a decree in M S No. 31/46 of the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar for dower-debt and then purchased defendant, Abdur Rahman's share in the Money Execution Case No. 34/48 on 7-4-48; that in pursuance thereof obtained delivery of possession in the suit-land i.e. in Abdur Rahman's share after auction purchase. Subsequently she settled six kanis of land out of her auction purchased land with defendants No. 4-9 on 28-7-55 on the basis of a patta vide Ext. 1; that the defendants No. 4-9 possessed the said six kanis of land and thereafter defendant Nos. 4-6 and 8 sold their four kanis of land out of the said holding to the plaintiff on the basis of a registered kabala dated 24-12-58 vide Ext. 2; that plaintiffs vendor later on executed an antedated kabala in favour of the defendant No. 10 in respect of their share in the suit-land in collusion with defendant No. 1 Abdur Raham to defeat plaintiffs title; that the plaintiff possessed the suit-land but the same was wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 Abdur Rahman Hence the suit by the plaintiff for declaration of title and for partition and allotment of saham in respect of the said schedule of land of the plaint.

3. The present appellant as defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit by filing written statement and denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff got no cause of action; that the suit was not properly valued; that the suit was barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver, and acquiescence and also limitation; that the suit was not maintainable in the present form; that the contesting defendant was not aware of any purchase of the suit-land by defendant No. 3 Syeda Khatun in execution of any money decree and that Syeda Khatun or the plaintiff or plaintiffs predecessor did never possess the suit-land and that defendant No. 1 had been in possession of the suit-land all along; that the plaintiff brought MS No. 45/1957 for contribution which ended in a decree against the present defendant and other co-sharers, wherein plaintiff himself admitted defendant's title in the suit-land that the plaintiff also put the decree of that MS 45/57 in execution in M Execution Case No. 63/61 wherein plaintiff also admitted defendant Abdur Rahman's title in the suit holding and put the share of defendant No. 1 Abdur Rahman and others to sale in respect of which the defendant Abdur Rahman deposited the share of his contribution which the plaintiff had withdrawn in that money execution case; that in the above circumstances the plaintiffs suit was barred by the principle of estoppel and it was liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. Upon the above pleadings of both the parties, the following issues were framed :

1. Is there any cause of action?

2. Has the suit been properly valued?

3. Is the suit barred by limitation, estoppel and acquiescence?

4. Is the suit maintainable in the present form?

5. What relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to?

5. In support of their respective cases, both the parties examined witnesses and filed some documents. The learned Munsif on consideration of the facts of the case and the evidence on record decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiff and decreed the suit on contest against defendant No. 1 and ex parte against the rest with costs in the preliminary form and declared plaintiffs title in respect of 1.60 acres of land described in the schedule of the plaint entitling him to get a saham for four kanis i.e. 1.60 acres of land out of the 2nd schedule-land as described in the plaint and the parties were directed to effect partition of the suit-land within two months amicably, failing which plaintiff would be at liberty to have the suit land partitioned through court with the help of a pleader commissioner by his judgment and decree dated 30-7-1965.

6. Being aggrieved by the same, the contesting defendant Abdur Rahman preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Chittagong which was transferred to the 2nd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for disposal. The appeal was numbered as Partition Appeal No. 271 of 1965. The learned Subordinate Judge then fixed only one point for the determination in the appeal which was to the effect as to whether the plaintiff respondent had title to the suit-land and whether he was entitled to possess the same. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the sides and on consideration of the materials on record however observed that the claim of the plaintiff could not be defeated or barred by limitation and decided the above point for determination in favour of the plaintiff but found that the learned Munsif made an error in giving the plaintiff a decree to the extent of 1.60 acres of land instead of 1.44 acres. He accordingly allowed the appeal in part on contest with costs and modified the judgment and decree of the trial Court to the following effect that the plaintiff would get only 1I6th of 8.65 acres of land as recorded in schedule 2 which was equivalent to 1.44 acres of land and not 1.60 acres. The learned Subordinate Judge thus affirmed the decision of the trial Court only with the above modification of the quantum of land by his judgment and decree dated 29-4-67. Being aggrieved by the same the contesting defendant Abdur Rahman preferred the present second appeal in this court.

7. Mr. Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate appeared for the defendant appellant and Mr. Masuk Hossain Ahmed the learned Advocate appeared for the plaintiff respondent.

8. It appears from a reading of the memo of the second appeal that on behalf of the appellant only four grounds have been taken. The 1st one is about miss appreciation of the evidence on record by the courts below, the 3rd ground is to the effect that the judgment of the appellate court below is not a proper judgment of affirmance; the 4th one is to the effect that the judgment of the court below is otherwise bad in law, and the second one is however, to the following effect:

For that in view of the fact that plaintiff respondent brought MS 45/57 for contribution in respect of the arrears of jama for the present holding against the defendant appellant and others and obtained a decree and the defendant deposited his share of dues in M Exn. Case No. 63/1960 to prevent the sale of his interest in the suit holding, the courts below ought to have held that the defendant appellant was not aware of the sale of his share in the suit holding in M Exn. Case No. 34/48 and the purchase of the same by Syeda Khatun and, as such, the defendant appellant is not bound by the same and that plaintiff-respondent therefore, has got no right, title and interest in the suit land by purchase from Syeda Khatun and on the basis thereof should have dismissed the suit.

9. Now, at the hearing of the appeal the learned Advocate for the appellant however tried to argue firstly on the point of estoppel though no such specific point or ground appears to have been taken in the memo of appeal.

10. Mr. Masuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned advocate for the respondent, then raised serious objection to the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant on the point of estoppel contending that as no such ground has been taken specifically in the memo of appeal by the appellant, the learned Advocate for the appellant should not be allowed to make any submission on the above point of estoppel. He has drawn my attention in this connection to rule 2 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs thus:

"The appellant shall not, except by leave of the court, urge or be heard in support of any ground of objection not set forth in the memorandum of appeal; but the Appellate Court, in deciding the appeal, shall not be confined to the grounds of objection set forth in the memorandum of appeal or taken by leave of Court under this rule:

Provided that the Court shall not rest its decision on any other ground unless the party who may be affected thereby has had sufficient opportunity of contesting the case on that ground."

11. Admittedly, no specific ground on estoppel had been taken in the present memo of appeal by the appellant, but it appears from the judgment of the trial Court that such plea on estoppel waiver acquiescence were taken in the pleading of the contesting defendant and the trial Court framed issue on the same also and thereafter decided the question of estoppel on the materials on record, of course, against the contesting defendant holding that the suit was not barred by estoppel, waiver or acquiescence. Now from a reading of the ordinary copy of the memo of appeal of the court of appeal below it appears that such ground on estoppel was taken on behalf of the defendant-appellant but it appears from the impugned judgment that there has been no discussion and finding on the same in the said judgment. Thus it is not a case that the point on estoppel is being urged for the first time in this court in second appeal. From a perusal of the relevant provision of law namely, rule 2 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it appears that the appellant shall not urge or be heard in support of any ground of objection not set forth in the memorandum of appeal except by leave of the court. But the appellate Court, in deciding an appeal, shall not be confined to the ground of objection set forth in the memorandum of appeal or taken by leave of the court under this rule provided the party who will be affected thereby is given sufficient opportunity to contest the case on that ground, that means, the power of the appellate Court in hearing any other ground beyond the memorandum of appeal, appears to be wide enough and the thing which is necessary for urging such ground or grounds before the court is that leave of the court must be taken before doing the same and sufficient opportunity to be given to the party affected thereby to contest the case on that ground.

<u>12. Mr. Mustafa Niza Muhammad, the learned Advocate for the appellant, however contends that a question of law, whether taken in the memorandum of appeal or not, can be urged at any stage of the proceeding. In support of his contention he has referred to a decision in the case of Mongal Muchi, at present Mahram Ali vs. Abu Musa Ahmed Mustafa and others, reported in 9 DLR 577. He has also relied on a decision in the case of Khairun Nessa Khatun Chowdhury vs. Golam Moktadir Chowdhury reported in 14 DLR 745. He further contends that the lower appellate Court appears to have made no finding on the question of estoppel, but the said question was taken as a ground and urged before that court. Hence, when that is a question of law it can be urged in this second appeal though not taken as a ground in the memo of appeal and that the other side will also not be prejudiced thereby.</u>

<u>13. Mr. Masuk Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has however relied on a decision in the case of Ramlarmi Ranchhodlal vs. Bank of Baroda, Ltd., reported in AIR 1955 Bom, 50 in support of his contention.</u>

<u>14. Now, from a reading of the above decisions cited at the Bar and the relevant provisions of law it transpired that with the leave of the court any ground can be urged before the court and particularly a ground on a question of law can be urged at any stage of the proceeding provided the other side is heard on the said ground without being prejudiced.</u>

<u>15. It further appears from another decision reported in AIR 1938 Madras 405 (Suppan Chettiar, vs. Rangen Chetty and others) that:</u>

<u>"Where a question of law is raised for the first time, upon the construction of a document or upon facts either admitted or proved beyond controversy, it is not only competent but expedient, in the interests of justice, to entertain the plea."</u>

16. Therefore in view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions as discussed above, I deem it fit and proper to allow the learned Advocate for the appellant to argue on the question of estoppel before me, though not taken as a ground in the memo of second appeal.

17. Then Mr. Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, the learned Advocate for the appellant, took me through the judgments of both the courts below and submitted that the trial Court framed issue on the said point of estoppel and also decided the same, of course, against the defendant-appellant, but the learned lower appellate Court has not made any discussion whatsoever on the said question of estoppel, though it was taken as a ground in the memo of appeal and this has caused a miscarriage of justice and, as such, the judgment of the lower appellate Court should be set aside.

18. Mr. Masuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that it is true that there has been no discussion by the learned appellate Court on the question of estoppel, but from the conduct of the appellant and the impugned judgment of the lower appellate Court, it appears that the appellant purposely did not take that point on estoppel herein the memo of appeal and also did not press the point rather abandoned it in the court of appeal below and, as such there is no fault with the impugned judgment of the court of appeal below for making no discussion or any finding on the question of estoppel.

19. Mr. Niaz Muhammad, the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant however cited 2 decisions one in the case of MP Krishnawami Pillai vs. Chockalingam Chettiar and others reported in AIR 1943 Madras 455 and another in the case of Sarjaraz Ali Khan vs. Abdul Ghafur Khan and others, reported in AIR 1929 Lahore 81 to show that as because there is no discussion by the court below on a certain point in the judgment it cannot be concluded that the point was not raised or argued in the court below, I however, respectfully agree with the view as taken in the above decisions and differed with the contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent and, as such, it cannot be held conclusively that the point on estoppel was not raised by the defendant-appellant in the court of appeal below because of the absence of any discussion or finding on the same in the impugned judgment. Now, it is the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that as regards other points involved in the case namely, whether the defendant-appellant had knowledge of the Money Suit of defendant No. 3 i.e. MS No. 31/46 and the M Execution case No. 34 of 1984 and in pursuance thereof the auction purchase by defendant No. 3 vide Ext. 6 and then the transfer of the land by her by a Patta to defendant Nos. 4-9 vide Ext. 9, thereafter the purchase by the plaintiff vide Ext. 2, he does not like to make any submission as the same has been concluded by finding of facts by both the courts below. But his main grievance is with regard to the question of estoppel. His submission is that admittedly the plaintiff-respondent along with others instituted a money suit for contribution being Money Suit No.45/57 against the contesting defendant Abdur Rahman as well as some other co-sharers and the same was decreed and in pursuance thereof Money Execution No.63/61 was started and in that Money Execution Case, the contesting defendant Abdur Rahman paid his share of the contribution money in court which was withdrawn by the plaintiff and as such he admitted the contesting defendant's title and interest in the suit-holding and hence the subsequent suit brought against him i.e. the contesting defendant, and others by the plaintiff is barred by estoppel in view of section 115 of the Evidence Act, but unfortunately this point has been wrongly decided against the defendant by the trial Court with a finding that the suit was not barred by estoppel and the lower appellate Court failed to consider this vital point of estoppel at all but somehow affirmed the decision of the trial Court only with some modification with regard to the quantum of land of the schedule and hence the impugned judgment is not a proper and valid judgment which is liable to be set aside.

20. Mr. Masuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that on the question of estoppel the trial Court in consideration of the materials on record rightly came to the following finding:

"The admissions in the execution petition cannot be said to be express because present plff. decree-holder as he stated described deft's name according to the entries of names in RS record. So it appears to me that the admission made by plff. in the execution case about defdt's title is mere admission which does not preclude him for explaining the correct state of affairs. The admissions made by the plaintiff will not also act as estoppel as deft. Abdur Rahman did not have to change his position. Since the position of deft. Abdur Rahman did not alter as a judgment-debtor by the admission of the present plff. as decree-holder, the admission cannot be treated as estoppel. From the evidence discussed earlier I am of opinion that Abdur Rahman was well aware of the sale of his interest. So, the representation made by plaintiff was known to the defendant Abdur Rahman as unfounded one and it cannot act as estoppel against the plaintiff."

<u>21. Now, it appears that the lower appellate Court has not discussed this question of estoppel which is a mixed question of law and fact, though the trial Court framed an issue on the point and decided the same with a finding that the suit was not barred by estoppel. Hence on the above situation, it may be a case for remand of the appeal to the lower appellate Court for rehearing and for consideration and decision on the said point but the suit being too old and the necessary facts and other materials being already on record, this court in second appeal in exercise of it's power under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure instead of sending the appeal back on remand to the lower appellate Court for decision on the above point, should itself discuss and decide the same.</u>

<u>22. It may be pointed out the estoppel is based on equity and good conscience and its object is to prevent fraud and secure justice between the parties by promotion of honesty and good faith, consequently where one person makes a representation to the other about a fact he would not be shut out by the rule of estoppel, if that other person knew the true state of facts and must consequently not have been misled by the representation. Further, the person setting up estoppel against another must show that his position was altered by reason of the representation or conduct of the later, otherwise even the general principle of estoppel cannot be invoked by him. The above view has been expressed in the case of R S Maddanappa (deceased) after him by his Legal Representatives vs. Chandramma and another reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 1812. At the same time the burden of proving the ingredients of section 115 of the Evidence Act lies on the party claiming estoppel vide AIR 1970 (SC) 426 in the case of Bennett Coleman and Co. Pvt. Ltd., vs. Punya Priya Das Gupta, and further for the purpose of estoppel, there should be clear and distinct pleading of the defendant stating the facts on which an estoppel should be founded and it is also settled principle that estoppel must be strictly construed.</u>

23. Now, keeping in view the above settled principles, let me proceed to examine the question of estoppel as raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant in this appeal.

<u>24. Mr. Masuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondents, however, contends that	the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge) has correctly decided the question of estoppel in the instant case and rightly held that the suit is not barred by estoppel. The learned Advocate has relied on a few decisions in support of his contention, one in the case of Radhasyam Gope vs. Aktarunnessa Begum and others reported in 6 PLR Dacca 181, wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"In order to find an estoppel, the representation, i.e., a party's declaration, act or omission, must be clear, definite, unambiguous and unequivocal and that the person making the representation should so conduct himself that a reasonable man would take the representation to be true and believe that it was meant that he should act upon it."</u>

<u>25. The contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent is that the plaintiff even before his purchase was a co-sharer along with the other defendants and the money suit for contribution was not instituted by plaintiff alone, it was instituted by the plaintiff along with some other co-sharers against the contesting co-sharer defendant and some other defendant-co-sharers, and so far the status of the contesting defendant is concerned, it is not disputed that he is a co-sharer in the suit-holding but his interest to the extent of 4 kanis of land which the defendant No. 3 first auction-purchased in execution of a money decree and then transferred it to defendant Nos. 4-9 by a patta who again sold out the same to the plaintiff-respondent by registered deed and thereby the right, title and interest of the contesting defendant was already extinguished and the same ultimately devolved upon the plaintiff-respondent and this was well within the knowledge of the contesting defendant and thus the subsequent suit for contribution by the plaintiff and others as against the defendants, particularly the defendant No. 1, cannot be constituted as any actual admission of his right, title; interest in the said 4 kanis of land of the plaintiff. The contesting defendant might have some interest of some share in the suit-holding as his co-shareship in the same was not disputed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff- respondent is however concerned only with his own share of 4 kanis of land in the schedule property which he purchased from defendant Nos. 4-6 and 8. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent. further contends that' the institution of the suit for contribution and its execution thereof has not changed or altered the condition or position of the contesting defendant even in respect of his possession in some portion over the same. The learned Advocate in support of his contention has cited two decisions, one in the case of Kista Chandra Mandal and others vs. Mt. Amita Bala Dasi and others reported in Para 19 in AIR 1968 Pat. 487 wherein it has been observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Estoppel is a rule of evidence by which a person in not allowed to allege and prove a thing under certain circumstances. The application of this principle in India is embodied in section 115 of the Evidence Act. Before the plaintiff could be held bound by the rule of estoppel, it must be established that the defendants have acted on his representation, act or omission: Where the defendant's position has not altered even the least on account of any act on the part of the plaintiff, the principle does not apply."</u>

<u>and another in the case of MP Krishnaswami Pillai vs. Chockalingam Chettior and others reported in AIR 1943 Mad. 455 where it has been held:</u>

<u>"Where the appellant has specifically raised a ground of appeal on a certain point but the court decides the appeal on another point and does not decide the former as being unnecessary, such point cannot be taken to have been abandoned by the appellant unless it is so stated in the judgment of the appellate Court."</u>

<u>The learned Advocate for the respondent has further referred to another decision in the case of Gyasi Bai and others vs. Dhansukh Lal and others reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 1055 in which the principles of estoppel have been specifically laid down in the following terms in para 8 of the decision.</u>

<u>"To invoke the doctrine of estoppel embodied in section 115, in Evidence Act, 1872, three conditions must be satisfied:</u>

<u>(1) representation by a person to another.</u>

<u>(2) the other shall have acted upon the said representation and</u>

<u>(3) such action shall have been detrimental to the interests of the person to whom representation has been made. Where the first two conditions are satisfied but the third is not, there is no scope to invoke the doctrine of Estoppel."</u>

<u>The learned Advocate for the appellant has further relied on an unreported decision of our Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 86 of 1981 in the case of Rashid Ahmed and others vs. Nurul Islam and others, wherein it has been observed:</u>

<u>"From the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court Division came to the conclusion that the representation was genuine and made in fact and the defendants changed their position acting on the plaintiffs representation and, as such, the plaintiff is estopped from claiming title to the suit land."</u>

<u>Now, even from the above decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant, it is clear that unless the defendant's position is changed or altered due to the representation made by the plaintiff, there will be no application of the doctrine of estoppel. In the present case from the facts and circumstances and the materials on record, it is not found that due to the contribution suit and the execution of its decree by the plaintiff and others, in fact there was any change or alteration of the position of the contesting defendant in respect of the lands concerned and further he (the contesting defendant) was fully aware of the extinction of his right on the suit land through the process of auction sale in execution of the money decree by Sayeda Khatun defendant 3, former wife of the defendant No.1.</u>

26. Therefore in the facts and circumstances of the case and the principles of estoppel as enunciated in the above decisions I am of the view that the conditions required for the application of the doctrine of Estoppel were not fully satisfied in the present case and hence the trial Court rightly held that the suit was not barred by estoppel. I therefore find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant and there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below and the same do not call for any interference by this court

27. The appeal is therefore dismissed without any order as to costs.

Let the lower court records be sent down expeditiously.

End.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J:- This Appeal is directed against Order No. 169 dated 7.11.84 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 106 of 1978 passing an order of abatement of the suit for specific performance of contract as a whole for non-impleading the heirs of deceased DefendantNo. 17. 

2. The relevant fact that will be necessary for disposal of this appeal may be narrated as follows :- 

The plaintiff-appellant filed the suit for specific performance of contract. The plaint case, is that the defendant No.1 who is the owner of Schedule 'A' land proposed to sell 5 kanis viz. 100 gondas of Schedule 'A' land to defendant No.2 who is the owner of the contiguous land. The defendant No. 2 being alose not in a position to purchase the suit land approached the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 3-5 and they agreed to purchase the same. In pursuance of that, negotiation went on between the parties and an agreement was entered into between the defendant No.1 as seller and the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 2-5 as buyer on 18.5.76. The consideration for the aforesaid land was scold at Taka 3,15,000/= (Tk Three lac fifteen thousand). In pursuance of that contract earnest money was paid and the purchasers got possession of the suit land. According to the plaint case it was agreed in the agreement of contract that defendant No. 1 shall sell gondas of land to defendant No. 2 and the balance of 90 gondas of land will be sold to plaintiffand defendant Nos. 3-5 in equal share. It is further stated in the plaint that on the basis of the part performance-of the contract the purchasers are in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff after the filing of the suit Having come to know that the defendant Nos. 2f5 and others have transferred a part of the suit land to some other purchasers filed an application on 28.9.78 for impleading defendant Nos. 15-17 as parties in the suit. Thereafter vide Order No. 6 dated 29.9.78 the defendant No. 17 was added as a party. The said defendant: No. 17 died on 5.7.83 leaving behind legal heirs. The legal heirs of defendant No. 17 were not substituted by the plaintiff and consequently the defendant Nos. 2-4 filed an application on 3.5.84 for passing an order of abatement of the suit under Order 22 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff filed an objection petition stating that the suit being one for specific Performa rice of contract executed between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 2-5 on the one hand as purchasers and defendant No. 1 on the other hand as seller; the other defendants are not necessary party and they are mere proper parties. Further in the application the plaintiff-appellant asserted that for non-substitution of the heirs of defendant No. 17, the whole suit shall not abate and the suit may abate only against defendant No. 17 and the same shall not affect the suit at all as effective decree can be passed in the absence of the said defendant. The matter was heard by the trial Judge and on due consideration of the application and objection as filed by the parties; by order No. 159 dated 15.8.84 the trial Judge dis- posed of the applications of the parties dated 3.5.84 by observing as follows: 

"Both the parties file haziras. The record is put up today for hearing pendent 3.5.84. Hd. the suit is abated against the deft. No. 17 only (V.O.P). Whether the entire suit has abated will be decided at the time of hearing of the suit." 

3. Thereafter, the defendants 2-5 again re-agitated the matter for reviewing the earlier order by filing an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order 47 rule 1 of the Code. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order passed the order of total abatement of the suit for non-impleading the heirs of deceased defendant No. 17. 

4. Mr. Abdul Mannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant submits that the defendant NO.17 is neither a necessary nor a proper party in this suit for specific performance of contract. The learned Advocate further submits that in the absence of deceased defendant No.17 an effective decree can be passed and as such the order of the learned Subordinate Judge abating the suit as a whole is totally illegal and misconceived in the facts of the present case. The learned Advocate of course has very candidly submitted that he has impleaded defendant No. 17 as a party under section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act as a measure of abundant precaution thinking this defendant is a subsequent transferee for value without notice of the original contract so he was a proper party in his estimation. 

5. The learned Advocate for the appellant next contends that the share of the purchasers namely, the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 2-5 being distinct and separate, there is no possibility of any conflicting decree in the absence of the heirs of defendant No.17. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that defendant No. 17 has purchased the share of defendant No. 2 who was an original purchaser in the original contract dated 18.5.76 and in that view he is also not a subsequent purchaser. 

6. Mi. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared for the defendant Nos. 2-5 and Mr. Syed Moazzem Hossain appeared for the defendant No. 14 and other defendants are also represented before this count by their respective Advocates. 

7. Mr. Syed Moazzem Hossain submits that defendant No.17 is a necessary party in this suit for specific performance of contract and without impleading the heirs of deceased defendant No. 17, no effective decree can be passed against the living persons and the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly passed an order of total abatement of the suit. The learned Advocate further submits that if the decree is allowed to be passed in the present suit without the heirs of deceased defendant No.17 being added as party then there will be inconsistent and conflicting decree in the suit which will adversely affect the heirs of deceased defendant No.17. Mr. Syed Moazzem Hossain, the learned Advocate has also cited the case of Wall and others Vs. Manak Ali and others reported in 17 D.L.R (SC) 536 for elaborating his argument in support of his argument for total abatement of the aforesaid suit. 

8. The material point for consideration in this appeal, is whether the suit will abate as a whole or the suit will abate against the defendant No. 17 alone for non-impleading the heirs of the said deceased defendant. 

9. It may be mentioned here that under the agreement dated 18.5.76, defendant No. 2 agreed to purchase 10 gondas of land and out of this 10 gondas he sold 6 gondas to defendant No. 17. The deceased defendant No.17 appeared and filed written statement where in paragraph 11 he stated as follows: 

"That, according to the plaint case the defendant No. 2 is entitled to get 10 gandas in R.S. Plot No. 576. The allegation regarding the entitlement of defendant No. 2 to 10 gandas in R.S. Plot No. 573, if for argument sake, is taken to be correct the purchase of 6 gandas of suit lands from defendant No. 2 this defendant is not and cannot be affected by the alleged contract." 

10. We will consider that question hereinbelow in the light of the facts as stated above and the issue of law involved in this question. A reference to Order 22 rule 4, sub rule (3) reads as follows:- 

"Where within the time limited by law no application is made under sub-rule(1), the suit shall abate as against the deceased defendant." 

11. This is all that we find in the four-corners of the Code of Civil Procedure as to the question of abatement. In the light of this we are to understand what do mean by the term total abatement as has been enunciated by various courts. Here we may profitably refer to a passage from the illuminating judgment of Kaikaus, J: reported in 17 D.L.R. (SC) -536. In that decision it has been observed as follows: 

"Total abatement will be justified only if it becomes impossible to proceed with the suit or appeal on account of its abatement as against the deceased parties. By "total abatement" of a suit is meant that on account of the situation that is created by the abatement of the suit as against the party the suit or appeal cannot for one reason or the other proceed at all." 

12. Keeping this in mind, we will now proceed to see what are the real tests for determination that in the present case, the suit will abate as a whole or will abate against the deceased defendant No.17 alone. The real test is whether an effective decree can be passed against the living party and whether the decision on the merits may result in conflicting and inconsistent decrees. There is, of course, another test that whether the suit is imperfectly constituted in the absence of the deceased party. So, we will see whether leaving aside the heirs of deceased defendant No.17 in effective decree can be passed in the present suit or specific performance of contract and whether the decree if at all passed by the trial Court will be conflicting or inconsistent in nature. 

13. This being a suit for specific performance If contract, in such a suit the parties to the contract re necessary and sufficient parties. The plaintiff having come to know after filing of the suit that the defendant No. 1 in collusion with the defendant Nos. -5(the original purchasers) of the contract sold the asland to other defendants impleaded them as a arty under section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Acthues it appears that the plaintiff while impleading ie subsequent purchasers as defendants in the suit misdeed them to be proper parties and impleaded them as defendants as stated hereinabove. Further we also find from the fact of the case that the defendant No. 17 purchased a portion of share from defendant No.2 one of the original purchasers. Thus in the facts of the present case we find that the defendant No.17 is not a necessary party. Further, in spite of the objection raised during the continuance of the trial, the plaintiff did not implead the heirs of deceased defendant No. 17 as the plaintiff considered that the defendant No.17 was not a subsequent purchaser as he purchased only 6 gandas of land from defendant No. 2 who agreed to purchase 10 gondas by the original agreement. Truly speaking by his purchase by defendant No. 17, the plaintiffs share was not at all affected and even without impleading defendant No. 17, the plaintiff can get a decree in respect of his specific share. Thus, we find that in the facts of the present case defendant No. 17 is in fact not a necessary party and without impleading the heirs of defendant No. 17 an effective decree can be passed in the facts of the present case. Thus, the first point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the suit can proceed and an effective decree can be passed in the absence of heirs of defendant No. 17 has got substance. 

14. Further in the present case, the plaintiff has come for enforcement of his contract in respect of his share of 22--1/2 gondas of land in Schedule 'A'. According to the plaintiff the contract is in respect of 100 gondas of land, of which the defendant No.2's share is specified as 10 gondas and the share of plaintiff and other purchasers namely, defendants No. 3-5 are specified as 22--1/2 gondas of land in each share. Thus in the frame of the present suit, the question is whether the suit abates in its totality or not will depend upon the nature of relief claimed in the suit. We also find that the defendant No. 17 is a purchaser at a subsequent point of time from one of the original purchasers namely, defendant No. 2 and the share being specified and ascertainable in the facts of the present case, we do not find that in any way there will be any inconsistency in the event of a decree being passed. Thus, we are of the view that on a total misconception of law the trial Judge wrongly held that the suit abates as a whole. In the judgment of 17 D.L.R (SC) an elaborate discussion has been made with regard to the nature of the suit wherein the question of abatement and total abatement has been discussed at length. In that reported decision it has been observed as follows: 

"An example of a suit where the nature of the relief asked for requires an-adjudication between all parties in a suit for partition of property. A partition can take place only as between all the co-sharers though it may be clarified here that after a decree for partition is passed the dispute may in appeal become confined to some out of the co-sharers. A suit for accounts of partnership is also an example of this kind but not a perfect one for a case is conceivable where there have admittedly been profits and two parties are claiming their share of profits against the third partner who is the accounting party. An example of a case where law requires one decision of a dispute between all parties in a suit for pre-emption. Though there be more than one vendee only a single suit can be filed with respect to one sale and the law does not permit an-adjudication as between the pre-emption and one of the vendees. Here the law envisages only one cause of action and only one decision of a dispute and a partial adjudication is not possible." 

15. In another decision reported in P.L.D. 1967 Lahore-613 wherein this judgment of Kaikaus J, : was considered at length. Wherein it has been observed as follows: 

"The principle of law that emerges from the above authorities is this: If the interest of the parties are distinct, divisible or ascertainable and the cause of action is not such that it can continue only in the presence of all the parties or their legal representatives the appeal will abate only partially." 

16. Mr. Syed Moazzem Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.14 cited some decisions for our consideration. The learned Advocate cited the case reported in 21 D.L.R. 437. In that decision it was held that when an appeal becomes incompetent for being improperly constituted due to lack of necessary parties the court cannot enter into merits of the case and decide any other question relating to the appeal for no appeal is pending in the eye of law. This decision has no manner of application as we have already held that defendant No. 17 is not a necessary party in the present suit. The next case cited is reported in 26 D.L.R. 35. That was a case wherein it was held that if the decree is indivisible then on the death of one of the parties interested in the decree, the appeal as a whole will become infructuous. This case is also not applicable to the facts of the present case as the share in respect of which the suit for specific performance of contract has been filed is distinct and separate and the interest of deceased defendant No. 17 is totally different and distinct and in the event of a decree being passed, the share of deceased defendant No. 17 will remain unaffected and the defendant No. 17 has also made categorical averment in the written statement as indicated above. 

17. We have carefully perused the impugned order wherein the trial Judge came to a finding that defendant No. 17 is a necessary party and consequently he came to the conclusion that the suit abates as a whole. But we have given our anxious consideration to the frame of the suit and the relief claimed in the suit and we are of the view that the defendant No. 17 is not a necessary party at all and an effective decree can be passed in the case against the living party. Consequently, the suit abates as against this defendant No. 17 only. 

18. Before parting with the case, it is to be stated that the trial Judge. on a total misconception of law and fact passed the impugned order and consequently the impugned order is set aside and the suit will proceed. Accordingly, this appeal is allow without any order as to costs. 

Send down the LC records at once. 

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated May 5, 1981 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 263 of 1981.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim CJ : I have gone through the judgments written by Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Shahabuddin Ahmed, JJ. I concur with the decision of Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J, Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J,- This appeal by special leave raises an important question of public importance namely whether the principle of acknowledgement of sonship under the Muslim Law has been correctly appreciated by the High Court Division as well as by the courts below.

<u>2. Facts are as follows: Plaintiff respondent instituted a suit being OC Suit No. 457 of 1977 for a declaration that the defendant appellant was a child of unknown parentage and also for a declaration that the plaintiff is the only eldest son of late Amir Ali Mia who was the Mutwalli of Salamat Mia Wakf Estate at Rajshahi and eligible for the Mutwalliship of the Wakf Estate in terms of the Wakfnama.</u>

3. One Salamat Hossain created a Wakf deed dated 1-7-30 and the Wakif was the first Mutwalli. After his death Amir Ali Mia, the brother's son of the Wakif became the Mutwalli in 1933 and continued as such till his death on 5-4-1967. After the death of Amir Ali a dispute arose with regard to the Mutwalliship of the Wakf Estate. The plaintiff claimed that he is the surviving eldest son of Amir Ali Mia by his third wife Mst. Meher Shamsun Nahar. He, in terms of the wakf deed, was entitled to be appointed as Mutwalli on the death of his father. The defendant No. 1 Khorshed Alam also claimed to be the eldest son of Amir Ali Mia by his alleged second wife namely Monwara Khatun.

4. Both the plaintiff and the defendant applied to the Wakf Administrator for being appointed as Mutwalli. The Wakf Administrator appointed plaintiff as Mutwalli by his order dated 5-12-67 and the defendant preferred an appeal before the District Judge; Rajshahi but the appeal was dismissed on contest. Thereafter, the defendant moved the High Court Division and succeeded in getting an order in his favour. The plaintiff thereafter moved the Supreme Court but the order of the High Court Division was upheld. It was observed that the question of legitimacy of the defendant would be decided by a competent civil court and till such decision the defendant was to continue as the Mutwalli (vide 29 DLR). The first round was thus over.

5. Now the second round. The plaintiff brought the aforesaid suit for the declaration mentioned above. His case was that Amir Ali Mia had three wives. His first wife Sakina Bibi had several issue but all of them died during their infancy. His second wife was a tribal lady from Siliguri named Zohura Khatun who had no issue and as such she with the permission of her husband Amir Ali Mia adopted a son of a prostitute called Baramoni of Natore. The plaintiff stated that this adopted son is defendant Khorshed Alam and it was contended that defendant Khorshed Alam was never the legitimate son of Amir Ali Mia and, as such, was not entitled to be the Mutwalli, Plaintiff's further case was Amir Ali Mia married for the third time in 1939 Mst. Meher Sharnsun Nahar from Bogra and 3 sons and five daughters were begotten out of the third marriage. The plaintiff is the eldest son by this wife and is entitled to be the Mutwalli of the Wakf Estate on the death of his father.

6. The defendant No. 1 Khorshed Alam contested the suit contending that Amir Ali had four wives: His first wife was Sakina Bibi, second wife was Monowara Khatun, mother of the defendant No. 1 and his third wife was Zohura Khatun and the 4th wife was Mst Shamsun Nahar, the mother of the Plaintiff. The defendant stated that Monowara Khatun, the mother of the defendant No. 1 was married by Amir Ali Mia at Calcutta in 1929 and the defendant No. 1 Khorshed Alam was born out of the wedlock in 1933 and, as such, he is the eldest son of Amir Ali. Defendant further contended that at the old age of Amir Ali when he was ailing and was completely under the influence of his 4th wife Shamsun Nahar he began to disown the defendant No. 1 as his son though all along acknowledge defendant as his son.

<u>7. On these averments the suit was fought out and the trial court came to the conclusion on evidence that the defendant No. 1 was not the son of Amir Ali nor Amir Ali acknowledged him "as his legitimate son". The learned Munsif further held that it could not be proved that Monwara Khatun, mother of defendant No. 1 was one of the wives of Amir Ali. The appellate Court below affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif. It was held that the plaintiff proved his case that the defendant was not the legitimate son of Amir Ali. The Appellate Court below further found that there was no proof of marriage of Amir Ali Mia with Monowara Khatun. The appellate Court below further noticed that as far back as 1965 defendant No. 1 could not give the name of his mother or the place where he was born. In this view of the matter, the judgment of the trial court was affirmed. The matter came before the High Court Division in Civil Revision being CR No. 263 of 1981, the learned Single Judge noticed such a contradiction of the defendant in his previous deposition as to the name of his mother and place of his birth and further noticed plaintiff's positive case by observing:</u>

<u>"We may notice that the plaintiff has come up with case that the defendant No. 1 was not the son of Amir Ali but only adopted by his second wife Zohura Khatun and he were adopted from one Baramoni of Natore and he was not begotten by Amir Ali”</u>

<u>The learned Single Judge further noticed that the very existence of Monowara Khatun was challenged by the plaintiff and the defendant has not been able to prove marriage between Amir Ali Mia and Monowara Begum and as such "the alleged marriage of Amir Ali with Monowara Begum has been disproved." And concluded that the question of acknowledgement by Amir Ali of the defendant No. 1 "as his son" is of no avail.</u>

<u>Leave was granted on the following terms:</u>

<u>"It appears that the decision of the case hinges on the question whether the claim to sonship of Amir Ali by the petitioner is established by the acknowledgement of Amir Ali claiming the former to be his son. The point for consideration is whether the learned judge of the High Court Division has correctly decided the principle of acknowledgement under Muslim Law".</u>

<u>Plaintiff is the respondent. He brought the suit:</u>

<u>(a) For a decree of declaration to the effect that the defendant No. 1 is the child of some unknown parentage other than that of Md. Amir Ali Mia; and</u>

<u>(b) For a decree of declaration that the plaintiff is the only eligible person to be appointed as Mutwalli of the Salamat Hossain Wakf Estate enrolled in EG No. 4028 of Rajshahi in terms and conditions of the Wakf deed thereof;</u>

<u>8. As has been noticed that this is a second round and on previous occasion over the Mutwalliship the controversy in issue was more or less the same namely, that the defendant Khorshed Alam is the child of some unknown parentage other than that of Md. Amir Ali. In paragraph 15 of the plaintiff it is stated that "the defendant is an illegitimate child of an unknown parentage who was only reared up by Md. Amir Ali Mia by way of a token of love to his said 2nd barren wife Zohura Khatun who died in the year 1965. Plaintiff examined 16 witnesses. The evidence of the plaintiff is more or less the same, namely, that Khorshed Alam is a son of one Baramoni of Natore and Amir Ali adopted his as his son. Amir Ali had three wives and no wife by the name Monwara Khatun as contended by the defendant. The defendant's case is that Amir Ali had 4 wives, the first wife Sakina, died in 1941-42 who had given birth to number of children but all were dead. He married Monwara in 1929 and the defendant Khorshed Alam was born in the wedlock of this marriage, 1933. Monwara died in 1935. Thereafter, Amir Ali married Zohura Begum in 1935 and she died on 6-2-66. The 4th wife plaintiff's mother Mst Meher Shamsun Nahar who was married to Amir Ali in 1939 and she is still alive. Be it noted that Amir Ali died in April, 1967 about a year after the death of Zohura. The contention of the plaintiff is that Amir Ali adopted this child. Khorshed Alam when he was a boy 2 years old and gave him to Zohura for rearing him up. This was done only to comfort Zohura who was a barren woman. Evidence was led that Khorshed Alam actually is the son of prostitute namely Baramoni of Natore who is still alive. PW 1 and the plaintiff himself stated: the said Zohura had no issue and she was barren. At Natore she got one boy about 2 years old in adoption from one Baramoni a prostitute of Natore and that boy is defendant No. 1". That was the main case of the plaintiff. It is not necessary for this court to go into the details of evidence that was led by the parties for it is apparent that the bone of contention between the parties over the Mutwalliship was so severe that the witnesses can safely be discarded as being partisan witnesses. They were obviously hostile to one another and it is clear that neither was over scrupulous in what he swore to. One may be fairly set of against the other as neither can be safely trusted. But the battle was fought on the ground that Khorshed Alam is son of Natore. Onus was heavily on the plaintiff but this onus was not discharged. The evidence of the mother clearly shows this and none of the witness could make any positive case to prove the theory that Khorshed Alam is the son of Baramoni. Moti Sk PW 5 claimed that Baramoni gave the son of her to Amir Ali and Amir Ali took the son at the request of Raja Birendra. He served as a Pakhawala in the Rajbari. In cross-examination he conceded that the boy was not hand over at the Rajbari nor was he present when the boy was handed over to Amir Ali by Baramoni. The rest of the witnesses on this point can better be ignored because they all gave a parrot-like story to suit the plaintiff's case. Baramoni was not cited as witness by the plaintiff though she is alive.</u>

<u>9. It is the question of status of an individual. When that status is assailed by a positive case much higher degree of proof was necessary and the courts below unfortunately had overlooked this point completely. The trial court ought ret to have allowed such evidence to be led in when mere verbal statement damaging the social status of a person is being made. The entire plaintiff's evidence on this point ought to have been discarded by the trial courted the court of appeal over looked the fact that the court below had ignored the presumption of law and such presumption can only be rebutted by positive fact and not by mere assertion or ipsi dixit. It is the plaintiff who brought the suit and he took up the positive stand that the defendant is a son of one Baramoni and since this onus was not discharged the plaintiff ought to have been non-suited. Unfortunately that did not happen. The courts below have decreed the suit and we shall come to this later as to whether such suit can at all be decreed.</u>

<u>10. The defendant took a consistent case that his mother was Monowara who was married by Amir Ali in 1929 at Calcutta. She gave birth to this son, the defendant, in 1933 and 2 years later she died in 1935. It is true that the boy was reared up by Zohura the 3rd wife of Amir Ali whom he married in 1935 and died on 6-2-66, there was no onus on the defence to prove the maternity. To be more clear, law has not placed any onus on him to prove as to in whose womb he was born. The fact is that he was born obviously in the womb of a woman. He was reared up according to his own statement by Amir Ali who introduced him in the society as his son and he was reared by Zohura who admittedly had no issue From 1935 right upto 1953 not a word was said by any group challenging the acknowledgement of a sonship by Amir Ali. Formal evidence was led by the defendant to show that Amir Ali had acknowledged the defendant as his son. He was admitted to a school and the Headmaster of that School gave certificate to that effect e.g. Exhibit B which shows the defendant as son of Amir Ali Exhibit C is the deposition by Amir Ali before a Magistrate on 14-11-335 where he stated "Shah Alam aged 2-1/2 is my son by my second wife". Kabinnama Exhibit D dated 23-3-51 when Khorshed Alam married Jahanara Begum, his first wife and he was shown as the son of SK Amir Ali and the marriage was solemnized in the house of Amir Ali, (column 18). Khurshed Alam's first wife died and he married again in 1953. This time he was married to Nazle Begum @ Zorna and the Kabinnama is dated 13-3-53. There he was shown as son of Amir Ali. And who is Nazle Begum. She was none but the daughter of the sister of the plaintiff's own mother, in other words, the plaintiff's first cousin (Khalato sister and Amir Ali was himself one of the witnesses of this marriage age. Rent receipt Exhibit E series between 1953 to 1957 show that Khorshed rented a part of the wakf property from his father Amir Ali and he was shown as first son of Amir Ali The most important document Exhibit G Ekrarnama for Hiba-bil-ewaj executed by Amir Ali on 19-3-533 where he stated:</u>

<u>“আমার জ্যেষ্ঠ পুত্র খোরশেদ আলম ওরফে শাহ আলমের শুভ বিবাহ আপনার জ্যেষ্ঠ কন্যা মোসাম্মৎ নাজনি বেগম ওরফে ঝরনা বেগমের সহিত প্রস্তাব করিলে আপনি উক্ত প্রস্তাবে নিম্ন লিখিত স্বত্ত্বে বিবাহ দিতে রাজী হইলেন। আমি এতদমুলে নিম্ন লিখিত স্বত্ত্বে এই একরায়ে আবদ্ধ হইয়া শুভ বিবাহের কাজ আগাম করিয়াছি। অর্থাৎ ২৫০০১ পঁচিশ হাজার এক টাকা দেন মোহর ধার্য্য হইয়া তৎপক্ষে হাজিরান মজলিশে সোনার অলংকার আদি দ্বারা নগদে মং ১০০০ টাকা পরিশোধ করিয়া দিয়া অবশিষ্ট ১২০০১, বার হাজার এক টাকা তলম মত আদায় ও অবশিষ্ট ১২০০০ বার হাজার টাকা বিবাহ দিয়ে থাকাতক ক্রমান্নয়ে পরিশোধের অংগীকার এবং নিজ ও পৈত্রিক স্থাবর সম্পত্তি আমার যাহাতৎ মর্যাদায় আমার অবর্তমানে ভবিষ্যতে কোন প্রকার গোলযোগ উপস্থিত না হয় এবং ইহা ও শুভ বিবাহের কল্য মধ্যে হেতু এই স্বীকার ও অংগীকার করিতেছি যে, আমি যতশীঘ্র সম্ভব আমার নিজ মোকাম রাজশহী গিয়া আমার ওয়ারিশান ও স্থলাভিযিকগনের নিম্ন লিখিত সত্যে হেবাবিল এওজ দলিল সম্পাদন ও জেজিষ্টী করিতে বাধ্য থাকিলাম। অন্যথায় চুক্তি ভংগ অপরাধে দন্ডণীয় হইবে। আমার নিজ মোকাম রাজশাহী শহরে রানী বাজারে রানপুর বোয়ালিয়া মৌজায় আমার স্বকৃত আমির মঞ্জিল নামীয় ত্রিতল অট্টালিকা আমার ১মা স্ত্রী মোছামৎ জহুরা খাতুন ও জ্যেষ্ঠ পুত্র খোরশেদ আলম ওরফে শাহ আলম এবং নবপুত্র বধু মোছামৎ নাজনি বেগম এই ৩জনকে তুল্যাংশে দান করিলাম। এবং উক্ত স্ত্রী জহুরা খাতুন অভাব হইলে তাহার যাবতীয় স্বর্তে আমার উক্ত জ্যেষ্ঠ পুত্র বধু মাতা নাজলি বেগমের উপর তুল্যাংশে বত্তিবে। এবং অবশিষ্ট উক্ত মৌজায় পুকুর পাড়ের স্তিত আমার স্বকৃত ত্রিতল অট্টালিকা আমার ২য় স্ত্রী বেগম শামছুন্নেহার এবং তাহার গর্ভজাত ২ পুত্র ও ৪ কন্যা এবং ভবিষ্যতে আরও যদি খোদা এনায়েত করেন তাহা সকলে উক্ত ত্রিতল বাড়ীর স্বত্ত্বাধিকারী ও কারিনী হইবেক। এবং আমার বাবা মরহুম ছালামত আলী সাহেব কৃত ওয়াকফ সম্পত্তির যাহা বর্তমান আমি নিজে মতোল্লী আছি। তাহা ও আমার অবর্তমানে আমার ২ স্ত্রী বেগম শামছুনেহার (অস্পষ্ট) এর গর্ভজাত পুত্রগনের মধ্যেই যে বড় (অস্পষ্ট) তাহাকেই আমার স্থলে মতোল্লী মনোনীত করিলাম।</u>

<u>We shall deal with the later part of this Ekrarnama in connection of the point of disclaimer of the acknowledgement or its repudiation at the appropriate place. Affidavits sworn by Bibi Gauharun Nessa Exhibit H, Exhibit H(1) by Roushan Aker Firoza Ahmed who was the relation of the family have proved the case beyond the doubt that the defendant was always acknowledged as the son of Amir Ali. Series of letters were produced between the father and the son written in the year 1953, 1954, 1955 and 1956. Exhibit L series which are the letters between the father and the son concerning family affairs. Khorshed Alam contested an election and evidence was led to show that his father Amir Ali asked Mussalli after Jumma prayer to support candidature of his son. Apart from the oral evidence that was adduced by the defendant to show that Amir Ali acknowledged Khorshed Alam as his son, this judgment proceeds on the basis of the written acknowledgement of the sonship and the legal consequence thereof.</u>

<u>11. Baillie says that the acknowledgement by a man of a child is valid under the following circumstances: first, the ages of the parties must admit of the party acknowledged being born to the acknowledger: as otherwise he would be manifestly a liar. Second, the descent of the person acknowledged must not be already established from another; for if it were so, that would prevent its establishment from any but him. 3rd, he must confirm the acknowledger in his acknowledgement if he can give an account of himself; for one he can do so in his own power contrary to the case of a child who cannot account for himself. (A digest of Mohammedan Law-Baillie P 405).</u>

<u>12. Amir Ali Acknowledged Khorshed Alam as his son and Khorshed Alam acknowledged Amir Ali as his father. So the conditions Nos. 1 and 3 are fulfilled. Now what about second condition. It says that the descent of a person acknowledged must not be already established from another. Has anybody proved that Khorshed Alam is a son of another person? None whatsoever. On the contrary. Plaintiff's own case was that Khorshed Alam was of unknown parentage. That was the specific case in the plaint though evidence was led to say that Khorshed Alam was son of one Baramoni, but it was not established, whereas the second condition says that the descent of a person acknowledges must not be already established from another. Thus the second condition is also fulfilled for rendering the acknowledgement valid. In Dural Mukhtar it is stated thus:</u>

<u>"(i) If a person makes an acknowledgement in favour of a stranger whose parentage is unknown and thereafter acknowledges him to his son, and the latter verifies it which he is one of those who are fit to make such a verification, his descent is established with reference to the time of his being begotten.</u>

<u>"(ii) If a person makes an acknowledgement in favour of a youth whose parentage is unknown whether at his birth place or in the town where he is, that the latter is his son, and the acknowledgers and the acknowledged are such in age that the later may be born of the former as a son, and the youth verifies it, he being capable of discretion (because otherwise his verification is not necessary as already stated) thus his descent is established, though the acknowledger be in sickness; and when the descent is so established, the youth will participate with the other heir". (CS 10 All 312).</u>

<u>Hedaya sums up the Law upon the subject:</u>

<u>"If a person acknowledge the parent- age of a child who is able to give an account of himself, saying "This is my son" and the ages of the parties be such as to admit of the one being the child of the other, and the parentage of the child be not well known to any person. It is well settled that the acknowledgement of parentage under the Mohammedan Law rests upon a footing higher than that of ordinary admission as pure matters of evidence. The rules of acknowledgement of parentage is based upon the words of Al-Qua-ran-Call them after their father".</u>

<u>"(Sura 33.4) Muslim Jurists have testified to this and the author of the Kifaya explains that such acknowledgement is sufficient because the burden of the obligation in respect of the child rests especially on the father, and the latter acknowledgement effects him personally and is thus accepted without any verification by the mother".</u>

13. An author celebrated commentary on the Hedaya Fathual Qadir in explaining the rule quoted above as to the condition that the acknowledged child should be of unknown parentage, goes on to say that the condition has been imposed because otherwise the descent of the acknowledged child could not be established from the acknowledger since "descent after it is established is not susceptible of the annulment." In other words the acknowledged child should be of unknown parentage.

<u>14. In the case of Md Alladat Khan vs Md. Ismail Khan 10 ILR Allahabad 289 the Court considered the following questions:</u>

<u>"The question then is whether in cases like the present, where the paternity of a child, that his, his legitimate descent from his father, cannot be proved by establishing a marriage between his parents at the time of his conception or birth, the Muhammadan Law recognises any other method whereby such marriage and legitimate descent can be presumed inferred, or held to be established as a matter of substantive law for purpose of inheritance". (at page 330).</u>

<u>Mahmood, J noticed the leading cases namely 3 Moore IA 295, 8 Moore JA 136, 11 Moore IA 94 then answered the question as in the following manner:</u>

<u>"All the cases which their Lordships had before them were cases in which the question of marriage itself was a matter in dispute and involved in obscurity with reference to the legitimacy of the child. In other words, those cases were such as left either the fact or the exact time of the alleged marriage a matter of uncertainty, that is, neither proved nor disproved; and their Lordships in dealing with those cases applied the principle of the Muhammadan Law of acknowledgement of parentage with reference to legitimacy for purposes of inheritance." (at page 334)</u>

<u>But this view is not applicable in the case of children born of Zina and such children can never be legitimated or entitled to inherit from their father. In the present case the plaintiff failed to prove that the defendant is the son of another person and therefore he could not be acknowledged validly as son of Amir Ali On the contrary, the plaintiff himself brought the suit for a prayer that the defendant is of unknown parentage other than Amir Ali In that prayer plaintiff itself invites the rule of acknowledgement of parentage in Muslim Law.</u>

<u>15. The defendant stated that he was born in the womb of Monwara Begum who was the second wife of Amir Ali The plaintiff contested it and stated that there had been no wife by name Monwara of Amir Ali Straight, J sunned up;</u>

<u>"But where there is no proof of legitimate birth or illegitimate birth and the paternity of a child is unknown in the sense that no specific person is shown so have been his father, then his acknowledgement by another, who claims his as his son, according to the authorities I have quoted from, afford a conclusive presumption that the child acknowledged is the legitimate child of the acknowledger and place him in that category" (10 All p. 317).</u>

<u>If the defendant failed to prove the marriage of his mother that will not create an impediment to the acknowledgement itself, and since the plaintiff did not take up the plea that the marriage between Amir Ali and Monowara could not have been possible it being within prohibitory degree or off spring of Zina. The force of the logic therefore upholds the contention of the defendant for the doctrine of acknowledgement to come into play. Mahmud, J in his celebrated judgment in 10 Ali 289 (which was upheld by the Privy Council in the case of Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Altaf Ali Chowdhury and others, 48 IA 114) pointedly answered the question: HI repeal that the rule is limited to case of uncertainty of legitimate descents and proceeds entirely upon an assumption of legitimacy and establishing such legitimacy by the force of such acknowledgement" (page 537), the learned judge summed up the fact of that case:</u>

<u>"that the entire question of the descent, birth and legitimacy of Alladat is involved in obscurity owing to the exact date of his mother marriage with Ghulam Gaus being unascertainable and that therefore, this case presents all these conditions to which the Muhammadan Law as to the acknowledgement of parentage is most appropriately applicable and further the requisite acknowledgement in words and by treatment was made by Ghulam Gaus without any such intimation of Alladat being the offspring of illicit intercourse as would vitiate the effect of the acknowledgement according to the text" (page 338-339).</u>

16. Such acknowledgement could being effective by proving (1) that the acknowledged son is an offspring of Zina,(2) that the marriage between the acknowledger and the mother of the child was impossible or did not exist at the time would make the child legitimate. The Plaintiff did not prove either of these two essentials which would vitiate the acknowledgement of Amir Ali that Khorshed Alam is his son.

17. In the case of Sadek Hussain Khan vs Hashim Ali Khan, 43 IA page 212 the Privy Council considered the oral evidence of 4 witnesses who supported the acknowledgement of Sultan Mirza by his father Zaigham-ud-Doula, Their Lordships scoffed at the criticism passed upon their evidence that the boy Sultan Mirza was only introduced to each of them once, and therefore their recollection is unreliable by observing "as it is was to be expected that a father would naturally introduce a son to a friend as his son more than once"(Page 233). Their Lordships re-emphasised the law:

"no statement made by one man that another (proved to be illegitimate) is his son can make that other legitimate, but where no proof of that kind has been given such a statement or acknowledgement is substantive evidence that the person so acknowledged is the legitimate son of the person who makes the statements provided his legitimacy be possible" (page 234),

<u>18. This proposition of law was reiterated in the case of Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Altaf Ali Chowdhury, 48 1A 114. It raises a presumption which may be taken advantage of by either wife-claimant or son-claimant, Being however, a presumption of fact, and not jurisdiction jure, it is, like every other presumption of fact, capable of being set-aside by contrary proof. The Privy Council says in a formula as under:</u>

<u>"The result is that a claimant son who has in his favour a good acknowledgement of legitimacy is in this position. The marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. Until the claimant establishes his acknowledgement the onus is on him to prove the marriage. Once he establishes an acknowledgement, onus is on those who deny a marriage to negative it in fact."</u>

<u>(This principle was reiterated, in Mahabbat Ali Khan's case 56 IA at page 207. Here is the key to be problem, Khorshed Alam has proved the acknowledgement and a written document Exhibit H backed by enormous documentary evidence that Amir Ali acknowledged him as his son. The onus is on those who deny a marriage of his mother Monwara Begum to Amir Ali (to negative it in fact). The plaintiff failed miserably on this score as well. Then the case of Mahabbat Ali Khan vs Muhammad Ibrahim Khan 56 IA 201 the Privy Council considered the question of acknowledgement by a father, their Lordships observed:</u>

<u>19. "The present case accordingly is one of an acknowledgement by the father, an acknowledgement which involves the assertion that he, the father Khurshid, was married to Musammat Babo, the appellant's mother. Such acknowledgement undoubtedly raises a presumption in favour of the marriage and of the legitimacy." (Page 206).</u>

<u>The Privy Council reiterated the principle laid down in the case of Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Alta] Ali Chowdhury, 48 1A 114. The dictum was reiterated with approval:</u>

<u>"A claimant son who has in his favour a good acknowledgement of legitimacy is in this position: The marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. Until the claimant establishes his acknowledgement the onus is on him to prove a marriage. Once he establishes an acknowledgement, the onus is on those who deny a marriage to negative it in fact." (page 207).</u>

<u>It would appear accordingly that it rests upon the respondent in this case to establish that there was no marriage with Monwara. The plaintiff-respondent did not discharge the onus and therefore acknowledgement by Amir Ali and his treatment of the defendant-appellant Khorshed Alam as his son holds the field. The Privy Council in 56 IA 201 considered the documents which had been produced and observed:</u>

<u>it is sufficient to say that they appear to demonstrate with clearness both the sonship and the legitimacy of the appellant. The father took much interest in his upbringing and there are letters between both the father and the son, on the one hand, and other members of the family on the other, showing that the interest in his upbringing and education was shared by these relations. Throughout the transactions and correspondences referred to, no suggestion of any kind appears to the effect that Mahabbat was illegitimate. The entire body of facts is confirmatory of his legitimacy." (Page 205-206).</u>

<u>20. Precisely that is the position here in this case. Khorshed Ali was acknowledged as son and he was reared up and treated as such and to cap it all he was married to Nazneen, his Khalato sister (first cousin), daughter of plaintiffs mother's sister and upon her death her younger sister was married to him. What more is expected to show that Khorshed Alam was treated legitimate son of Amir Ali. The crisis came in 1966 and now we shall deal with that chapter. The evidence is that plaintiff by now had become a major. He was born in 1945 in the womb of his mother Meher Shamsun Nahar who was married in 1939 to Amir Ali Be it noted that Zohora who reared up Khorshed Alam was married in 1935 and died in 1966. It appears that Amir Ali filed a money suit being MS 33 of 1965 for realization of rent of Taka 900 being the arrears of rent from 1962 to 1965. This suit was filed on 16-8-65 and it was filed against Khorshed Alam describing him as Khorshed Alam @ shah Alam, (Possa Putra of Amir Ali). The word (Possa) was written in bracket in the decree Exhibit 4. The deposition of Amir Ali is Exhibit 5 and he deposed on 26-4-66 just about two months after death of Zohura Begum. In his evidence he did not say a word that Khorshed Alam was his adopted son. Though in cross-examination he disputed the genuineness of the Heba-bil-Ewaj Exhibit H Khorshed Alam deposed as defendant and stated that he took lease of the entire building for the purpose of running residential hotel and he stated that he lived in the Amir Manzil on the second floor with his father who lived on the first floor. He was cross-examined as to his place of birth, name of his mother and a suggestion that the plaintiff was not his father. Amir Ali himself died in April, 1967. High Court Division and the courts below gave much emphasis on this fact that the appellant was shown as "Possa Putra" in the cause title and the appellant in cross-examination could not give the name of his mother and his place of birth. Amir Ali himself deposed; he did not say a word in his evidence as to the acknowledgement of sonship or Khorshed Alam this way or the other. Defendant himself explained that at this time at the instigation of the plaintiff and his mother a ground was being prepared for disowning him as the eldest son of Amir Ali in view of prolonged aliment of Amir Ali and having an eye on the question of Mutwalliship after his death. Perusal of the documentary evidence and oral evidence adduced by the plaintiff show that towards the end of 1965 the scheme was made for dislodging Khorshed Alam from the family and the rent suit for recovery of amount of Rs. 900 was merely a device for letting in some evidence for the purpose of discarding legitimacy and acknowledgement of Khorshed Alam. As the Privy Council mentioned in 561 lA. at page 209 that such evidence ought not to have been allowed by the trial court and we are also of the same opinion that in a Money Suit the question as to the paternity of the defendant ought not to have been allowed by the trial courts. This evidence is therefore discarded. To fail back upon the dictum of the Privy Council, "Once he establishes an acknowledgement the onus is on those who deny a marriage to negative it in fact." That acknowledgement has been well proved in this case by oral evidence and documentary evidence that since his childhood Amir Ali brought him up, gave him education and was a little boy 2-1/2 years old when his mother Monwara Begum died (1935). Amir Ali married Zohura in 1935 and this Zohura reared him up since 1935 and she died on 6-2-1966. Be it noted that Mst. Shamsun Nahar, the 4th wife of Amir Ali was married to him in 1937, Between 1935 and 1939 Amir Ali only one wife namely Zohura. Meher Shamsun Nahar's sister gave her daughter Nazneen in marriage to Khorshed Alam in 1953. <u>The evidence that was led shows clearly that this Heba-bil-Ewaj was acted upon and Zohura was described as his first wife because at that time she was the first wife and Alam was mentioned as the eldest son and his newly wedded wife Nazneen Begum was given a proportionate share in the three storied houses namely" Amir Manzil".
