<u>21. That clinches the whole issue Khorshed Alam was not only mentioned as his eldest son but he was given the status of a defacto guardian of the entire family in the business of Amir Ali till step-brother born through his second wife comes of age, What more is expected to show that the acknowledgement of sonship of Khorshed Alam admits of no doubt.</u>

22. The next question comes that where there is a valid acknowledgement whether such acknowledgement could be repudiated. In the case of Ashrufood Dowlah vs Hyder Hossain Khan, 11 MIA 94 there had been no continuation of treatment upto the time of the father's death. On the contrary, there has been absolute denial of paternity by the father. There was no proof of any acknowledgement but there was proof of treatment strong enough to prove legitimacy in the ordinary case. In these circumstances their Lordships Hele: "That the acknowledgement was not proved satisfactorily for sonship and further held that the onus of proof of his illegitimacy was upon the further held that a denial of a son either of a Nikahee (regular) or Mootaher (irregular) marriage after acknowledgement is untenable though supported by a disclaimer and repudiation by the father. In that case the plaintiff-appellant denied the marriage and the disclaimer of acknowledgement by the Nowab of the respondent as his son and relied upon deed of disclaimer and the repudiation of the respondent executed by the Nowab in his life time denying that the respondent was his son was held to be untenable, Their Lordships however found that the defendant failed to establish acknowledgement. In the case of Mohammad Baikder Hossain Khan Bahadoor vs Shurfoon Nessa Begum, 8 IA 136 the question was whether the appellant was the son of Nowab of Karnataka by his Nika wife Amin Shaheba. The respondent challenged the marriage who according to them was a slave girl observed:

"According to the Mohammedan Law, the law, which regulates the rights of the parties before us, the legitimacy or legitimation of a child of Mohammedan parents may properly be presumed or inferred from circumstance without proof, or at least without any direct proof, either of a marriage between the parents, or of any formal act of legitimation" (page 159).

In that case, it was held, there was absence of circumstances sufficient to find or justify such a presumption or such an inference.

23. Mr Khondaker Mahhubuddin Ahmed appearing for the respondent argued strenuously on the Exhibit 8 Ekramama and questioned as to why Amir Ali nominated the eldest son of his second wife to be the Mutawalli as far back in 1953. To quote Lord Bowen, Devil knows not what is in the mind of a man. It is not permissible in law to speculate. When the person himself has spelled out in writing as to the disposition of his properties and as to, the happening after his death that till the son of the second wife comes of age. Khorshed Alam whom he described as his eldest son was to manage the affairs. In his background he mentioned that after his death the eldest son of second wife will be the Mutawalli is left in the field of speculation and though Amir Ali lived for about 14 years thereafter, he never clarified the position. It was only in 1967 just a month before his death that he declared: I nominate my eldest son Amir Sultan Ali Hyder as the next Mutwalli after me and he is educated, religious minded and fit to be Mutwalli of the suit wakf Estate.

<u>24. That one Khorshed Alam alias Shah Alam is not my son and I reared him and never acknowledged his as my son and he is separate from (Exhibit lid dated 6-3-67) me. By that time Zohura was dead and interesting enough by this time Khorshed Alam was described as "my adopted son, is very dishonest, mischievous and for his nefarious activities, I drove him out from my family and I have no connection with him." (Exhibit 1 dated 14-3-66). Towards the end of 1966 and beginning of 1967 various representation were made denouncing Khorshed Alam. For instance Exhibit 1/d dated 6-3-67 where Khorshed Alam was disowned as son and furthers it is stated that he was never acknowledged as his son. These are products of grand design which will be evident when a petition filed by Md Solaiman in considered. This Solaiman submitted an objection dated 23-8-77 praying not to appoint Khorshed Alam alias Shah Alam as he is illegitimate son of unknown person and adopted son of late Md Amir Ali (vide Exhibit 1/e dated 23-8-77). By that time the battle was on over Mutwalliship. Solaiman described himself as son of late Sk Salamat Hossain. In paragraph 1 he says that he is the only son of Salamat Hossain Khan who created Salamat Hossain Wakf estate and he stated that his cousin brother late Md Amir Ali was the ex Mutwalli of Salamat Ali Wakf Estate after his father. And not that Amir Ali died on 5-4-67, he joined with the plaintiff supporting his candidature for Mutwalliship as against Khorshed Alam. He denounced Khorshed Alam on the same pattern as was done by plaintiff himself and prayed for the appointment of the plaintiff as Mutwalli. Why this unusual zeal on the part of the person named Solaiman who described himself as only son of first wakif yet he was not appointed Mutwalli. Answer in not far to seek. Amir Ali himself has given the answer in his life time and it will be useful to consider Exhibit S (1) petition by Amir Ali dated 12-12-49. In respect of Misc. Case No.6 of 1944 before the Wakf Commissioner who initiated the proceeding on various allegations by Solaiman Mia and Amir Ali posed the question "who is this Solaiman Mia?" (at page 118 of volume 11 of the Paper Book). He mentioned son of the Wakif Salamat Mia in his advanced age Nika Married one Wahidan Bewa who was born and brought up at Patna. This Solaiman wanted to be Mutwalli and he initiated series of proceeding against Amir Ali and Amir Ali states: "It is very recently the Mutwalli was attacked and the Mutwalli has been obliges to file a petition under section 107 Cr PC for protection before the SDO on 2-9-49. Such is the man Solaiman Mia". Amir Ali him- self posed the question and gave answer to it and the less said the better, because Solaiman was never appointed as Mutwalli tough he has now taken up the cudgel on behalf of the plaintiff to dislodge Khorshed Alam who had been acknowledged as eldest son of Amir Ali by Amir Ami himself throughout his life. These subsequent affidavits in and around 1966-67 expose the design which is now paved for dislodging Khorshed Alam then proving any disclaimer or repudiation. As the Privy Council in 43 IA 212 considered such documents are of no avail and the acknowledgement having been proved such documents composed many years subsequent to the dates of acknowledgements deposed to by the four witnesses mentioned and concluded that the evidence of the four witness is not rebutted or discredited "by these documents" (at page 234),</u>

<u>Issue No. 2 was framed as under:</u>

<u>"Is the defendant No. 1 a man of unknown parentage other than that of Amir Ali Mia?"</u>

<u>While the trial court initially started by placing the onus on the plaintiff answered the question that the defendant was never a legitimate son of late Amir Ali Mia but he was a foster son of him and of unknown parentage and Amir Ali Mia 'intended to establish him in the society as his son and simply acknowledged him." In passing placed the onus on the defendant to prove that Monwara Khatun was the mother of the defendant No. 1 and she was married to Amir Ali Mia.</u>

<u>25. The lower appellate Court approached the question from another angle namely, that the plaintiff's case was that defendant Khorshed Alam is the son of one Baramoni, a reputed prostitute of Natore and that he was adopted by Johura Khatoon, the second wife of Amir Ali Mia who was a tribal lady from Siliguri. It was noticed that this onus was not discharged by the plaintiff and that Baramoni who was still alive was not adduced as a witness by the plaintiff. The appellate Courts suggests "that Baramoni as mother of the defendant could not come forward to assert her mother hood of the defendant at this stage which may doom the further of the defendant the defendant also did not produce her in supported of his case, it is the therefore well proved that the defendant is not a legitimate son of late Amir Ali" (page 194 of Paper book). The suggestion is unwarranted and the conclusion is arbitrary being contrary to all presumption of law built up over the last 150 years! The appellate court below took the view from Exhibit G the Ekramama that 'why then Amir Ali wanted to disprove Khorshed Alam from Mutwalliship as back as 1953 which was due to him if he is a real son of Amir Ali Mia."</u>

26. Before proceeding further both trial court and the lower appellate court erred in law and failed to take notice of the presumption in the matter of personal status which will be considered presently.

<u>27. The High Court Division further noticed that Exhibit 5 (a) and 6, deposition of the defendant in case No. 5/66 show that the defendant contradicted himself as to the place of his birth and origin, Notwithstanding the challenge that was given by the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant appellant as to the admissibility of Exhibit 5 and 6 which have been treated as substantive evidence, the High Court Division took the view that those previous statements are admissible for the purpose of the contradiction. With respect, this conclusion is not founded in law. Exhibit 5 and 6 are inadmissible evidence and they cannot constitute as admission within section 19 of the Evidence Act. The High Court Division then dealt with Exhibit G and concluded that because Amir Ali wanted to deprive from the Mutwalliship as far back as in 1953 question of defendant No. 1's relationship cropped up in the mind of the relations of Nazlee Begum, wife of defendant No. 1 and this document Exhibit G was executed as safe guard for the defendant and his wife. This finding is based on conjecture which was recorded overlooking the provision of sections 91 and 02 of the Evidence Act. The High Court Division also viewed as the appellate Court below did that the defendant could not prove the marriage of Monwara Begum with Amir Ali Mia and concluded 'as such the alleged marriage of Amir All Mia with Monwara Begum has been disproved," This finding again has been recorded contrary to the well-settled principle of law and of Evidence Act. That the marriage between Monwara Begum and Amir Ali Mia was pleaded, no doubt, by the defendant, but the onus is never upon the defendant to prove the factum of marriage. As it has been already mentioned Mahmood, J after noticing the Privy Council cases namely, 3 MIA 295, 8 MIA 836 and 11 MIA 94 observed:</u>

<u>"In other works, these cases were such as left either the fact or the exact time of the alleged marriage a matter of uncertainty, that is, neither nor disproved".</u>

<u>But the well-settled proposition of acknowledgement of sonship is attracted unless it could by shown that the child is born out of Zina or of adultery and that onus is heavily upon the person who alleges. The plaintiff in this case stated as a positive case that defendant is a son of one Baramoni but gave up the case. Then the Court of appeal below onus on Khorshed Alam to prove the marriage and it was an erroneous allocation of onus because long line of cases does not place any onus on the evidence in a case of clear acknowledgement of parentage. Once acknowledgement is established the Privy Council says in 56 IA at page 201:</u>

<u>"A claimant son who has in his favour a good acknowledgement of legitimacy is in this position; The marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. Until the claimant establishes his acknowledgement the onus is on him to prove a marriage. Once he establishes an acknowledgement the onus is on those who deny a marriage to negative it in fact."</u>

<u>The onus was clearly upon the plaintiff to establish that there was no marriage. The plaintiff failed both on the court that defendant is the son of one Baramoni and also on the court that there was no marriage of Amir Ali with Monowara Begum. All the findings which have been arrived at by the courts below follow from misconception of law which have been laid down in the decision already mentioned since nineteenth century. In Srimati Bibabati Devi vs Kumar Ramendra Narayan Roy, 5 CWN 98 the Privy Council considered the nature of special circumstances which would allow a departure from the rule of the concurrent finding of fact. It was held:</u>

<u>"that there must be some miscarriage of justice of violation of some principle of law or procedure, that miscarriage of justice means such a departure from the rules which permeate all judicial procedure as to make that which happened not in the proper sense of the word judicial procedure at all. That the violation of some principle of law or procedure must be such an erroneous proposition of law that if that proposition be corrected the finding cannot stand: or it may be the neglect of some principle of law or procedure, whose application will have the same effect. The question whether there is evidence on which the Courts could arrive at their finding in such a question of law.</u>

<u>28. All the Courts below in the facts and circumstances of the case had misplaced the onus on the defendant for proving the marriage of Monowara Begum with Amir Ali Mia where as the settled principle of law is that the person who deny it will have to be established. In other words, it was for the plaintiff to prove that there was no marriage with Monowara Begum as alleged. As such, the concurrent findings in fact are no findings in the eye of law.</u>

29. Secondly, the Muslim dictum of acknowledgement was not appreciated by the Courts below and unfortunately the High Court Division also overlooked the settled proposition that is laid down in 6 IA page 201 that the marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. The High Court Division unfortunately mentioned that the defendant has not been able to prove the alleged marriage with Monwara Begum and concluded as such "alleged marriage of Amir Ali with Monwara has been disproved." Evidence Act deals with the concept, 'proved or not proved or disproved". Had the onus been on the defendant then the High Court Division could have said that the marriage was not proved, but the Privy Council settled that as onus is upon the plaintiff to disprove the marriage and if he establishes it, marriage is disproved. These legal concepts ate to be applied in the facts and circumstances of the cases, and any derailment by way of allocation of onus bound to cause a miscarriage of justice and the findings of fact arrived at are in contravention of the presumptions of law and therefore such finding of facts cannot stand as noticed by the Privy Council in 51 CWN Much emphasis was given by the plaintiff on Exhibit G to show that Amir Ali Mia as far back as 1953 denied Mutwalliship to Khorshed Alam and nominated that after his death the eldest son by his other wife should be the Mutwalli. Strenuous arguments were advanced by Mr Ahmed that this shows that the Mutwalli Amir Ali did not intend Khorshed Alam to be the Mutwalli. This document read as a whole belies the contention; on the other hand, Khorshed Alam was appointed as de facto guardian during the minority of the plaintiff. True that Amir Ali intended that Mutwalliship should pass on the issue of his other wife but wakf nama has not reserved such power to him which says:

“খোদা না করেন আমার জীবদ্দশায় উক্ত শ্রীমান আমীর আলীর অভাব হইলে তাহার পুত্র সন্তানগণের মধ্যে বার্ষিক ও সৎচরিত্র ও বয়োজেষ্ঠ ব্যক্তিপুঙ্খানুক্রমে---হইতে থাকিবেন।

Further he said that-

“উক্ত শ্রীমান সেখ আমীর আলীর অভাবে উক্ত শ্রীমান সেখ আমীর আলী ও শ্রীমান সেখ ছোলেমানের পুত্রগণের মধ্যে বয়োজেষ্ঠ ও সর্বাপেকক্ষা ধার্মিক ও সৎচরিত্র হইবে তিনি মতওয়াল্লী হইবে।”

That was the instrument of the Wakif. It has already been noticed that Solaiman Khan was not appointed, on the other hand, the wakif appointed his brother's son Shah Alam as Mutwalli. No power was reserved to the Mutwalli to vary the terms of the Wakf deed for choosing the line of Mutwalliship. It is admitted, that Solaiman is now dead and he has no male issue. Now condition is-

“উক্ত শ্রীমান সেখ আমি আলীর অভাবে উক্ত শ্রীমান আমির আলী ও শ্রীমান সেখ ছোলেমানের পুত্রগন মধ্যে যিনি বয়োজেষ্ঠ ও সর্বাপেক্ষা ধার্মিক ও সৎচরিত্র হইবে তিনি মোতয়াল্লী নিযুক্ত হইবেন।”

Now that Solaiman had no issue. Only sons of Amir Ali can claim Mutwalliship. The Wakif mentioned there conditions-

“যিনি বয়োজেষ্ঠ সর্বাপেক্ষা ধার্মিক ও সৎচরিত্রবান হইবেন।”

It is relevant for the purpose that the prayer No.2 of the plaint was to the following effect:

"For a decree of declaration that the plaintiff is the only eligible person to be appointed as Mutwalli of the Salamat Hossain Wakf Estate."

Since the prayer No. 1 that the defendant No.1 is the child of some unknown parentage other than that of Md. Amir Ali Mia cannot be granted view of the proposition of law mentioned above, the second prayer does not come for consideration inasmuch as, the conditions for appointment of Mutwalli, are mentioned in the Wakf deed itself and it is for the statutory functionary namely, the Administrator of Wakf to consider whether these conditions have been fulfilled by any individual. It is enough to notice that the assessment is to be made by the Administrator of Wakf Estate in Judicial manner (29 DLR. Page) Such jurisdiction exclusively conferred upon him by the law but his decision is not immune from challenge on the ground of malafide or arbitrariness.

30. To sum up the conclusions:

1. Plaintiff though set up a positive case that the defendant is the son of Baramoni had given it up and the onus that was on him was not thus discharged.

2. Acknowledgement of Amir Ali Mia raises a presumption in favour of the defendant as to his sonship.

3. Written acknowledgement was made in 1953 and that was never re-validated nor in law such acknowledgement could be invalidated by repudiation or disclaimer (vide Privy Council in 11 MIA. 94)

4. Having proved the acknowledgment of Amir Ali there is no onus on the defendant to prove marriage of his mother Monwara Begum with Amir Ali. The onus is on him who denies such marriage, namely the plaintiff and this onus was also not discharged. Marriage of Monwara Begum is thus neither "disproved" nor "proved" and, in such, circumstances the dictum of Mahmood, J in 10 Allahabad comes into play.

5. All evidence that has been adduced by the plaintiff challenging the status of defendant is around 1966 and 1967 and it may be noted that Amir Ali died in April, 1967.

6. Social relationship with the family of Amir Ali, and Khorshed Alam and that of the plaintiff raises strong circumstance in favour of the presumption of acknowledgement inasmuch as Khorshed Alam married to first cousins one after another of the plaintiff. The affidavit of plaintiff's mother's mother (Nani) though of 1967 throws light as to how controversy arose over the Mutwalliship only for which the plaintiff went to length of denying the acknowledgement of sonship by Amir Ali Mia.

7. In the Wakf deed no power was reserved to Mutwalli for diverting the line of Mutwalliship - the only condition was that the Mutwalli should be, “যিনি বয়োজেষ্ঠ সর্ব্বপেক্ষা ধার্মিক ও সৎচরিত্রবান হইবেন।”

All these qualities are to be evaluated by the statutory functionary e.g. Wakf Administrator while choosing the Mutwalli. It is for him to resolve the problem of solution if any of these requisite qualifications are lacking.

8. Lastly, the present suit was misconceived and on plaintiff's own showing such declaration namely, that Khorshed is of unknown parentage cannot be made as that is contrary to law nor the second prayer can be allowed which calls for objective determination of fact by the statutory functionary and as such the plaintiff has to be non-suited.

In the result, therefore this appeal is allowed and all the judgments and orders of the Court below are hereby set-aside and the suit is dismissed. No costs.

Shahabuddin Ahmed J : I have had the opportunity to read and consider the judgment of my learned brother, BH Chowdhury, J I very much regret that I am unable to agree with him on the views expressed and the decision arrived at in his judgment on the real question that calls for determination in this appeal. The real question is whether the presumption raised by late Amir Ali's acknowledgement that the appellant in his eldest son has been rebutted or set-aside by contrary proof adduced by the respondent an admitted son of late Amir Ali. Respondent filed the suit for this particular purpose in pursuance of this Court's earlier judgment in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975, reported in 29 DLR (SC) 295. Both the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court, on a concurrent finding of facts, decreed the suit holding that defendant appellant is not a legitimate son of Amir Ali, and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, on a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, did not find any ground to interfere with the concurrent finding of fact. Now it is to be seen whether the learned Single Judge rightly refused to interfere with the concurrent decision of the Courts below.

<u>32. At the outset. I would refer to the judgment of this Court in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975 in order to make it clear that the principle of law governing this suit was already determined and finally settled by this Court in that appeal, and thereafter, the party interested was advised to file a suit to rebut by contrary proof the presumption raised in favour of the defendant-appellant by late Amir Ali's acknowledgement that the defendant was his son. The said appeal also related to the same dispute that arose between the appellant and the respondent on the Mutwalli ship of the "Salamat Hossain Wakf Estate." On Amir Ali's death both the appellant, Khorshed Alam, and the respondent, Amir Sultan Ali, claimed the Mutwalliship as the eldest son of Amir Ali. The Commissioner of Waqfs, later on designated as Administrator of Waqfs, provisionally accepted the claim of the respondent Amir Sultan Ali and appointed him the Mutwalli in terms of the Waqf deed treating him as he eldest son of Amir Ali, the late Mutwalli, and expressed the view that the question as to who is the eldest son of the late Mutwalli should be decided in a properly constituted suit and till that decision the respondent would work as Mutwalli. This decision, as we have seen, was act aside by the High Court Division in a previous Revisional Application and its judgment was confirmed by this Court in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975 and it was held that in view of Amir Ali's acknowledgement" the appellant should be prima-facie treated as Amir Ali's son and he would hold the office of Mutwalli till the presumption of legitimacy in his favour is rebutted in a properly constituted suit, in that judgment this Court observed:</u>

<u>"The Muhammadan law does not recognize legitimation, and acknowledgement cannot create or confirm the status of a legitimate son in favour of or upon a person, who as a matter of fact, is not or is disproved to be the legitimate son of the acknowledger. But in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, an acknowledgement raises a presumption, the rebuttal of which is the burden of the person who disputes it, and such a presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be the legitimate son of the acknowledger. The principle which seems to be well established is that an acknowledgement has the effect of raising presumption of legitimacy excepting where illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt by reason of the marriage of its parents being either disproved or found to be unlawful. Having regard to this principle the High Court came to the conclusion that prima facie, in view of the earlier acknowledgement by Amir Ali, respondent (Khorshed Alam) should be accepted as the legitimate eldest son of Amir Ali until the contrary is proved in a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. The respondent should be treated as the eldest son and as such entitle to succeed, in terms of the Waqf deed, to the office of Mutwalli, until it is established in a properly framed suit that in spite of such acknowledgement there had been in fact no marriage between the mother of the respondent and the deceased Mutwalli."</u>

33. This judgment was announced on 1 July 1977 and within a short time respondent, Amir Sultan Ali, filed the suit-OC suit No. 457 of 1977 seeking declarations that defendant (Khorshed Alam) is the son of unknown parentage and not the legitimate son of late Amir Ali and that the (plaintiff) is the eldest son of Amir Ali, and he being pious and of good character as such being eligible for the office of Mutwalli, is the fit person to be appointed the Mutwalli.

34. Case of plaintiff is that he is the eldest son of Amir Ali through his third wife Meher Shamsunnahar and that the defendant is not the son of Amir Ali but is his foster son only. The plaintiff alleged that his father Amir Ali, who was a Member of the Bengal Legislative Assembly for about 10 years, had only three wives, Sakhina Khatun of Patna, Zohura Khatun, a tribal lady brought from Darjeeling and converted to Islam and Meher Shamsunnahar of Bogra, and that Amir Ali had no other wife than these three ladies. Sakhina Khatun, the first wife, had 8 children all of whom died in their infancy and she died some time in 1940. Amir Ali had a fruit business at Natore and in connection with that business he had gone to Darjeeling and from there he brought a tribal lady who embraced Islam, took the name 'Zohora Khatun' and was married to Amir Ali. She was barren and childless and decided to foster a son to look after her in old age. One Baramoni, a professional dancer-cum-prostitute of Nature had an infant son aged about 11/2 years; from her Zohora Khatun took this infant and reared him with the consent of Amir Ali who also extended to the child his love, affection and care. It is this boy who is the defendant, Khorshed Alam; he was given education by Amir Ali as he were his own son-Subsequently, at the time of Khorshed Alam's marriage when his status and position in society were questioned, Amir Ali executed an Ekramama in favour of one Hafizuddin, father of Nazlee Begum, Khorshed Alam's bride, admitting him as "his eldest son" and promised to make a gift of one of his houses in favour of Khorshed Alam, Zohora Khatun and Nazlee Begum. In the same document, Amir Ali made it clear that his son, (the plaintiff) through his third wife, Shamsun Nahar, would succeed him in the office of 'Mutwalli' in terms of the Waqf deed which provides that the Mutwalli's eldest son would be the next Mutwalli" Amir Ali at a later stage recalled the "acknowledgement" and described the defendant in different documents as his "foster son". About a year before his death, Amir Ali made an application to the Commissioner of Waqf stating that the plaintiff being his 'eldest son' would be the next Mutwalli after him, and explained that the defendant was not his real son but was a foster son not eligible for this office.

<u>35. Defendant (Khorshed Alam) contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the allegation that he was the foster son of Amir Ali and his wife Zohora Khatun and claimed that he is Amir Ali's real as well as the eldest son. He contended that Amir Ali had four wives, the second of whom was one Monowara Begum of Park Circus, Calcutta and was married to Amir Ali in 1929 and from this wedlock he was born in 1933 and those two years thereafter his mother Monowara Begum died. The plaintiff born of Meher Shamsunnahar, the 4th wife of Amir Ali, according to him, is not the eldest son of his father. Defendant further contended that Amir Ali acknowledged him as his son during his life time in a number of documents and also told many persons, on different occasions that he was his eldest son. He contends further that Amir Ali, at the fag end of his life, became physically and mentally weak and fell under the influence of his wife Shamsunnahar and that at her direction, Amir Ali repudiated the acknowledgements and filed an application to the Waqf Commissioner requesting him to accept the plaintiff as his eldest son for the office of the Mutwalli. This subsequent repudiation of the acknowledgement, he contended, got no legal effect upon the acknowledgement of legitimacy through his father's life.</u>

<u>36. On these pleadings the trial Court approached the case with the following observation:</u>

<u>"This acknowledgement raises a presumption that defendant Khorshed Alam is the legitimate son of late Amir Ali Mia and this presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be legitimate son of the burden is on the person who disputes, i.e. here in this case this onus lies on the plaintiff. Now let us see how far the plaintiff has been able to discharge the onus on him."</u>

<u>Plaintiff-examined 16 witnesses including himself and produced a number of documents. He deposed that the defendant was not and could not have been a son, far less a legitimate son, of his father Amir All in that his father had only three wives, Sakhina Khatun, Zohora Khatun Meher Shamsunnahar, but the defendant was not admittedly born of any of their wives. He contended that the defendant was fostered and reared up as a son by Zohora Khatun who was admittedly barren and that Zohora Khatun had taken him from his mother Baramoni of Natore when he was about 1-1/2 years old. Defendant, on the other hand, examined 10 witnesses including himself to prove that he was not a foster son of Zohora Khatun but he was born of Monowara Begum, one of the wives of Amir Ali, and that Amir Ali had in fact four wives. Besides oral evidence he produced a great number of documents all of which except one relate to the acknowledgment of Amir Ali which has already been accepted by the trial Court as prima-facie evidence in favour of the defendant's legitimacy. On consideration of the evidence, oral and documentary, adduced by both the parties, the trial Court came to a clear finding that Amir Ali had only three wives, Sakhina Khatun, Zohora Khatun and Meher Shamsunnahar, that he had no wife named Monowara Begum nor any Monowara Begum was ever in existence, but that Monowara Begum, as claimed to be his mother for the first time in his Written Statement, is a fictitious person, and that he not being the offspring of Amir Ali through any of his wives is not a legitimate son of Amir Ali and, on this finding, decreed the suit. On appeal, the learned Additional District Judge also arrived at his independent finding that Amir Ali had only three wives, that he had no wife named Monowara Begum whose very existence was not established, that 'Monowara Begum' was invented as a wife of Amir Ali for the first time in the written statement of the defendant and that he, not having been born of any of the married wives of Amir Ali is not a legitimate son of Amir Ali. On this finding, the learned Additional District Judge dismissed the appeal and maintained the decree of the Trial Court.</u>

<u>37. This decree, based as it is, on concurrent finding of the two Courts below was challenged by a Revisional application being Civil Revision No. 263 of 1981. Before the learned Single Judge who heard the matter only two grounds were urged by the appellant namely, (i) the courts below treated certain documents, such as Exhibits 5 (a) and 6, which are his depositions in a previous case, as substantive evidence in this case and that theses courts did not consider all the evidence particularly documentary evidence produced by the defendant and, as such, the concurrent finding was not sustainable in law. The learned Single Judge referred to the evidence on record and found no substance in either of the grounds nor did he find any illegality or material irregularity which called for interference in revision with the finding of facts, pure and simple. I have considered Exhibits 5 (a) and 6 to see if they were used as substantive evidence in the suit. These documents are depositions of the defendant (DW 1) in two previous suits-MS No.5 of 1966 and OC Suit No. 381 of 1966 filed against him by late Amir Ali respectively for recovery of rent and ejectment. In these suits Amir Ali had shown him as his 'foster son'. Defendant in his depositions stated, among other things, that he did not know name and whereabouts of his mother or whether she was dead or alive. But in this suit when he claimed that Monowara Begum was his mother and that she hailed from Calcutta, be was confronted with his depositions, Exhibits. 5 and 6. That right the opponent got under section 145 of the Evidence Act. To test the veracity of his testimony, particularly when he for the first time, set up the claim that Monowara Begum was his mother. These depositions were not used as any substantive evidence in this suit. As to the second ground, I have examined his documents were considered by the courts below.</u>

<u>38. In this appeal by special leave the appellant did not take the grounds that he had taken before the High Court Division, but raised again the question of legitimacy by the acknowledgment which was already accepted as a prima facie proof of his claim to son-ship by the courts below in pursuance of this Court's previous decision. The sole duty of these courts was therefore to see if the prima facie proof was nullified and rebutted by contrary facts Leave granted was to see whether the appellants "claim to son-ship of Amir Ali is established by the acknowledgment of Amir Ali claiming the former to be his son. The point for consideration is whether the learned Judge of the High Court has correctly decided the principle of acknowledgement under Muslim Law". This question is superfluous, for in the previous decision of this Court the principle of acknowledgement under Muhammadan Law was explained, presumption of legitimacy by acknowledgement was taken in favour of the appellant and it was the respondent on whom the onus was laid to rebut the presumption by contrary proof. The question thus raised in the suit was whether the defendant was born of any valid marriage between Amir Ali and any woman claimed by him to be his mother. This was purely a question of fact which fell for determination by the Courts below. These Courts were not called upon to re-state the principle of law as to acknowledgement and its effect. The appellant, it appears, has raised the question of acknowledgement against to create a smoke screen in an attempt to escape from the adverse finding of facts, which he otherwise could not challenge.</u>

<u>39. The law applicable to the question is well settled, as already indicated by this Court in the judgment in Civil Appeal No. 27 of 1975. It is that when the paternity of a person is uncertain and another person acknowledges him as his son, then this acknowledgement is a substantive evidence of the fact that the person acknowledged is his legitimate son; such acknowledgement raises a presumption that the person acknowledged is born of a valid union between the acknowledger and the mother of the person acknowledged. But being a presumption of fact and not of juris at jure, it is like every other presumption of fact capable of being set-aside by contrary proof. Onus of such a proof is upon the person who challenges the acknowledgement. His onus may be discharged by bringing evidence that the person acknowledged is not the legitimate son of the acknowledger became he was not the offspring of any valid marriage between the acknowledger and mother of the acknowledged or because it is impossible for the acknowledger to beget the acknowledge or the marriage between him and the mother of the acknowledged is prohibited by law. In elaborating this principle it is found that to become a legitimate son on the strength of an acknowledgement the following ingredients are necessary, namely the acknowledge was born of the loin of the acknowledger, that is, the former is the descent from the latter; the age difference between them is such that the acknowledger must have attained puberty at the time he allegedly begot the son; the mother of the acknowledge was legally married wife of the acknowledger at the relevant time; the marriage between these two is not prohibited by law, that is, the wife is not within the prohibited decree in relationship. Any offspring other than from such valid union is illegitimate being the offspring of zina that is, adultery, incest or fornication. In a nutshell, a valid marriage between the parents is the essential precondition for legitimacy. If such marriage is disproved. Acknowledges case falls straightaway, and no amount of acknowledgement shall make the acknowledge a legitimate son.</u>

<u>40. In Md Allahdat Khan vs Md. Ismail Khan, 10 All 289 Straight, J elaborating "acknowledgement" observed:</u>

<u>"The rules of Muhammadan Law relating to acknowledgement by a Muhammadan of another as his son are rules of the substantive law of inheritance. Such an acknowledgement, unless certain impediments exist, confers upon the person acknowledged the status of a legitimate son capable of inheriting. Where there is no proof of legitimate birth or of illegitimate birth, and the paternity of a child is unknown, in the sense that no specific person is shown to be the father, then the acknowledgement of him by another who claims him as him son affords a conclusive presumption that he is the legitimate child of the acknowledger, and places him in that category"</u>

<u>Mahmood J, in the same case, observed:</u>

<u>"So far as inheritance through marriage is concerned, the existence of consanguinity and legitimate descent is an indispensable condition precedent to the right of succession, and such legitimate descent depends upon the existence of a valid marriage between the parents. Where legitimacy cannot be established by a direct proof of such marriage, acknowledgement is recognized as a means whereby marriage of the parents of legitimate descent may be established as a matter of substantive law, Such acknowledgement would proceed upon the hypothesis of a lawful union between the parents ... a child whose illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt by reason of the marriage of his parents being either disproved of found to be unlawful cannot be legitimized by acknowledgement."</u>

<u>Facts of the case related to a dispute between the appellant Allahdat Khan and his step-brother Ismail Khan over inheritance from their father Golam Ghous Khan. Ismail Khan was admittedly a son of Golam Ghous Khan through his first wife, and Allahdat Khan claimed that he was a son of Golam Ghous Khan through his another wife named Moti Begum. It was contended by Ismail Khan that Moti Begum was married to Golam Ghous Khan long after the birth of Allahdat Khan and, as such, the latter was born, as an illegitimate son of his father, Form the evidence adduced the date of Moti Begum marriage could not be ascertained with certainty. But Golam Ghous Khan had acknowledged Allahdat Khan as his son during his lifetime. In these circumstances it was held that presumption as to legitimacy by acknowledgement remained unrebutted and consequently Allahdat was held to be a legitimate son of Golam Ghous Khan.</u>

<u>41. In Sadek Hossain Khan vs Hashim Ali Khan, AIR 1916 PC 27=43 1A the legitimacy of one Sultan Mirza came up for consideration. He claimed to be a son of Zohora Kainam, whom, he claimed, the Nowab had married in Mota form, Zohora Kainam was an Abyssinian slave girl and was brought home by the Nawab's father from Mecca. But the sons of the Nowab through his admitted wives averred that Zohora Kainam was not legally married to their father, and, as such, Sultan Mirza was not a legitimate son as claimed. It was found from evidence that the Nawab, during his lifetime, treated Sultan Mirza as his son in the marmer, which suggested his acknowledgement of Sultan Mirza as a legitimate son. But it was found that there was no lawful marriage between the Nawab and Zohora Kainam but that she was a mere mistress of the Nawab, and, as such, Sultan Mirza was not his legitimate son. In these circumstances it was observed by their Lordship of the Privy Council:</u>

<u>"No statement made by one that another (Proved to be illegitimate) is his son can make that other legitimate, but where no proof of that kind has been given, such a statement or acknowledgement is substantive evidence that the person so acknowledged is the legitimate son of the person who makes the statement, provided his legitimacy be possible."</u>

<u>42. In Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs Altaf Ali Chowdhury, AIR 1922 PC 159, their Lordships considered a similar question as to legitimacy viz-a-viz legitimation under the Muhammadan Law and observed that "legitimacy" is a status which results from certain facts, whereas "legitimation" is a procedure which creates a status which did not exist before and that under Muhammadan Law there is no legitimation because. Under Muhammadan Law, "a person to be legitimate son of another person must be the offspring of a marriage between his mother and his alleged father and that any other offspring is the off-spring of zina, that is, illicit connection and cannot be legitimate." In that case the appellant claimed to be a legitimate son of Abdus Sobhan, Nawab of Bogra, stating that he was born of Mozelle Cohen, a Jewish lady, who he claimed was a legally married wife of the Nawab. Nawab's grandson through the daughter of his first wife and others disputed the claim contending that Mozelle Cohen was never married to the Nawab. It was found from evidence that the Nawab lived and cohabited with her for a long time but she was never married to him, and that she was Nawab's concubine only. It was held that though the Nawab had acknowledged the appellant as his son during his lifetime no marriage between those parents having been provided, the appellant was not a legitimate son of the Nawab.</u>

<u>42A. The crux of the instant case is whether the appellant was born of any legally married wife of Amir Ali and if the answer is in the negative his claim to sonship shall fail straight-away and the acknowledgement of Amir Ali will be of no avail and the presumption as to legitimacy raised by the acknowledgement shall stand rebutted. It is only to rebut this presumption that the suit has been brought, and weather the appellant is the offspring of any lawful union between Amir Ali and Monowara Begum whom the appellant claims to be his mother is purely a question of fact. By a concurrent finding the trial Court and the lover Appellate Court held that there was no woman like Monowara Begum but she was invented for the purpose of the suit and that Amir Ali had no wife named Monowara Begum, Now it is to be seen whether a Court exercising Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 CPC can interfere with this finding. A finding of fact is immune from revision unless is shown that the finding is based on gross misreading of evidence or on nor-consideration of material evidence or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or on misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to evidence on record. To see whether this finding suffers from any such weakness. I would go straight to the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by both the parties.</u>

<u>43. Oral evidence led by the plaintiff aimed at substantiating his averments that Amir Ali had only three wives and had no wife named Monowara Begum, that the defendant was the foster son of Zohora Khatun and Amir Ali and that the defendant had been taken for that purpose from his mother-Baramoni of Natore when he was a child of 1 1/2 years old. Defendant's oral-evidence was directed towards falsifying these averments and to establish his claim that Amir Ali had another wife, besides the admitted three, of whom he was born. Plaintiff's claim was supported, in respect of the first two points, by PWs 3, 4, 11, 12, 14, 15, and 16 and in respect of the third point by PWs. 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. Of these witnesses PW 16 is the Plaintiff's mother Meher Shamsunnahar and as such is interested in his case, but the remaining witnesses are found to be respondent and disinterested persons having no grudge or enmity with the defendant whatsoever. Of them PW 4, aged about 79 years, is a retired Secretary of Rajshahi District Board, claiming to be acquainted with Amir Ali, having occasionally visited Amir Ali's house. PW 4 (76) is a retired teacher of a Government High Madrassa and Amir Ali's neighbor having personal knowledge about Amir Ali's family and his wives, PW 10 (80) was the Secretary of Saheb Bazar Mosque in Rajshahi town and thereafter, its Imam and was a friend of Amir Ali, and PW 11 (70) is a retired Sub-Inspector of Police who was Officer-in-Charge of Rampur Boalia Police Station in 1952/53 and had personal knowledge about Amir Ali's family, PW 12 was a Car assistant of Amir Ali having personal knowledge about Amir Ali's family; PW 14 (70) was Amir Ali's neighbor having personal knowledge about his family, PW 15 was a clerk of Amir Ali from 1941-46 and had personal knowledge about Amir Ali's family and his wives. On the other hand PW 1 is defendant Khorshed Alam himself; his claim was supported by DWs 4, 5 and 7. Of them DW 5 did not depose from his personal knowledge, but he, as Ward Chairman, held an enquiry in course of which he met Baramoni of Natore who told him that the defendant was not her son. He however admitted during cross-examination that he had held the enquiry without serving any notice upon the parties and that he secretly met Baramoni who then told him that the defendant was not her son. This part of his evidence is inadmissible being hearsay, DW 4 said that when he was a student he had seen Monowara Begum, mother of the defendant and called her Chachi-Amma; DW 7 an Advocate, stated that he had heard from the late Amir Ali that the defendant was his eldest son. DW 8 a Junior Advocate, was examined to prove an affidavit, Exhibit H (2) sworn by one Dr RU Khan, a retired Food Controller in that affidavit the deponent stated before another advocate (to whom DW 8 was a junior) that in 929 or so he had attended Amir Ali's marriage with Monowara Begum. But the affidavit was sworn on 6-2-68 when the dispute already started; the deponent not being examined in support of the affidavit it got no evidentiary value as it has been challenged.</u>

<u>44. Having considered these two sets of evidence the Courts below disbelieved the evidence of the DWs. Particularly DW 1 the defendant, and came to the finding that Amir Ali had no wife named Monowara Begum, that she defendant was foster son of Zohora Khatun and Amir Ali and that the defendant was son of Baramoni of Natore. I find that rejection of the evidence of DW 1 is not arbitrary, but is founded on cogent reasons and proper appreciation of the evidence according to rules of evidence. DW 1 made inconsistent statements vis-a-vis his depositions in the two previous suits in 1966 regarding his mother's existence, name. Whereabouts, as well as addresses and whereabouts of any relations of his mother, etc. it 1966 he even could not give the name of his mother or say whether she was alive or dead; but in this suit filed in 1977, he claimed that Monowara Begum of Calcutta was his mother and that she was a married wife of Amir Ali. He contradicted himself in respect of his own place of birth, saying that he was born in Calcutta whereas in the Money Suit he stated that he was born in Amir Manzil, Rajshahi. He also contradicted himself about the place of his mother's death saying in one of the previous suits that his mother had died in Rajshahi Town, but now saying that she had died in Calcutta. He could not produce his birth-register or his mother's death register or any Kabinnama of his mother's marriage or any relation of her mother. The courts below particularly considered the fact that though he went to Calcutta on many occasions, he never visited the house of his maternal grandfather, nor did he ever try to ascertain who was his maternal grand-father or where did he live or what was he and no member of Amir Ali's family or his relations came forward to say that Amir Ali ever got a wife named Monowara Begum.</u>

<u>45. As against the oral evidence as discussed, I shall look into the documents filed by the parties, these documents relate to the acknowledgement of Amir Ali as well as its annulments. The courts below, as already pointed out, proceeded on the assumption that the defendant got in his favour a good acknowledgement of Amir Ali and cast the onus to nullify the acknowledgement upon the plaintiff. Contention of the plaintiff is that the documents apparently evidencing 'acknowledgement' are in fact not any documents of acknowledgement but were intended to give the defendant a status in life and society and to avoid embarrassment. Exhibit C is a copy of deposition of Amir Ali in a criminal case between other parties in 1933. There Amir Ali stated in cross-examination that the boy Khorshed Alam aged about two years was his son. This statement Amir Ali made when he denied that he had brought a woman from Darjeeling, meaning his wife Zohora Khatun who was admittedly brought from Darjeeling. The next documents as to acknowledgement are Exhibit D, a Kabinnama dated 23-3-51 and Exhibit D (1), another Kabinnama dated 13-3- 53. These two Kabinnama relate to the first and the second marriage of the defendant and in those kabinnamas Amir Ali appeared as a wit- ness stating that 'Khorshed Alarn was his son.' The most important document regarding the acknowledgement is Exhibit G, an "Ekrarnama" executed by Amir Ali on 19 March, 1953 in favour of one Hafizuddin whose daughter Nazle Begum was married to Khorshed Alarn under the Kabinnama Exhibit D (1). There Amir Ali stated that Khorshed Alam was "his eldest son" and promised that he would execute a Heba-deed in favour of Zohora Khatun, Khorshed Alam and Nazle Begum each of them 1/3 rd share of his three-storied building known as 'Amir Manzil". In the same Ekrarnama Amir Ali made it clear that his son through Meher Shamsunnahar would be the next Mutwalli on his death. This document is sought to be interpreted by both the parties to get support to their rival claims-the defendant saying that it was a clear admission of father-hood and the plaintiff saying that if the defendant were really Amir Ali's eldest son, he would have become the next Mutwalli in terms of the Waqf deed, Exhibit 11, which reserved the Mutwalliship for Amir Ali's eldest son, Exhibit E series are rent-receipts in respect of a hotel housed in a part of the Waqf property; in these rent-receipts the defendant was shown as Amir Ali's son. There are the documents, which contain Amir Ali's statements admitting the defendant as his son. The other documents are papers like income-tax receipts, nomination papers, private letters, etc. in which the defendant was referred to as Amir Ali's son, but these papers did not contain any statement of Amir Ali; nevertheless, these documents relating to different matters and transactions spread over a considerably long period of time upto the year 1964. Considering all these documents a reasonable conclusion can be drawn that Amir Ali had acknowledged the defendant as his son, sometimes as his eldest son, from 1933 to 1964.</u>

46. Thereafter, from 1965 till his death in 1967, Amir Ali made statements denying that the defendant was his son but contending that he was his foster son. The plaintiff produced documents containing those statements. Exhibit 3 is a certified copy of the plain of Money Suit No. 33 of 1965, renumbered as MS No. 5 of 1966, which was filed by Amir Ali against the defendant claiming arrears of rent in respect of a part of the Waqf Estate In that plaintiff the defendant was shown as his foster son. Exhibit 7 is the plaintiff of another suit-OC Suit No. 381 of 1966, filed by Amir Ali for ejecting the defendant stating that the defendant's parentage was unknown, Exhibit 5 is Amir Ali's deposition in MS No. 5 of 1966 where he said that the defendant was his foster-son. Exhibit 1 is a petition dated 14-3-66 of Amir Ali addressed to the Commissioner of Waqf in which he stated that the defendant (Khorshed Alam) was not his son but was his foster son, that the plaintiff Amir Sultan Ali was his eldest son and eligible for appointment of Mutwalli in terms of the Waqf deed. Exhibit 1 (a) is an affidavit sworn Amir Ali on 6-3-67 in respect of his petition Exhibit 1 in which he reiterated that Khorshed Alam was not his son but was his foster son. About one month thereafter Amir Ali died and thus the struggle for succession to Mutwalliship began. It was argued in the Courts below that the question of legitimacy was raised and the acknowledgement was annulled at the instance of plaintiff's mother before Amir Ali's death. Evidence however shows that this question was raised as far back as 1933 when the defendant was a child of two years that is seven-years before the marriage of plaintiff's mother. As to acknowledgement, subsequent annulment got no legal effect. But the plaintiff has not built up his case on the annulment; he has built up his case on positive evidence of competent witnesses that the defendant was not born of any of Amir Ali's wives. The trial Court and the lower Appellate Court on consideration of the evidence found that the presumption of sonship raised by the acknowledgement has been rebutted by the unimpeachable oral evidence that the defendant was not born of any wife of Amir Ali. This finding of fact is based on impregnable mass of good evidence and appreciation of this evidence being correct and proper the finding is as strong as granite pillar, which is too strong to be dented by the fragile weapon of revisional jurisdiction. Interference with this finding in revision will be disobedience to the direction of law.

<u>47. In this appeal the appellant challenged the finding that he was born of Baramoni of Natore taking the ground that Baramoni, though alive, was not examined by the plaintiff. PWs 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 gave testimony from their personal knowledge that the defendant was son of Baramoni from whom he was taken by Zohora Khatun. Linking Zohora Khatun with the defendant in the Ekrar Exhibit G provides support to the claim that she had fostered him. Of these witnesses PW 5 was a Pankha Puller of Natore Rajbari, for about 22 years; he said that sometime in 1933 he saw Baramoni frequently visiting the Rajbari carrying a little boy and that on the advice of the Raja who was a friend of Amir Ali the latter took that child, aged about 1/2 years, to be fostered by his second wife Zohora Khatun. PW 5 was an Assistant of Amir Ali in his fruit shop at Natore. He claimed to have known Baramoni personally, and deposed that the defendant was Baromoni's son. These witnesses being dis-interested their evidence was accepted by the Courts below as reliable. As to Baromoni's non-examination in this case, the plaintiff got cogent reasons not to call her as a witness, since she was not expected to give evidence which would certainly affect her own son's interest, besides ranking the past. Disclosure of the real fact by her would at once disentitle the defendant to claim inheritance from late Amir Ali. This recalls the case of the two women putting up claim to sonship of an infant before king Solomon. When the King decided that the infant would be cut and divided into two pieces-one for each of the claimants, the real mother abandoned her claim in order to save the life of her son. Even if it is taken that Baramoni was not the defendant's mother. Still the plaintiff's case would not suffer and the defendant's case would not improve in any way. For, plaintiff's failure to prove that the defendant was Baromoni's son will not mean that the defendant was born of Monowara Begum and that Monowara Begum was a married wife of Amir Ali. That claim of the defendant has been disproved by strong evidence. "Legitimacy from marriage follows the bed" as has been observed by the Privy Council in Ashraf-ud-Daula vs Hyder Husain, 11 M. IA 94, "Bed" means relationship of husband and wife by a valid marriage under Muhammadan Law. Such relationship between Amir All and alleged Monowara Begum has been disproved in view of the fact that she was held to be a fictitious person. In the case of Azmat Khan v Lalli Begum, 9 IA 8 and also in the case of Allahdat Khan, as referred to above, the claim of legitimacy by acknowledgement was accepted by the Court when the marriage concerned was 'neither proved nor disproved". But this is not the case here. Facts of those two cases as well as of the case of Habibur Rahman Chowdhury and Sadeq Hossain, already referred to above, are altogether different from that of the instant cases. In none of these cases, maternity of the person acknowledged was questioned: in each such case the mother was a definite woman, but her marriage with the acknowledger was in dispute. In the instant case, the defendant's claim of being born of Monowara Begum was disputed, and now disproved, and consequently the acknowledgement of Amir Ali is useless. It must be borne in mind that 'acknowledgement' in Muhammadan Law is no substitute for 'adoption' in Hindu Law or Roman Law. Under Muhammadan Law relationship by consanguinity is a pre-requisite for legitimacy and the latter is dependent upon a valid marriage of the parents. If Amir Ali had acknowledged the defendant as his son, then he knew better who was the defendant's mother-but that woman not being any of his three wives the defendant is not his legitimate son. That ends the whole matter. The learned Single Judge is found to have rightly refused interference with the finding of the courts below, which stands on a solid rock.</u>

48. In the result, the appeal is dismissed. I do not make any order as to costs.

Chowdhury ATM Masud J : I have gone through the judgments written by Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Shahabuddin Ahmed JJ. I concur with the decision of Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.

ORDER OF THE COURT

By the majority opinion the appeal is allowed and all the Judgments and Orders of the court below are hereby set-aside and the suit is dismissed. No. costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: This appeal by the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 5 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.1.1982 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Manikganj in Title Suit No. 37 of 1981 decreeing the suit for declaration of title in the suit land. The respondent Nos. 1-3 as plaintiffs filed the said Title Suit against the appellants and some others for declaration of their title in suit land measuring 1.26 acres described in the schedule to the plaint.

2. The case of the plaintiffs, inter alia. is that the suit land originally belonged to Gour Chandra Biswas and others and by several sale deeds dated 3.4.58, 24.10.73, 24.10.73, 14,11.57, 2.7.73, 14.11.73, 7.2.74 proforma defendant No.7 Sree Pran Nath MondaI and his wife proforma defendant No. 8 Sreemati Rashmoni Dashya purchased the same and possessed the same by mutating their names in the RS Khatian and record of right and they were in peaceful possession therein of for more than 12 years. Thereafter, the said proforma defendants Nos. 7 and 8 entered into an agreement to sell the said land at a consideration of Tk. 24,000.00 to the plaintiffs on 28.1.76 corresponding to 14th Magh, 1383 BS and on receipt of Tk. 19,500.00 executed a written contract in favour of the plaintiffs and transferred possession of the said land in their favour agreeing to execute and register the sale deed on or before 1st May, 1978 on receipt of the balance amount of the consideration. Their further case is that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of all concerned including the defendants by living in the two little huts in the suit land and growing crops by cultivating other land. Thereafter on 25.4.78 the said defendant Nos. 7 and 8 executed and registered three separate sale deeds in favour of the plaintiffs on receipt of the balance consideration from the plaintiffs; that on 24.6.78 the defendant Nos. 1-6 tried to take forcible possession of the suit land but with the help of local Matbars the plaintiffs managed to remove them from the suit land. The defendants claimed to have agreement of purchase from the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 but they could not produce anything in support of their claim. Further case of the plaintiffs is that after the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 left Bangladesh for India the defendant Nos. 1-6 might have created some forged signatures upon some white papers to claim the suit property and if any such papers or documents appear to be created by or in the name of the proforma defendant Nos. 7 and 8 that will have no legal force in the eye of law as because they had already transferred their right to the suit land by registered deeds in favour of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs mutated their names in the Khatian. Upon these allegations the plaintiffs prayed for declaration of title in the suit land.

3. Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 5 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations. Their case is that the suit land originally belonged to defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and they sold the same to defendant Nos. 1-2 at a consideration of Tk. 53,000.00 by executing and registering two sale deeds, one on 15.12.76 and other on 27.1.78. After sale of the suit land to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 the proforma defendant Nos. 7 and 8 had no subsisting interest to sell the same to the plaintiffs. The alleged bainapatra and sale deeds in favour of the plaintiffs is nothing but forged, ante-dated, without consideration and on the basis of the same the plaintiffs have not acquired any right, title and interest in the suit property. The plaintiffs in collusion with others in the last part of March, 1979 forcibly trespassed upon 7/8 decimals of the suit land and removed two huts of the defendants and constructed two ghars thereon and residing therein and the remaining suit land is in possession of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Defendant No. 5 is the care-taker of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 who live outside the village in connection with the service, etc. and defendant No. 5 is residing in the residential house on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 as borgadars of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have been possessing the same. Defendant Nos. 6 has no personal interest in the suit land. There is no question of these defendants forcibly entering into the suit land as they are in possession. The kabalas in favour of the defendant No. 1 and 2 are valid, legal and for consideration and they have right, title and possession in the suit land. The false suit of the plaintiffs is liable to be dismissed.

4. Upon the said allegations the following issues were framed:

"1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form ?

2. Is the suit bad for defect of parties ?

3. Is the suit barred by limitation as alleged ?

4. It the suit barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act?

5. Have defendant Nos. 1 and 2 acquired any right, title and interest upon the suit land on the basis of their alleged deeds?

6. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get decree for declaration as prayed for?

7. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiffs, entitled?

5. The plaintiffs examined plaintiff No. 1 Wazed Ali Fakir as PW 1, Abdul Aziz, an attesting witness of the Bainapatra as PW 2 and plaintiff No. 1's brother Khaimuddin Fakir as PW 3 in support of their case. The plaintiffs also filed and proved Bia-deeds of their vendors, Exts. 1-1 (h) and three sale deeds in their favour Exts. 1(i) to (k), copy of RS Khatian No. 555 in the name of Pran Nath Mondal, Gaya Nath Mondal and another in respect of 0.88 acre of land of Mouza Bhakum marked Ext.2, true copy of the Mutation Khatian No. 117/1 of Mouza Bhakum in respect of 1.27 acres of land mutating the names of plaintiffs as Ext. 2(a); Duplicate Carbon Receipt dated 24.7.78 as Ext. 3, two rent receipts dated 10.12.79 and 24.7.72 as Exts. 4 and 4(a) respectively; one certificate of the local Chairman as Ext. 5 and Bainapatra dated 28.1.76 executed by defendant Nos. 7 and 8 as Ext. 6.

6. The defendants in support of their case examined defendant No. 1 as DW 1, one Hossain Miah as DW 2, defendant No. 4 Elem Biswas DW 3, defendant No. 5 Habibur Rahman Khan as DW 4 and another Badsha Fakir as DW 5. They also produced and proved in evidence sale deed dated 15.2.76 executed and registered by defendant Nos. 7 and 8 in favour of defendant No. 2 Asia Khatun marked Ext. A and sale deed dated 27.1.78 executed by defendant No. 7 in favour of defendant No. 1 Abdus Samad Khan, defendant No.2 Asia Khatun as Ext. A(1) and map of Mouza Bhakum marked as Ext. B.

7. Mr. Gaur Gopal Saha, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, placed before us the plaint written statements, evidence on record as well as the impugned judgment.

8. He submits that admittedly the kabalas of the defendants dated 15.12.76 and 27.1.78 are prior to the kabalas of the plaintiffs dated 25.4.78 and as such the common vendors of both the parties, proforma defendant Nos. 7 and 8 had no subsisting interest in the suit lands at the time of transferring the same to the plaintiffs by three kabalas Exts. l(i) to 1 (ka) on 25.4.78. He also submits that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 had title in 3 decimals of lands in suit plot No. 747 and the same was inserted in the plaintiffs kabalas only to enable them to register the said sale deeds at Savar far away from the suit land having no jurisdiction to register the deeds in respect of the remaining lands and as such registration of plaintiffs kabalas at Savar instead of at Singair was void. Therefore, the claim of plaintiffs title to the suit land having not been established the court below was wholly wrong in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.

9. Mr. Abul Quasem, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, submits that the plaintiffs entered into the agreement on 28.1.76 vide Ext. 6 with the vendors proforma defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and in part performance of that agreement they arc in possession of the suit land from the date of the said agreement and in pursuance of that agreement the plaintiffs purchased the suit land by three registered sale deeds on 25.4.78 and admittedly they arc in possession in part of the land by living in the two huts and as such the kabalas of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 arc nothing but fraudulent ones and cannot stand in the way of declaration of plaintiffs title in the suit land. He further submits that insertion of 3 decimals of lands in plaintiffs sale deed from Savar area will not affect registration of the said sale deeds though the plaintiffs could not produce any document in, support of the title of the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 therein since the contesting defendants admitted their title therein in their written statement and did not raise the same in the court below.

The learned Court below in the impugned judgment while deciding the issue Nos. 5 and 6 held that the plaintiffs have been able to prove the Bainapatra Ext. 6 and they are in possession of the suit land from the date of Bainapatra on 28.1.76 and they continued in possession in pursuance of the same till execution and registration of the sale deed on 25.4.78 and as such the plaintiffs acquired possessory right in the suit land from 28.1.76. He further held that the total area of the suit plot No. 636 is 22 decimals and there is no clash between the plaintiffs' claim of 18 decimals of the suit land and the remaining "areas of 4 decimals of land of defendant No.2 of that plot on the basis of Ext A dated 15.12.76. He further held that Ext A(I) dated 27.1.78 was only executed by defendant No.7 as such the title of the defendant No. 8 in the suit property could vest with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on the basis of the said document. He also held that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were aware of the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land and obtained the kabala dated 27.1.78 Ext. A (1) and included the suit plots therein. He therefore, concluded that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 obtained the said sale deed from defendant No. 7 without consideration and he is not bonafide purchaser for value and the same did not affect right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in the suit land.

10. "The title of defendant Nos. 7 and 8 in the suit land is admitted but the extent of their title has neither been explained in the pleadings nor in the evidence. It appears on consideration Ext: 1 (b) and 1 (g) the only deeds in favour of proforma defendant No.8 that she acquired only .6 decimals of land in suit plot No. 636. Learned Advocate of both the parties do not dispute that the proforma defendant No.8 had interest only in 6 decimals of land of plot. No. 636 arid she had no interest in other suit plots.

11. It is admitted that the total area of the suit plot No. 636 is 22 decimals. Admittedly entire land of plot No. 636 belonged to both the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and as such after deduction 6 decimals lands of defendant No. 8 remaining 16 decimal of that plot along with the remaining lands of other suit plots belonged to defendant No.7. By kabala dated 15.12.76 Ext. A both the respondents No. 7 and 8 sold 4 decimals of lands of suit plot No. 636 along with other lands to the defendant No. 2. Since there is nothing in the said deed as to the extent of the share of the vendors to be transferred under the said deed as per the provisions of section 47 of the Transfer of Property Act the vendors' share in the land sold will be proportionate to the extent of their share in the suit plot Since the defendant No.8 was the owner of 6 decimals of land of plot No. 636 under the said kabala about 1 decimal of land from her share from the suit plot No. 636 was transferred to defendant No.2 and she was left with 5 decimal of land in that plot after her sale to defendant No. 2.

<u>12. Admittedly both the kabalas of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are prior to the kabalas of the plaintiffs. Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act is as follows:</u>

<u>"48. Where a person purports to create by transfer at different times right in or over the same immovable property, and such rights cannot all exist or be exercised to their full extent together, each later created right shall, in the absence of a special contract or reservation binding the earlier transferees, be subject to the rights previously created".</u>

<u>From the above provisions of the Transfer of Property Act it is clear that the earlier kabalas will taka precedence over the subsequent kabalas. Therefore, the plaintiffs have not acquired any right title and interest in the suit and on the basis of their subsequent sale deeds in respect of the properties already sold to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by the same vendors. We have already noticed that sale deed dated 27.1.78 was executed and registered by defendant No. 7 alone in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and by that deed title of defendant No. 8 in 5 decimals of land in suit plot No. 636 was not transferred to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2.</u>

<u>13. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondents vehemently argued that the plaintiffs had been in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of the defendants in part performance of the agreement for sale since 28.1.76 as found by the court below and as such the sale deed of the defendants though prior to the sale deeds of the plaintiffs cannot stand in the way of plaintiffs' title in the suit land. The learned Advocate could not show any provision of law in support of his contention that title on the basis of subsequent sale deeds will take effect from the date of agreement. We, therefore, find no merit in the said contention.</u>

14. Let us now consider the evidence on record regarding possession Ext. 6, unregistered deed of agreement dated 28.1.76 shows that the possession of the suit land was delivered to the plaintiffs in part performance of the said agreement for sale. The learned Advocate of the appellants vehemently contended that the writings “যাহার দখল -গ্রহীতাগণের বরাবরে ছাড়িয়া দিলাম” written after the schedule of the lands in the last portion of the said Ext. 6 is a subsequent interpretation made by the plaintiffs after taking back the said document from the court when their prayer for temporary injunction was refused by the Court below on 28.2.79 on the finding that the plaintiffs failed to establish their claim of possession on the basis of the said agreement for sale. The learned Advocate further contended that the said writing is in different ink and different hand. None of the PWs were cross-examined about the same at the time of trial. It appears from the order sheet that plaintiffs' prayer for temporary injunction was rejected by the trial Court on 28.2.79 with the observation that there is no such recital in the deed of agreement that possession was delivered to the plaintiffs. Thereafter on 18.3.79 the plaintiffs received back the deed of agreement from the court on condition of refilling the same and thereafter on 3.9.81 the plaintiffs refilled the same in Court. In spite of the same it is difficult to uphold the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants though the said writings appear to be in different ink and also soaked. Even if in the said agreement there is stipulation that possession was delivered to the plaintiffs, let us see whether in fact any such possession was delivered of the plaintiffs.

15. The plaintiffs in support of their possession examined three witnesses Plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1. He has stated that he is cultivating the entire suit land on behalf of the plaintiffs and possessing the same since the date of bainapatra. PW 2 is a relation of plaintiff No. 3 and he admitted in cross-examination that Arman Khan (plaintiff No. 3) cultivates the suit land and also possess through borgadar. PW 3 is a brother of plaintiff No. 1 and supported PW 1. All these PWs are inter-related and interested. Let us now consider the recitals regarding possession in plaintiff's sale deeds. In the three sale deeds Exts. 1(i) to 1(k) there is recital to the effect that on 28.1.76 the vendors received part of the consideration as advance and on receipt of the balance consideration they transferred their right, title and possession in the lands in favour of the plaintiffs. There is no recital in the said deeds that possession was delivered to the plaintiffs on 28.1.76.

16. The defendants have also examined 5 DWs. In support of their claim of possession in the suit land defendant No. 1 as DW 1 has stated that defendant No. 5(DW 4) lives in the homestead as their caretaker and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 cultivate the agricultural land as their borgadars. DW 2 who is not related to the defendants is a resident of the same village supported the case of possession of the defendants. PW 3 (defendant No. 4) one of the borgadars of the lands also supported the case of possession of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. DW 4 (defendant No. 5) is a relation of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and he has also supported the case of possession of the defendants. Except DW 5 all the DWs admitted that the plaintiffs are in possession of 7 or 8 decimal of land with two huts standing thereon constructed by them after removing the huts of the defendants 1 and 2 in suit plot No. 636. DW 5, who is another resident of the same village and not related to the defendants, has also supported defendant's possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs could not examine a single disinterested witness in support of their case of possession whereas the defendants examined at least two disinterested witnesses in support of their possession. The learned court below did not also consider the evidence of possession adduced by the defendants. On consideration of the above evidence we have no manner of hesitation to hold that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the entire suit land except an area of 7 or 8 decimals in the homestead portion in plot No. 636 and the plaintiffs has or had no possession in the remaining portion of the suit land. Therefore, plaintiffs suit for declaration of title only in the present form is not maintainable and barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in respect of the remaining land in which they have no possession.

17. As already noticed that the proforma defendant No. 8 was owner of 6 decimals of land out of which 1 decimal was transferred to the defendant No. 2 on the basis of sale deed dated 15.12.76 Ext. A and she was left with 5 decimals of land of plot No. 636. Therefore, by sale deeds dated 25.4.78 the plaintiffs acquired title only in 5 decimals of land of suit plot No. 636. The plaintiffs could not acquire title in the remaining suit lands on the basis of their subsequent Kabalas dated 25.4.78 as the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 had already transferred their right, title and interest therein to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2.

<u>18. The plaintiffs have not made out any case either in the plaint or in evidence that the kabalas of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, specially kabala dated 27.1.78 Ext. A (1) was either without consideration or fraudulent. Therefore, the learned court below was not justified in holding that the said kabala was without consideration and fraudulent and the defendants were not bonafide purchasers for value without notice. The doctrine of bonafide purchaser for value without notice is applicable in a case when the plaintiff wants to enforce the agreement for sale not only against the vendor but also against transferee of the vendor's title arising subsequent to the plaintiffs' agreement for sale. Plaintiffs' suit is not such a suit but is a suit for simple declaration of title in the suit land as such we are of the view that the said doctrine is not applicable in the present case.</u>

19. Had the plaintiffs file a suit for declaring defendants kabalas as fraudulent, without consideration and not binding upon them and led evidence to that effect the learned Court below would have been justified to come to such a finding but in the absence of such case made out either in the pleading or in evidence the court was not justified in making out a third case to decree the suit. Court is to decide the case on the basis of the pleadings of the parties and evidence on record and not on the basis of its own assumption making out a third case.

20. Hence the appeal succeeds in part.

In the result the appeal is allowed in part. The impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court is modified and the suit is decreed in part and plaintiffs title to the extent of .5 decimals of land over which their two huts are standing in plot No. 636 is declared and their claim in respect of the remaining 1.21 acres of the suit land is dismissed. Parties will bear their respective costs althrough.

End.
